head: AGENTS.md — VS Code Git Worktrees > Project Overview
text: **VS Code Git Worktrees** is a VS Code extension that wraps Git worktree operations with an interactive UI, letting developers add, list/switch, and remove worktrees without leaving the editor. TypeScript, targets VS Code `^1.65.0`, requires Git `≥ 2.34.1`.

head: AGENTS.md — VS Code Git Worktrees > Essential Commands
text: > **Before submitting a PR**: run `yarn typescript && yarn lint && yarn jest-test --watchAll=false`.

head: AGENTS.md — VS Code Git Worktrees > Architecture
text: The extension registers four VS Code commands at activation time (`src/extension.ts`). Each command delegates to a dedicated operation module under `src/git/operations/worktree/`. Those modules orchestrate calls to the helper layer, which encapsulates all Git CLI execution, VS Code UI interactions, and string utilities.

head: AGENTS.md — VS Code Git Worktrees > Code Conventions
text: -   **TypeScript strict mode** is enabled (`"strict": true` in `tsconfig.json`).

head: AGENTS.md — VS Code Git Worktrees > Code Conventions
text: -   **Module system**: CommonJS (`"module": "commonjs"`), target ES2020.

head: AGENTS.md — VS Code Git Worktrees > Code Conventions
text: -   All source lives under `src/`; compiled output goes to `out/` (gitignored).

head: AGENTS.md — VS Code Git Worktrees > Code Conventions
text: -   Git CLI is invoked via `executeCommand` (uses `child_process.exec`) or `spawnCommand` (uses `child_process.spawn` for streaming). Both are in `src/helpers/helpers.ts`.

head: AGENTS.md — VS Code Git Worktrees > Code Conventions
text: -   VS Code UI calls are centralised in `src/helpers/vsCodeHelpers.ts` — do not call `vscode.window.*` directly from operation modules.

head: AGENTS.md — VS Code Git Worktrees > Code Conventions
text: -   All user-facing strings and URLs are constants in `src/constants/constants.ts`.

head: AGENTS.md — VS Code Git Worktrees > Code Conventions
text: -   Use the `logger` helper (not `console.log`) for any diagnostic output; it writes to a VS Code output channel and is toggled by the `toggleLogs` command.

head: AGENTS.md — VS Code Git Worktrees > Code Conventions
text: -   Pre-commit hook runs `lint-staged` (ESLint + Prettier on staged files) via Husky v4.

head: AGENTS.md — VS Code Git Worktrees > Testing
text:
| Suite       | Runner                          | Location                | Purpose                                         |
| ----------- | ------------------------------- | ----------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| Unit        | Jest + `ts-jest`                | `src/helpers/*.test.ts` | Pure helper functions (string ops, git helpers) |
| Integration | Mocha + `@vscode/test-electron` | `src/test/`             | VS Code extension host tests                    |

head: AGENTS.md — VS Code Git Worktrees > Testing
text: VS Code API is mocked via `__mocks__/vscode.js`. Jest config is in `jest.config.js`.

head: CLAUDE.md — Deploy Center (Server) > 🔧 v3.0 Stack-Specific Gotchas
text:
These are non-obvious things that have bitten us. Reference them before
working in the related area.

head: CLAUDE.md — Deploy Center (Server) > 🔧 v3.0 Stack-Specific Gotchas > Queue (BullMQ)
text:
- **Priority semantics**: BullMQ uses **lower number = higher priority**. The
  project standardizes on `QUEUE_PRIORITY` constants in
  [`Services/QueueService.ts`](./src/Services/QueueService.ts):
  `Rollback=1`, `Webhook=0`, `Manual=10`. Never hardcode literal numbers.

head: CLAUDE.md — Deploy Center (Server) > 🔧 v3.0 Stack-Specific Gotchas > Queue (BullMQ)
text:
- **Redis unreachable**: `QueueReadyMiddleware` short-circuits new deployment
  triggers with **503** when Redis is down — server does NOT crash; it retries
  with exponential backoff and auto-recovers.

head: CLAUDE.md — Deploy Center (Server) > 🔧 v3.0 Stack-Specific Gotchas > Queue (BullMQ)
text:
- **Bull Board** mounts at `/admin/queues` behind `AuthMiddleware` +
  `RoleMiddleware([Admin])`. Mount order in [`App.ts`](./src/App.ts) matters:
  it must be registered BEFORE the SPA catch-all.

head: CLAUDE.md — Deploy Center (Server) > 🔧 v3.0 Stack-Specific Gotchas > Database (Sequelize + MariaDB/MySQL)
text:
- **mysql2 returns JSON columns as raw strings**, not parsed objects.
  Defensive pattern:
  ```typescript
  const events = Array.isArray(row.Events)
    ? row.Events
    : (typeof row.Events === 'string' ? JSON.parse(row.Events) : []);
  ```

head: CLAUDE.md — Deploy Center (Server) > 🔧 v3.0 Stack-Specific Gotchas > Database (Sequelize + MariaDB/MySQL)
text:
- **Sequelize 6.37 + mariadb driver** has a `formatResults` bug on
  `removeColumn` / certain `INSERT` paths. The project switched the test
  dialect to `mysql` (mysql2 npm driver, wire-compatible with MariaDB) via
  `.env.test` to dodge it. In production migrations that need `removeColumn`,
  use raw `ALTER TABLE` via `sequelize.query(..., { type: QueryTypes.RAW })`
  (see [`Migrations/005_*.ts`](./src/Migrations/005_fix_deployment_paths_constraint.ts)
  for the pattern).

head: CLAUDE.md — Deploy Center (Server) > 🔧 v3.0 Stack-Specific Gotchas > Database (Sequelize + MariaDB/MySQL)
text:
- **All new migrations need working `up()` AND `down()`** — the
  `MigrationRunner` won't auto-rollback otherwise.

head: CLAUDE.md — Deploy Center (Server) > 🔧 v3.0 Stack-Specific Gotchas > Database (Sequelize + MariaDB/MySQL)
text:
- **Migration numbering:** v3.0 uses 009, 012, 013, 016, 017, 018, 019, 020,
  021, 999. **Numbers 010, 011, 014, 015 are RESERVED for v3.1** — do not use.

head: CLAUDE.md — Deploy Center (Server) > 🔧 v3.0 Stack-Specific Gotchas > Tests
text:
- **`.env.test` is the source of truth** for test env. It's loaded via
  `__tests__/jest.env.setup.ts` (Jest `setupFiles`) — this runs **before any
  test module import**, which matters because TypeScript hoists `require()`
  calls and `AppConfig` reads `process.env` at import-time.

head: CLAUDE.md — Deploy Center (Server) > 🔧 v3.0 Stack-Specific Gotchas > Tests
text:
- `jest.config.js` has `restoreMocks: true` — that means `jest.spyOn` setups
  in `beforeAll` are erased after test 1. Always put spy setups in
  `beforeEach` (the Rollback / Deployments suites learned this the hard way).

head: CLAUDE.md — Deploy Center (Server) > 🔧 v3.0 Stack-Specific Gotchas > Tests
text:
- `jest.config.js` has `forceExit: true` — required because ioredis/BullMQ
  keep handles open. Do not remove without a replacement teardown.

text: This is the Dymension Hub repository (`d-dymension`), which serves as the settlement layer of the Dymension protocol. It's a Cosmos SDK-based blockchain written in Go.

head: CLAUDE.md > FACTS
text: - Cosmos SDK code all runs in a single thread, there is no multithreading

head: CLAUDE.md > FACTS
text: - Transactions rollback if there is any error, in this sense they are atomic: all or nothing. If they panic, nothing happens.

head: CLAUDE.md > FACTS
text: - BeginBlocker and Endblocker functions in module should never panic, it would cause a chain halt

head: CLAUDE.md > FACTS
text: - All cosmos validators must get the same result so the code should be deterministic

head: SlimServe repository guidance > Scope and ownership
text:
- We own the complete serving stack, including Python orchestration, vLLM,
  ROCm/HIP code, communication paths, generated kernels, and handwritten GPU
  kernels.

head: SlimServe repository guidance > Scope and ownership
text:
- Do not stop at an upstream-library boundary or classify a kernel failure as
  external. Reproduce it, isolate the first failing operation, and fix the
  responsible layer in this repository or the owned dependency tree.

head: SlimServe repository guidance > Scope and ownership
text:
- Long-running and concurrent workloads are correctness requirements. A short
  smoke test does not replace the exact workload that exposed a failure.

head: SlimServe repository guidance > GPU implementation scope
text:
- AITER is a supported dependency. Do not remove or replace a working AITER
  path solely to eliminate that dependency.

head: SlimServe repository guidance > GPU implementation scope
text:
- AITER and its kernels are part of the stack we debug and fix when a supported
  workload exposes a failure there.

head: SlimServe repository guidance > GPU implementation scope
text:
- Kernel work is in scope. Use serialized launches, device assertions,
  sanitizers, reduced reproducers, and targeted instrumentation as needed.

head: SlimServe repository guidance > Reference implementations
text:
Use these local trees when checking algorithms, layouts, bounds, and kernel
behavior:

head: SlimServe repository guidance > Reference implementations
text: - `~/QuixiCore/QuixiCore-ROCm`

head: SlimServe repository guidance > Reference implementations
text: - `~/QuixiCore/QuixiCore-Metal`

head: SlimServe repository guidance > SlimServe Orientation
text: - SlimServe is profile-driven. `slimserve/profiles.json` is the source of truth for supported models, quants, engine args, environment, and platform overrides.

head: SlimServe repository guidance > SlimServe Orientation
text: - Missing model files are not a blocker. Run `slimserve <profile> ... -y`; `slimserve.fetch` downloads or resumes required files into `$SLIMSERVE_CACHE` or `~/models`.

head: SlimServe repository guidance > SlimServe Orientation
text: - Do not hand-build unsupported serving commands when a profile exists. Use `slimserve <profile> --dry-run` to inspect and `slimserve <profile>` to run (serving is the default; `--serve` is still accepted).

head: SlimServe repository guidance > Agent Operating Discipline
text:
- Read the repo before deciding. Start from `AGENTS.md`, `perf/perf.md`,
  `perf/baseline_status.md`, `perf/optimization_status.md`, the relevant
  profile in `slimserve/profiles.json`, and the local implementation paths for
  the model/platform under discussion.

head: SlimServe repository guidance > Agent Operating Discipline
text:
- Do not confuse "the process started" with "the system works." A serving path
  is not validated until the real SlimServe profile reaches health, serves the
  benchmark workload, passes correctness checks, and produces recorded TPS.

head: SlimServe repository guidance > Agent Operating Discipline
text:
- Do not treat vLLM interval logger output as an authoritative benchmark.
  Interval logs are diagnostics. Use exact-token harness output, raw JSON, and
  reproducible commands for baseline or comparison claims.

head: SlimServe repository guidance > Agent Operating Discipline
text:
- Do not make a placeholder fix and describe it as the real fix. If a change is
  an interim diagnostic, say so in the notebook and keep the production target
  explicit.

head: SlimServe repository guidance > Agent Operating Discipline
text:
- Remove or clearly quarantine failed experiments. Do not leave disabled,
  memory-heavy, or misleading alternate paths in the serving code unless they
  are intentionally retained as documented diagnostics.

head: SlimServe repository guidance > Agent Operating Discipline
text:
- When the user points at a precedent, inspect it before implementing. For this
  repo that often means reading the optimized ROCm/Metal path, GLM 5.2 Ampere
  path, DS4 kernels, and the QuixiCore CUDA/ROCm code that is actually relevant
  to the active serving path.

head: SlimServe repository guidance > Agent Operating Discipline
text:
- Keep model downloads out of the reasoning loop. If SlimServe owns the
  download, run SlimServe and let it download or resume; do not block kernel or
  profile work because a model file is not already present.

head: SlimServe repository guidance > Agent Operating Discipline
text:
- State uncertainty precisely. If only startup, smoke, or synthetic parity has
  been run, call it that. Do not imply end-to-end correctness, production
  readiness, or final performance without the corresponding evidence.

head: SlimServe repository guidance > Agent Operating Discipline
text:
- Preserve user and prior-agent changes. The worktree may be dirty; understand
  nearby edits and build on them rather than reverting unrelated work.

head: SlimServe repository guidance > Agent Operating Discipline
text:
- Finish the loop: implement, build, smoke, run the real profile or explain the
  concrete blocker, update the performance notebook, and leave the next command
  obvious.

head: SlimServe repository guidance > Kernel Work
text: - Develop serving kernels in this repo first. Vendored code used by SlimServe belongs under `csrc/quixicore/` or `csrc/libtorch_stable/`; modify those copies, then port the finished used pieces to `/home/ubuntu/QuixiCore/QuixiCore-CUDA`.

head: SlimServe repository guidance > Kernel Work
text: - Vendor only kernels and headers on the actual serving path. QuixiCore is a large kernel library; do not copy broad directories just because they exist.

head: SlimServe repository guidance > Kernel Work
text: - QuixiCore, `ds4`, `llama.cpp`, and vLLM Marlin are references and inspiration, not finished answers. Study them for layouts, scheduling, quant decode, and tensor-core strategy, then implement and tune the SlimServe path that this model and hardware actually need.

head: SlimServe repository guidance > Kernel Work
text: - SlimServe owns the inference stack all the way down to CUDA/HIP kernels. Do not assume an upstream or vendored kernel is "already done" when profiling shows room to improve.

head: SlimServe repository guidance > Kernel Work
text: - The primary purpose of this repo is to optimize serving performance for the target model on the target hardware. Keep pushing until the remaining bottlenecks are measured and defensible.

head: SlimServe repository guidance > Kernel Work
text: - When inference is already thoroughly optimized on one platform, study that implementation before implementing another platform. Preserve the algorithmic wins, data layout choices, fusion boundaries, and profiling lessons unless the new hardware gives a measured reason to diverge.

head: SlimServe repository guidance > Kernel Work
text: - For DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731, the ROCm implementation is the baseline reference for the current Ampere A100 work.

head: SlimServe repository guidance > Kernel Work
text: - For DSV4 0731 on A100, the target is native fused MoE: IQ2_XXS gate/up from vLLM's combined `[expert, gate|up, packed]` GGUF layout or split/aligned artifacts, SwiGLU, Q2_K down, and final weighted reduce.

head: SlimServe repository guidance > Kernel Work
text: - Do not use dequant or standalone Q2_K GEMV as the production DSV4 answer.

head: SlimServe repository guidance > Kernel Work
text: - Lazy persistent repack caches can duplicate tens of GiB and break TP2 memory. Prefer load-time replacement, aligned artifacts, or byte-neutral layouts.

head: SlimServe repository guidance > GLM 5.2/Ampere Reference
text: - Use the GLM 5.2 Ampere path as the local precedent: route/align, expert-contiguous gather, grouped GEMM, grouped SwiGLU, and finalize.

head: SlimServe repository guidance > GLM 5.2/Ampere Reference
text: - For quantized A100 kernels, follow the Marlin lessons in `csrc/quixicore/a100_glm52_design.md`: layout-only repack, in-register narrow scale decode, `cp.async` staging, fp16 fragments, tensor cores for `M >= 2`, and aggressive decode-node fusion.

head: SlimServe repository guidance > GLM 5.2/Ampere Reference
text: - The parked `q2k_moe_ampere.cuh` GEMV is diagnostic only; it was measured too small a win to be the serving solution.

head: SlimServe repository guidance > Validation
text: - Build native changes with `cmake --build build/temp.linux-x86_64-cpython-312 --target _C_stable_libtorch -j$(nproc)` and copy the rebuilt `.so` into `vllm/` for editable imports when needed.

head: SlimServe repository guidance > Validation
text: - Smoke imports with `import vllm._C_stable_libtorch` and inspect relevant `torch.ops` schemas.

head: SlimServe repository guidance > Validation
text: - End-to-end DSV4 performance must be measured through SlimServe profiles such as `dsv4-2` and `dsv4-4`, because those profiles own downloads, parser settings, DSpark/FP8 environment, KV dtype, and CUDA graph settings.

head: SlimServe repository guidance > Performance Notebook
text: - Rigorously record inference experiments and optimization data using the method in `perf/perf.md`, adapted from `/home/ubuntu/QuixiCore/QuixiCore-Metal/perf/perf.md`.

head: SlimServe repository guidance > Performance Notebook
text: - Before changing or benchmarking performance-sensitive code, read `perf/baseline_status.md` and the relevant entries in `perf/optimization_status.md`. Know how the current profile compares with the other platform/profile baselines before interpreting a new number.

head: SlimServe repository guidance > Performance Notebook
text: - Treat large throughput gaps as evidence, not background noise. If a profile that should be in the tens, hundreds, or higher tokens/s range produces 2 tok/s, assume something is wrong until the notebook and fresh measurements prove otherwise.

head: SlimServe repository guidance > Performance Notebook
text:
- Treat tensor-parallel scaling as a hard sanity gate. TP2 should be at least
  50% faster than TP1, TP4 should be at least 50% faster than TP2, and TP8
  should be at least 50% faster than TP4. These are minimum acceptable checks;
  the target should be better than that when the kernels, collectives, and
  scheduling are healthy.

head: SlimServe repository guidance > Performance Notebook
text:
- Similar TPS across TP levels is not fine. If TP2, TP4, or TP8 produce roughly
  the same throughput, treat it as evidence of a fundamentally wrong design, not
  just a local bug. Review how the better-performing SlimServe profiles and
  platform ports are implemented before inventing a new path.

head: SlimServe repository guidance > Performance Notebook
text:
- Stand on our own shoulders. Do not rediscover solutions we already built for
  another model, tensor-parallel size, or platform; start from the proven local
  design and adapt it with measurements.

head: SlimServe repository guidance > Performance Notebook
text: - Keep the running notebook in `perf/optimization_status.md` and stable baseline snapshots in `perf/baseline_status.md`.

head: SlimServe repository guidance > Performance Notebook
text: - Store raw benchmark logs and JSON under `perf/results/YYYY-MM-DD/<run-id>/`; `perf/results/` is git-ignored except for its `.gitignore`.

head: SlimServe repository guidance > Performance Notebook
text: - Every retained or rejected optimization must have a baseline, hypothesis, correctness result, measured throughput, decision, and raw artifact location.

head: SlimServe repository guidance > Profile validation
text:
- Live validation must discover every registry profile compatible with the
  current machine. Do not substitute one tensor-parallel size for another.

head: SlimServe repository guidance > Profile validation
text:
- Every supported profile must run with its registered DSpark drafter and
  registered draft KV configuration. FP8 is the only permitted KV cache
  quantization; TurboQuant is prohibited for targets and drafters.

head: SlimServe repository guidance > Profile validation
text:
- Enable vision on every profile whose model supports vision; validate both
  text and image requests.

head: SlimServe repository guidance > Profile validation
text:
- For vision profiles, test both text and image requests. For text-only
  profiles, test text requests.

head: SlimServe repository guidance > Commit authorship
text:
- Eric Hartford is the sole author. Do not add co-author or assistance
  trailers, and do not discuss automated assistance in commit messages.

head: AGENTS.md > Project Overview
text: Git Workers is an interactive CLI tool for managing Git worktrees, written in Rust. It provides a menu-driven interface for creating, deleting, switching, and renaming worktrees, with shell integration for automatic directory switching.

head: AGENTS.md > Development Commands > Commit Conventions
text: - Follow `Conventional Commits` for all commit messages

head: AGENTS.md > Development Commands > Commit Conventions
text: - Format: `<type>(<scope>)?: <description>`

head: AGENTS.md > Development Commands > Commit Conventions
text:
- Common types in this repository:
  - `feat`: user-facing feature additions
  - `fix`: bug fixes and behavior corrections
  - `refactor`: structural changes without behavior changes
  - `test`: test additions or test-only refactors
  - `docs`: documentation-only changes
  - `chore`: maintenance work with no product behavior impact
  - `ci`: CI or automation workflow changes
  - `build`: build system or dependency management changes

head: AGENTS.md > Development Commands > Commit Conventions
text: - Keep the subject concise, imperative, and lowercase where natural

head: AGENTS.md > Development Commands > Commit Conventions
text: - Do not mix structural changes and behavior changes in the same commit

head: AGENTS.md > Development Commands > Commit Conventions
text:
- Examples:
  - `refactor(app): move menu dispatch into app module`
  - `fix(create): preserve selected tag when creating worktree`
  - `test(rename): cover cancel flow in rename prompt`

head: CLAUDE.md > Overview
text: `load-generator` (binary name `lg`) is a generic, protocol-agnostic load testing tool written in Go. It drives load against HTTP, gRPC, Redis, MySQL, PostgreSQL, Cassandra (CQL), MongoDB, ClickHouse, SMTP, and Kafka endpoints. Each protocol is exposed both as a standalone subcommand and as a Lua module, so a single Lua script can mix protocols and have metrics collected per-call and in custom aggregations. Latency is tracked with HdrHistogram; SQL queries are fingerprinted so metrics aggregate by query signature rather than literal text.

head: CLAUDE.md > Common commands
text: Several `internal/*` tests (`cql`, `psql`, `lua`, `mongo`, `kafka`) use `ory/dockertest` and will start real containers — they need a working Docker daemon. `docker-compose.yml` provides the same backing services for manual testing (`docker compose up -d <service>`).

head: CLAUDE.md > Common commands
text: CI (`.github/workflows/testing.yml`) runs `make test` on PRs targeting `main`. Releases are built with GoReleaser (`make snapshot` / `make release`).

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture
text: The codebase has three layers: **`cmd/`** (CLI wiring), **`internal/runner` + `internal/loadgen`** (the concurrency/throughput engine), and **`internal/<protocol>`** (per-protocol generators). `internal/stats` is the shared metrics spine that everything writes into.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > The Generator contract
text: Everything that produces load implements `loadgen.Generator` (`internal/loadgen/loadgenerator.go`):

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > The Generator contract
text: A `NewGenerator` factory closure adapts each protocol's constructor to this interface. To add a new protocol you: (1) implement a generator in `internal/<proto>/`, (2) add a cobra subcommand in `cmd/<proto>.go` that builds options and a `NewGenerator` closure, then calls `runner.New(...).Run()`, and (3) if it should be scriptable, register it as a Lua module in `internal/lua/lua_api.go` (`preloadModules`) and add a `TraceType` in `internal/stats/stats.go`.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Runner: concurrency + throughput control
text: `internal/runner/runner.go` is the engine. `Run()`:

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Runner: concurrency + throughput control
text: - Spawns `concurrency` worker goroutines, each owning its own `LoadGenerator`/`Generator` instance (so connections are per-worker, not shared).

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Runner: concurrency + throughput control
text: - Uses a two-phase startup barrier: all workers run `Init()`, wait on a `WaitGroup`, then begin `Run()` together.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Runner: concurrency + throughput control
text: - A `ticker()` goroutine uses `golang.org/x/time/rate` to push work tokens onto `workChan` at `requestrate`/sec. Workers block on `workChan` and call `Tick()` per token. **`requestrate=0` means uncapped** — the ticker closes `workChan` and workers loop as fast as possible.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Runner: concurrency + throughput control
text: - If the channel backs up (target too slow to keep up), it logs "Target host is likely slow: missed request rate".

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Runner: concurrency + throughput control
text: - `warmupTimer()` calls `stats.ResetMetrics()` after the warmup window so warmup traffic is excluded from the final report; `durationTimer()` cancels the context after `warmup + duration`.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Runner: concurrency + throughput control
text: `concurrency` defaults to `requestrate` (then to 1) — see `PersistentPreRunE` in `cmd/root.go`.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Stats: the metrics spine (`internal/stats/stats.go`)
text: A single `Stats` object is shared across all workers, built on a **single-writer actor model**: exactly one goroutine (`statsCollector`) owns all mutable state (the metrics map, every HdrHistogram, `digestToQuery`). There are no mutexes on those structures. Two channels drive it:

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Stats: the metrics spine (`internal/stats/stats.go`)
text: - `statsChan` (buffered, size `requestrate*100`, min 10000) — the hot path. `RecordMetric()` just pushes a `*TraceInfo` and returns; all workers feed it.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Stats: the metrics spine (`internal/stats/stats.go`)
text: - `statsCmd` (unbuffered) — control plane. `Report`/`Export`/`Reset`/`ResetMetrics`/`Stop` each send a command with a `done` reply channel and **block** until the collector responds (synchronous rendezvous).

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Stats: the metrics spine (`internal/stats/stats.go`)
text: Implications: the collector is a hard serialization point that does real per-metric work (SQL fingerprinting, map lookups, histogram recording). When `statsChan` fills, `RecordMetric` blocks and **stats backpressure throttles load generation itself**.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Stats: the metrics spine (`internal/stats/stats.go`)
text: Data model: `MetricsMap = map[TraceType][Key][Subkey]*Metrics` — protocol → target(host) → operation(URL/query/command) → histogram bundle, lazily vivified by `getMetrics`. `TraceType` is the protocol (`http`, `grpc`, `sql`, `psql`, `cql`, `clickhouse`, `redis`, `mongo`, `smtp`, `custom`, `raw`). `custom`/`raw` back Lua's custom-metric aggregation.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Stats: the metrics spine (`internal/stats/stats.go`)
text: Key behaviors and footguns:

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Stats: the metrics spine (`internal/stats/stats.go`)
text: - **Latency is recorded in microseconds**, displayed in ms via `scale = 1000`. `RawTrace` is the exception: recorded as-is, displayed with scale 1.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Stats: the metrics spine (`internal/stats/stats.go`)
text: - **5-minute latency ceiling**: histograms are bounded `[1, 5min in µs]`. Slower responses are dropped with a warn — do not trust this tool for endpoints that can exceed 5 min.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Stats: the metrics spine (`internal/stats/stats.go`)
text: - **RPS is sampled, not counted**: a 1s ticker records instantaneous `Δcount/Δtime` into a *separate* `rps` histogram; `AvgRPS = rps.Mean()`. Zero-throughput seconds are **not** recorded, so `AvgRPS` is the mean over *active* seconds and overstates sustained throughput for bursty workloads. In **server mode the ticker is disabled** — the server's RPS comes only from imported client reports.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Stats: the metrics spine (`internal/stats/stats.go`)
text: - **SQL fingerprinting** (`sql`/`psql`/`cql`/`clickhouse`): the raw query Subkey is replaced by a percona `go-mysql` fingerprint Id, with `digestToQuery` mapping id→normalized query. All literal variants of a query aggregate under one signature.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Stats: the metrics spine (`internal/stats/stats.go`)
text: - **Warmup exclusion**: the runner calls `ResetMetrics()` after warmup, which throws away the whole metrics map and resets start/end times.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Stats: the metrics spine (`internal/stats/stats.go`)
text: - `Errors2` is overloaded — it is the gRPC deadline-exceeded counter, surfaced as the `deadline` column.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Output rendering
text: `Report()` takes a format chosen by the `--output table|markdown` persistent flag (`md` is an alias for `markdown`; the flag is validated in `cmd/root.go` `PersistentPreRunE` and applied via `Stats.SetOutputFormat`). The format is stored on `Stats` and read inside `print()` — `Report()` itself stays parameterless. `print()` emits two independent renderers per metric leaf:

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Output rendering
text: 1. **Summary table** via `tablewriter` **v1.0.9**. Default (`table`) uses the library's Unicode box-drawing borders (`┌─┬┐│`); `markdown` mode swaps in `renderer.NewMarkdown()` (pipe `|` columns + `---` header separator, valid GFM). Columns are assembled dynamically: a fixed base (`<label>, Avg, StdDev, Min, Max, p50, p95, p99, p99.99, Total`), then `AvgRPS, Errors` for everything except `raw`, then protocol-specific trailing columns (HTTP: `2xx/3xx/4xx/5xx`; gRPC: `deadline`). The first column label is protocol-specific (`Url`/`Method`/`Query`/`Command`/`Operation`/`Key`). In markdown mode the protocol-name/target labels render as `###`/`####` headings and the digest map becomes a `| Digest | Query |` table. **Note:** v1.x `Header` takes variadic `any` (not `[]string`) and is NOT API-compatible with the widely-documented v0.x `NewWriter`/`SetHeader`. Rows sort by ascending request count; targets sort alphabetically; protocol **sections print in a fixed canonical order** (`sectionOrder` in `stats.go`) — this is intentional so regenerated reports diff cleanly (the map was previously ranged directly, giving non-deterministic order).

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Output rendering
text: 2. **Response-time histogram** — hand-rolled ASCII (`getResponseHistogram`), not tablewriter. Bars scale to a max of 40 `■` chars; HdrHistogram's native bars are re-projected onto 10 linear buckets (`hdrHistBarsToBuckets`, the fiddliest function here — covered by `TestBarsToBuckets`). `raw` metrics print without the `Response time histogram (ms):` heading. In markdown mode each histogram is wrapped in a ```` ``` ```` fence so the ASCII bars stay valid Markdown.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Distributed (server/client) mode — two transport paths with different fidelity
text: `lg server :PORT` (`cmd/server.go`, `internal/server/`) runs a node that generates no load and serves a web UI (table, JSON, latency graphs at `/graphs`). There are two distinct merge/transport paths, and they are **not equivalent**:

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Distributed (server/client) mode — two transport paths with different fidelity
text: - **Live aggregation** — clients run with `--server host:PORT` and publish their `stats.Report` over Go `net/rpc` (`LG.ImportReport`) in `PersistentPostRunE`. `net/rpc` uses **gob**, which ignores the `json:"-"` tag on `Result.LatencySnapshot`, so the full HdrHistogram snapshot crosses the wire and `importReport` **merges histograms** for statistically correct combined percentiles. (Merge rules differ per field: latency merged, counters summed, RPS *added* assuming parallel clients, start/end time min/max, duration summed — the duration sum is dubious and flagged `// ??` in the source.)

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Distributed (server/client) mode — two transport paths with different fidelity
text: - **JSON `--export` / `--import`** — `Result.LatencySnapshot` is tagged `json:"-"`, so JSON keeps only the precomputed percentiles/buckets, **not** the raw histogram. JSON reports are therefore **display-only and terminal**: the server's `--import <file>` path renders them directly and never re-merges. You cannot aggregate JSON exports; use the RPC path for live multi-client aggregation.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Lua scripting (`internal/lua/`)
text: `lg script foo.lua` is the most powerful entry point. The Lua VM is `yuin/gopher-lua`; Go objects are bridged with `layeh.com/gopher-luar`. The compiled bytecode is compiled once and shared across all worker LStates.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Lua scripting (`internal/lua/`)
text: - A script defines global `init()`, `tick()`, and `finished()` functions, mapped to the `Generator` lifecycle. See `scripts/*.lua` for examples (`scripts/multiple.lua` mixes protocols; `scripts/http.lua` is the minimal template).

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Lua scripting (`internal/lua/`)
text: - `internal/lua/lua_api.go` `preloadModules` exposes each protocol as a `require`-able module (`http`, `grpc`, `redis`, `mysql`, `psql`, `cql`, `smtp`, `mongo`, `clickhouse`), each with `.Options()` and `.New()`. Globals `LG` (the `*LG` handle), `Log`, and helpers are injected.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Lua scripting (`internal/lua/`)
text: - Custom metrics: `LG:BeginCustomMetrics(keys...)` / `LG:EndCustomMetrics(keys...)` / `LG:RecordRawMetrics(...)` let a script group several calls and report them as one combined unit.

head: CLAUDE.md > Conventions
text: - Logging uses `logrus`; workers tag entries with their `Id` field. `--verbose` enables debug level; `--debug` is specifically for diagnosing hung Lua scripts.

head: CLAUDE.md > Conventions
text: - SQL-type generators (`mysql`, `psql`, `clickhouse`) fingerprint queries (via `percona/go-mysql`) so metrics aggregate by normalized query signature, not literal SQL.

head: CLAUDE.md > Conventions
text: - Context cancellation is the universal stop signal: `main.go` cancels on SIGINT, and that context flows through the runner into every generator's `Tick`. Generators should treat "context canceled" errors as a clean exit, not a failure (see `scripts/http.lua`).

- NEVER EVER EVER create a branch!!! branches are FORBIDDEN!!!
- NEVER EVER EVER delete the `bugdrop-screenshots` branch, locally or remotely. It is protected project history.
- NEVER create a worktree, UNLESS the user has specifically asked for it!

- NEVER delete files unless the user has specifically asked for it. If you think a file is misplaced, unrelated, or stale, that is an entirely separate request — ask first. "Looks unrelated to this task" is not authorization to delete.

- When the user gives a UUID and asks what is going on with it, treat it as an OmniHarness conversation/session lookup: check `sqlite.db`, starting with the `runs` row for that UUID, then inspect related `workers`, `messages`, `execution_events`, queued messages, and validation/plan records as needed.
- To delete all conversations and associated persisted artifacts, use `scripts/delete-conversations.sh`
- When the user says “write the plan”, “write a full plan”, or “write the implementation plan”, treat that as a request to persist the complete plan to a file, not merely display it in chat.
- If the user gives a path, write the plan there. Otherwise use `docs/superpowers/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-<kebab-case-feature-name>.md`, using the current date and a non-colliding filename.
- The saved file is the canonical full plan. The final response should link to it and summarize the result rather than replacing the file with a chat-only plan.
- This convention applies even when the current message omits the destination because “write the plan” is the project’s established shorthand for creating the plan artifact.
- If the same request explicitly says not to change the workspace or not to create a file, obey that more specific prohibition and ask for a destination when needed.
- After any UI/frontend change, always run `pnpm build:interface:web` before considering the work complete.
- When testing the app, use the already-running process if one exists instead of starting another server.
- The normal runner URL is `http://localhost:3050`; the Vite development interface is usually at `http://localhost:5173`.
- Clean up any test sessions/conversations and their associated persisted artifacts before finishing.

- For lifecycle / chaos-style regressions (reconnect, restart, FK-on-delete, plan-review leftover state), use `pnpm test:lifecycle`. Scenarios live under `tests/lifecycle/scenarios/` and drive the control plane via HTTP/SSE — no Chromium. To debug a specific reported bug, mirror it as a new scenario file.
- Read `docs/architecture/lifecycle-observability-and-testing.md` before adding new server-side state transitions. It is the spec all new code is held to.

- Worker conversation content (direct-control and supervisor-driven worker turns) lives in the unified worker stream — one append-only JSONL per worker at `app-data/run-data/<runId>/<workerId>.jsonl`. Persist new worker content through `appendWorkerEntry` in `src/server/workers/output-store.ts`; render it through `WorkerEntriesManager` and the `entries` prop on `Terminal`. Do NOT add a parallel persistence layer (a sibling JSONL, a new `messages.kind`, an in-memory cache that the frontend reconciles against the stream). See `docs/architecture/worker-conversation-stream.md`.
Lifecycle observability rules (full doc: `docs/architecture/lifecycle-observability-and-testing.md`):

- Every server-side decision (spawn, reattach, recreate, give up, refuse, delete, fail) emits a typed named event via `emitNamedEvent` from `@/server/events/named-events`. Silent early returns and bare `catch {}` are bugs.

- User-relevant failures additionally emit `error.surfaced` with a stable `code` (typed union in `named-events.ts`), `surface`, and at least one relevant subject id such as `runId`/`workerId`/`conversationId`/`accountId`. Never funnel through a blanket wrapper in `api-errors.ts`.

- All SSE frames carry an `id:`. Clients reconnect with `Last-Event-ID`; the server replays from the ring buffer or emits `stream.resync_required`. Snapshot bootstrap is `GET /api/events?snapshot=1` (anchor id in the `x-omni-last-event-id` response header).

- Dev-only event log: `GET /api/events/log?since=<id>&runId=<id>` returns the ring buffer as JSON. Use this when triaging "X didn't happen" bug reports — if the event isn't there, the server didn't do the thing, and the next step is finding the silent branch.
- Chaos is a client-side concern. Never add fault-injection code paths to server code.
- EVERY user-facing frontend string MUST live in `shared/locales/*.json` and be rendered with the `t()` function from `@/lib/i18n`.

- NEVER hardcode user-facing JSX text, button labels, dialog titles, aria-labels, titles, placeholders, empty states, status labels, help text, error fallback text, or visible option labels directly in components.

- For every new user-facing string, add the key to `shared/locales/en.json` and every other locale file in `shared/locales/` in the same change. Use stable dotted keys like `settings.runtime.recovery` or `conversation.sidebar.search`.

- Components that render translated strings and need to update when the language changes MUST subscribe to the i18n manager by calling `useI18nSnapshot()` from `@/lib/i18n`; then render text with the existing `t("key", params?)` function. The hook is only for re-rendering; `t()` is the translation API.

- Non-React modules that produce user-visible text must still use `t("key", params?)` at the boundary where text is produced. Protocol values, storage keys, API paths, CSS classes, model ids, and database values are not translation keys unless they are displayed as copy.
- Do not pass translated strings through transactions or persist translated UI copy. Store stable ids/values and translate at render time.
- MutableRefObject is deprecated in React; use RefObject instead.
- NEVER use require() to import modules. Use import instead.
- ALWAYS centralize all state in global single source of truth Manager classes. Components/listeners subscribe to updates from Managers and use Manager methods to update data.
- Always implement a custom data manager for any data structure. NEVER use separate state variables and arrays as the source of truth.
- NEVER send data around in transactions.
- Avoid using useEffect() to update state. Prefer useCallback() or Manager methods for explicit state transitions.
- Avoid callback hell, race conditions, and infinite loops.
- NEVER store string literals or UI settings for the frontend in the .env file. Use literals in files, inline arrays, or .json files instead.
- When debugging React: if a fix did not work, think hard about whether this is a race condition. Race conditions are common in React.

head: CLAUDE.md
text: This file provides guidance to Claude Code (claude.ai/code) when working with code in this repository.

head: CLAUDE.md > Overview
text: Chorus is a BDD (Behaviour Driven Development) test interpreter for testing distributed/microservice architectures. Unlike conventional BDD tools, Chorus allows components to **publish step definitions over the network**, so the interpreter can connect to running components and execute their steps remotely. It supports both Java (JVM) and JavaScript components.

head: CLAUDE.md > Running Tests
text: **Important**: The `:chorus` module has "selftests" that validate the interpreter's exact stdout output at INFO log level. If you add any `INFO`-level (or higher) log statements in the interpreter, existing selftest assertions will fail — update them to match the new output.

head: CLAUDE.md > License Headers
text: All `.java` files must include the MIT license header. Use the license plugin to fix or verify:

head: CLAUDE.md > Project Structure
text: Extensions are individually published to Maven Central. Services are internal utilities — not published.

head: CLAUDE.md > Core Architecture > Interpreter Entry Points
text: - **CLI**: `org.chorusbdd.chorus.Chorus` (main class); `org.chorusbdd.chorus.Main` (backwards-compat alias)

head: CLAUDE.md > Core Architecture > Interpreter Entry Points
text: - **JUnit**: `org.chorusbdd.chorus.ChorusSuite` extends `ParentRunner` — creates one JUnit test per feature

head: CLAUDE.md > Core Architecture > Key Abstractions
text: - **`@Handler`** — marks a class as a step-definition provider; discovered via classpath scanning

head: CLAUDE.md > Core Architecture > Key Abstractions
text: - **`@Step`** — marks a method as a step, with a regex or literal pattern to match feature file steps

head: CLAUDE.md > Core Architecture > Key Abstractions
text: - **Remoting** — handlers can be hosted in separate processes/components and discovered over the network at runtime

head: CLAUDE.md > Core Architecture > Key Abstractions
text: - **`ExecutionToken` / `FeatureToken`** — results model passed to `ExecutionListener` implementations

head: CLAUDE.md > Core Architecture > Key Abstractions
text: - **Subsystems** — pluggable internal services (e.g., process management, remoting) managed via `@SubsystemConfig`

head: CLAUDE.md > Core Architecture > Built-in Handlers (in `org.chorusbdd.chorus.handlers`)
text: Process management, Chorus context, remoting (network step definitions), timers, utilities.

head: CLAUDE.md > Core Architecture > Layered Architecture
text: ArchUnit tests in `interpreter/chorus/src/test/java/org/chorusbdd/chorus/archunit/` enforce package layering — check these if you see architecture-violation test failures after adding new dependencies between packages.

head: CLAUDE.md > Core Architecture > Output / Logging
text: The interpreter has two distinct output streams:

head: CLAUDE.md > Core Architecture > Output / Logging
text: 1. **Test results** — written via `ChorusOut` (standard output, structured result tokens)

head: CLAUDE.md > Core Architecture > Output / Logging
text: 2. **Diagnostic logging** — Commons Logging / Log4j (default level WARN; selftests run at INFO)

head: CLAUDE.md > Core Architecture > Output / Logging
text: Remote listeners can receive serialized result tokens as the suite runs (used by chorus-webagent).

head: lm-assist
text: Monorepo for the LM Assistant — a self-hosted control plane for Claude Code: session observability and control (web UI + REST API), fleet connectivity over the hub, an MCP server exposing the whole surface inside Claude sessions, missions/automation, cross-host memory, and service connectors.

head: lm-assist > Build-breaking pins — read before touching dependencies

head: lm-assist > Build-breaking pins — read before touching dependencies > Dependency pin — chokidar MUST stay `^3.6.0` (do NOT bump)
text: **chokidar 5 is ESM-only.** The core build is CommonJS (`core/tsconfig.json` → `"module": "commonjs"`), so `core/dist/*.js` does `require("chokidar")`. `require()` of an ESM-only module throws **`ERR_REQUIRE_ESM`** and **Core crashes on boot** — the Web UI still starts, but Core never binds `:3100` (prod) / `:3200` (dev). Symptom: services look half-up, `curl localhost:3100/health` fails, and anything the hub relays (the MCP) errors → "lm-assist MCP is down". Six call sites `require` it: `rest-server.ts`, `task-store.ts`, `session-cache.ts`, `memory-cache.ts`, `memory/cross-project-signpost.ts`, `rules/autosync.ts`.

head: lm-assist > Build-breaking pins — read before touching dependencies > Dependency pin — chokidar MUST stay `^3.6.0` (do NOT bump)
text: So v4 would `require()` fine. **v5 is the one that breaks**, and it breaks *selectively*: `require(esm)` exists on Node ≥ 20.19, so a bump looks healthy on a modern dev box and dies on a Node 18 user. Never validate this pin only on the machine you are sitting at.

head: lm-assist > Build-breaking pins — read before touching dependencies > Dependency pin — chokidar MUST stay `^3.6.0` (do NOT bump)

Keep it pinned in BOTH `package.json` and `core/package.json`.

text: **⚠️ Upgrade hazard (RESOLVED 2026-09-01):** npm `latest` (≥0.2.0) now carries `chokidar: ^3.6.0`, so `lm-assist upgrade` / `npm install -g lm-assist@latest` no longer breaks boot. Installing a version **≤0.1.70** still ships `^5.0.0` and needs the recovery above. A build/install from this repo is always fine (pin committed here).

head: lm-assist > Build-breaking pins — read before touching dependencies > Agent SDK (`@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk`) is ESM-only — `import()` must survive tsc
text: `/agent/execute` (the agent runtime in `sdk-runner.ts`) loads `@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk`, which is **ESM-only** (`type: module`, `exports.require: null`). The code imports it dynamically, but **tsc with `module: commonjs` downlevels `await import('pkg')` to `Promise.resolve().then(() => require('pkg'))`** — and `require()` of an ESM module throws **`ERR_REQUIRE_ESM`**. Result: every agent execution dies with **0 turns / empty result** on the dev build (`:3200`). Prod masks it only because its older npm-installed SDK is still `require`-able — a latent trap, same class as the chokidar one above.

head: CLAUDE.md > What this is
text:
Cobbler-Web is the Angular-based web UI for [Cobbler](https://github.com/cobbler/cobbler), a Linux provisioning
server. The UI talks directly to the Cobbler server's XML-RPC API from the browser — there is no
backend-for-frontend; all requests originate client-side.

head: CLAUDE.md > Workspace layout
text:
This is a single Angular CLI workspace (`angular.json`) with three projects that **must be built in dependency
order**:

head: CLAUDE.md > Workspace layout
text:
1. **`typescript-xmlrpc`** (library, `projects/typescript-xmlrpc`) — generic XML-RPC client: serializes/deserializes
   XML-RPC payloads over `HttpClient` (`AngularXmlrpcService`). No knowledge of Cobbler.

head: CLAUDE.md > Workspace layout
text:
2. **`cobbler-api`** (library, `projects/cobbler-api`) — depends on `typescript-xmlrpc`. `CobblerApiService`
   (`projects/cobbler-api/src/lib/cobbler-api.service.ts`) exposes one method per Cobbler XML-RPC call
   (get/find/save/remove/modify for every item type, background\_\* task triggers, auth, events...). It's several
   thousand lines and almost entirely repetitive boilerplate: each method builds params, calls
   `client.methodCall(...)`, and maps the `MethodResponse`/`MethodFault` union into a typed result or a thrown
   `Error`. When adding a new Cobbler XML-RPC method, copy the shape of a neighboring method of the same kind
   (getter / finder / background action) rather than inventing a new pattern. Item shapes live in

head: AGENTS.md
text: This file provides guidance to coding agents working in this repository.

head: AGENTS.md > Project Overview
text: Turing.jl is the user-facing entry point for the [TuringLang](https://github.com/TuringLang) probabilistic programming ecosystem. It is largely a translation layer between DynamicPPL models — which work with named, structured parameters — and inference algorithms that expect flat, vectorised samples (e.g. HMC/NUTS operate on `AbstractVector{<:Real}`). DynamicPPL's `LogDensityFunction` handles most of this translation; Turing provides the sampler wrappers that set it up and manage state across iterations.

head: AGENTS.md > Project Overview
text: Model definition lives in [DynamicPPL.jl](https://github.com/TuringLang/DynamicPPL.jl), parameter transformations in [Bijectors.jl](https://github.com/TuringLang/Bijectors.jl), and sampling interfaces in [AbstractMCMC.jl](https://github.com/TuringLang/AbstractMCMC.jl). Turing re-exports their APIs and provides concrete sampler implementations that wire everything together.

head: AGENTS.md > Building and Testing
text: Code formatting uses [JuliaFormatter.jl](https://github.com/domluna/JuliaFormatter.jl) v1 (not v2) with the **Blue style** (configured in `.JuliaFormatter.toml`). CI enforces formatting on all PRs. JuliaFormatter must be installed in the **global** Julia environment, not the project environment — do not use `--project`. See the [formatting guide](https://turinglang.org/docs/contributing/code-formatting/) for setup details.

head: AGENTS.md > Building and Testing
text: Tests use `SelectiveTests.jl` (in `test/test_utils/`) to filter by path. CI splits the suite into four shards: `mcmc/gibbs.jl`, `mcmc/Inference.jl`, `ad.jl`, and everything else. To run a subset locally:

head: AGENTS.md > Building and Testing
text: Use `--skip` to exclude files:
