head: CLAUDE.md > Critical rules
text: 1. **Never add features that don't capture signal.** If it doesn't help founders validate faster, reject it.

head: CLAUDE.md > Critical rules
text: 2. **Never build custom when VueUse/library exists.** Priority: VueUse → library → custom (last resort). Check composables.vueuse.org first.

head: CLAUDE.md > Critical rules
text: 3. **Validation ≠ Product.** Email sequences, auth, payment processing, gated content are product features — out of scope.

head: CLAUDE.md > Critical rules
text: 4. **Complexity budget:** max 50 lines per layer component (reusable); example-app components can run longer but extract composables at ~150 lines. Max 5 props, max 2 abstraction layers, max 3 nesting levels.

head: CLAUDE.md > Critical rules
text: 5. **Content in YAML/Markdown, not hardcoded.** Customers edit content files, not code.

head: CLAUDE.md > Critical rules
text: 6. **Ship first, optimize later.** Ship working → measure → optimize what data proves necessary.

head: CLAUDE.md > Critical rules
text:
Before building: does VueUse solve this? does an existing component handle it? is this a
real (not imagined) problem? will it capture signal faster? If all four are "no," don't
build it.

head: CLAUDE.md > Hard-blocked commands — do NOT retry
text:
`curl`, `wget`, inline HTTP (`fetch('http`, `requests.get(`, `requests.post(`,
`http.get(`, `http.request(`), and `WebFetch` are intercepted by a PreToolUse hook and
replaced with an error message. Do not retry them in Bash. Use
`ctx_fetch_and_index(url, source)` then `ctx_search(queries)` for web pages, or
`ctx_execute(language, code)` to run HTTP calls in the sandbox — only stdout enters context.

head: CLAUDE.md > Bash — short output only
text:
Bash is for short-output commands and mutations only (`git`, `mkdir`, `rm`, `mv`, `cd`,
`ls`, `pnpm install`). Anything printing more than ~20 lines — including `grep` over a large
tree — floods context if run directly; route it through `ctx_batch_execute(commands,
queries)` or `ctx_execute(language: "shell", …)` instead, so only the derived answer enters
context. Full tool-selection hierarchy and the `ctx` command table are in `CONTEXT.md`.

head: RVSpecFit: Automated Spectroscopic Pipeline
text: RVSpecFit is a Python-based automated spectroscopic pipeline designed to determine radial velocities and stellar atmospheric parameters (Teff, logg, [Fe/H], [alpha/Fe], vsini) from spectroscopic data. It employs interpolated synthetic spectral templates (primarily PHOENIX) and performs maximum likelihood fitting.

head: RVSpecFit: Automated Spectroscopic Pipeline > Project Overview
text: - **Core Functionality:** Performs radial velocity and general spectral fitting using interpolated templates.

head: RVSpecFit: Automated Spectroscopic Pipeline > Project Overview
text:
- **Key Technologies:**
    - **Language:** Python 3.6+
    - **Scientific Stack:** NumPy, SciPy, Astropy, Pandas, Matplotlib, Numdifftools.
    - **Data Handling:** H5py, PyYAML.
    - **Performance:** CFFI-based C extensions for spline interpolation (`py/rvspecfit/src/spliner.c`).
    - **Interpolation:** Linear, Voronoi-based, and Neural Network (PyTorch).
    - **Parallelism:** MPI support for distributed file processing (`mpi4py`).

head: RVSpecFit: Automated Spectroscopic Pipeline > Project Overview
text:
- **Architecture:**
    - `SpecData`: A fundamental class representing a spectroscopic dataset (wavelength, flux, error, resolution matrix).
    - `get_chisq`: The primary likelihood function that marginalizes over the polynomial continuum.
    - `spec_inter`: Handles template interpolation from pre-processed libraries.
    - `vel_fit`: High-level processing for maximum likelihood fitting.
    - `fitter_ccf`: Cross-correlation based initial parameter estimation.

head: RVSpecFit: Automated Spectroscopic Pipeline > Building and Running > C Extension Build
text: The project uses CFFI for performance. The C extensions can be built manually:

head: RVSpecFit: Automated Spectroscopic Pipeline > Building and Running > Testing
text: Tests are managed with `pytest`. Note that some tests require external data (PHOENIX templates, DESI data) which the CI fetches automatically.

head: RVSpecFit: Automated Spectroscopic Pipeline > Building and Running > Core Scripts
text: The project provides several CLI tools for template preparation and data analysis:

head: RVSpecFit: Automated Spectroscopic Pipeline > Building and Running > Core Scripts
text: - `rvs_read_grid`: Creates a template database from synthetic spectra.

head: RVSpecFit: Automated Spectroscopic Pipeline > Building and Running > Core Scripts
text: - `rvs_make_interpol`: Generates interpolated spectra for a specific instrument configuration.

head: RVSpecFit: Automated Spectroscopic Pipeline > Building and Running > Core Scripts
text: - `rvs_make_nd`: Constructs n-dimensional interpolators.

head: RVSpecFit: Automated Spectroscopic Pipeline > Building and Running > Core Scripts
text: - `rvs_make_ccf`: Prepares Fourier-transformed templates for cross-correlation.

head: RVSpecFit: Automated Spectroscopic Pipeline > Building and Running > Core Scripts
text: - `rvs_train_nn_interpolator`: Trains a neural network-based interpolator.

head: RVSpecFit: Automated Spectroscopic Pipeline > Building and Running > Core Scripts
text: - `rvs_desi_fit`: Specialized fitting tool for DESI (Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument) data.

head: RVSpecFit: Automated Spectroscopic Pipeline > Building and Running > Core Scripts
text: - `rvs_weave_fit`: Specialized fitting tool for WEAVE data.

head: RVSpecFit: Automated Spectroscopic Pipeline > Development Conventions
text: - **Data Representation:** Use `SpecData` objects to encapsulate spectra.

head: RVSpecFit: Automated Spectroscopic Pipeline > Development Conventions
text: - **Configuration:** Configuration is managed via `config.yaml`, handled by `rvspecfit.utils.read_config`. Default parameters are defined in `rvspecfit.utils.get_default_config`.

head: RVSpecFit: Automated Spectroscopic Pipeline > Development Conventions
text: - **Continuum Modeling:** Continuum is typically modeled as a polynomial (or RBF basis) and marginalized out during the likelihood calculation.

head: RVSpecFit: Automated Spectroscopic Pipeline > Development Conventions
text: - **Interpolation Methods:** Defaults to multi-dimensional linear interpolation. Supports Neural Networks (if `torch` is installed).

head: RVSpecFit: Automated Spectroscopic Pipeline > Development Conventions
text: - **Coordinate Systems:** Wavelengths are typically in Angstroms. Supports both air and vacuum conversions.

head: RVSpecFit: Automated Spectroscopic Pipeline > Development Conventions
text: - **Caching:** Extensive use of `functools.lru_cache` and custom LRU implementations (`LRUDict`) to optimize repeated likelihood evaluations.

head: RVSpecFit: Automated Spectroscopic Pipeline > Development Conventions
text: - **Safety:** Uses `frozendict` to ensure configuration and data objects remain immutable during processing.

head: ⚠️ STRICT CODE OF CONDUCT
text: *   **Fix the Bug, Don't Patch the Test**: When a test fails or an error occurs, investigate the *root cause* (e.g., missing import, broken logic, incorrect configuration) rather than applying a superficial patch just to silence the error or make the test pass.

head: ⚠️ STRICT CODE OF CONDUCT
text: *   **No "Band-Aid" Fixes**: Do not just comment out failing code, mock out essential logic without understanding it, or add broad `try/except` blocks that swallow important errors unless explicitly instructed.

head: ⚠️ STRICT CODE OF CONDUCT
text: *   **Verify the Solution**: After applying a fix, verify that it actually resolves the problem in the running system, not just in the test suite.

head: ⚠️ STRICT CODE OF CONDUCT
text: *   **Ask if Unsure**: If the proper fix is complex or risky, STOP and ask the user for guidance rather than applying a quick hack.

## 🏛️ **High-Level Architecture**

### Core System Flow
1. **File Ingestion** → Files enter through Downloads/Desktop monitoring or manual input
2. **Content Extraction** → `content_extractor.py` processes PDFs, DOCX, emails
3. **Semantic Analysis** → `vector_librarian.py` creates embeddings with ChromaDB
4. **Classification** → `interactive_classifier.py` determines categories with confidence scores
5. **User Interaction** → Low-confidence files trigger questions via web UI or CLI
6. **Organization** → `interactive_organizer.py` moves files to appropriate locations
7. **Rollback Safety** → `easy_rollback_system.py` logs all operations for undo

### Key Design Patterns
- **Hybrid Storage**: Google Drive as primary with local caching/streaming
- **Confidence-Based Actions**: 85% threshold for automatic filing
- **Learning System**: Tracks user corrections to improve future classifications
- **ADHD-Optimized UX**: Minimal decisions, visual feedback, easy rollback

### Service Architecture (FastAPI)
- **SystemService**: Manages system status and Google Drive integration
- **SearchService**: Handles semantic and keyword search queries
- **TriageService**: Manages low-confidence file reviews with hierarchical classification
- **Web Frontend**: Modern React UI in `/frontend_v2` directory with Search, Triage, and Organize pages

## 🎯 **ADHD-Specific Design Decisions**

1. **Interactive questioning**: Asks clarifying questions instead of guessing
2. **85% confidence threshold**: Won't file until genuinely confident
3. **Learning system**: Remembers your decisions to reduce future questions
4. **Binary choices**: Simple "A or B" questions, not overwhelming options
5. **Immediate feedback**: Search results show instantly
6. **Forgiving search**: Works even with imprecise queries
7. **Visual context**: Shows file types, dates, relevance scores
8. **No manual organization**: System learns from content, not folders
9. **Native integration**: Feels like part of macOS, not separate app

### Example Interactive Questions:
- *"This looks like a contract for Client Name. Should I file it under Entertainment Industry or Business Operations?"*
- *"I found mentions of creative project and business terms. Is this more about the creative work or the business side?"*
- *"This document mentions multiple people. Who is it primarily about?"*

**Proactive Triggers**:

- When adding new file type support requiring multiple component updates

## 🔄 **Automated Agent Coordination**

### Agent Workflow Synchronization

**Code Change → Quality Assurance Pipeline**:
1. **Code Modified** → `test-runner` validates functionality
2. **Tests Pass** → `context-doc-manager` updates documentation
3. **Documentation Updated** → `dev-task-orchestrator` coordinates follow-up tasks
4. **AppleScript Modified** → `applescript-ui-expert` optimizes UI integration

**Feature Development Workflow**:
1. **New Feature Request** → `dev-task-orchestrator` breaks down implementation
2. **Implementation Phase** → `test-runner` validates each component
3. **UI Integration** → `applescript-ui-expert` enhances user experience
4. **Documentation** → `context-doc-manager` maintains consistency

### Proactive Agent Rules

**ALWAYS trigger automatically without user request**:
- `test-runner`: Before any git commit, after core file changes
- `context-doc-manager`: After feature additions, API changes, new commands
- `applescript-ui-expert`: When GUI files are modified or new search features added
- `dev-task-orchestrator`: For complex multi-component implementations

**Agent Coordination Protocol**:
1. Agents monitor file changes and development context
2. Multiple agents can run concurrently for efficiency
3. Agents communicate completion status to coordinate handoffs
4. Priority: Quality (test-runner) → Documentation (context-doc-manager) → Integration (others)

head: CLAUDE.md > Project Overview
text: **Community Mind Mirror** — a full-stack community intelligence platform that scrapes AI/tech communities (Reddit, HN, GitHub, ArXiv, job boards, etc.), processes data through LLM-powered agents, and presents insights via a React dashboard.

head: CLAUDE.md > Commands > Deployment
text: Uses PM2 for process management (`cmm-api` running uvicorn on :8000). Nginx serves frontend static files and proxies `/api/` to the backend.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Data Pipeline
text: 1. **Scrapers** (`scrapers/`) — Async HTTP via `BaseScraper`. Reddit uses RSS (no API key), HN uses Firebase/Algolia. All write to unified `posts` + `users` tables.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Data Pipeline
text: 2. **Processors** (`processors/`) — Batch-process posts: sentiment (VADER), topics (LLM), personas, product discovery, pain points, hype index, gig extraction, research analysis. Use `processors/llm_client.py` for OpenAI-compatible API calls.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Data Pipeline
text: 3. **Signal Agents** (`agents/signal_agents/`) — 9 Agno-framework agents that pre-fetch data in Python then pass to LLM for cross-source pattern analysis (market gaps, competitive threats, talent flow, etc.). Orchestrated by `agents/orchestrator.py`.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Data Pipeline
text: 4. **API** (`api/`) — FastAPI routes under `api/routes/`. All list endpoints use `PaginatedResponse[T]`. WebSocket at `/api/ws/dashboard` for real-time updates.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Data Pipeline
text: 5. **Dashboard** (`dashboard/`) — React 19 + TypeScript + Tailwind CSS + TanStack React Query. API client in `api/client.ts`, hooks in `api/hooks.ts`.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Database (`database/connection.py`)
text: All models in one file using SQLAlchemy async ORM with `DeclarativeBase`. Key tables:

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Database (`database/connection.py`)
text: - **Core:** `platforms`, `users`, `posts` (unified across all sources)

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Database (`database/connection.py`)
text: - **Analysis:** `topics`, `topic_mentions`, `discovered_products`, `migrations`, `pain_points`

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Database (`database/connection.py`)
text: - **Signals:** `research_pipelines`, `traction_scores`, `market_gaps`, `competitive_threats`, `agent_runs`

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Database (`database/connection.py`)
text: - **Custom Research:** `research_projects`, `research_insights`, `research_contacts`

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Database (`database/connection.py`)
text: - **Jobs/Gigs:** `gig_posts`, `product_reviews`

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Database (`database/connection.py`)
text: Posts use `raw_metadata` (JSONB) for source-specific data. Session factory: `async_session()` (not a context manager — use `async with async_session() as s:`).

head: CLAUDE.md > Key Patterns
text: - **Scraper:** Inherit `BaseScraper`, implement `scrape()`. Use `upsert_user()`, `upsert_post()`, `fetch_url()`, `rate_limit()`. Posts deduplicate via `platform_id` unique constraint.

head: CLAUDE.md > Key Patterns
text: - **Processor:** Class with `async def run()`. Load unprocessed posts in batches, call LLM, store results. Return summary dict.

head: CLAUDE.md > Key Patterns
text: - **API Route:** FastAPI router, `async_session()` for DB, return Pydantic schemas. Pagination: `page`, `per_page` query params → `PaginatedResponse`.

head: CLAUDE.md > Key Patterns
text: - **Frontend Hook:** TanStack React Query hook per endpoint in `hooks.ts`. Mutations invalidate related query keys.

head: CLAUDE.md > Key Patterns
text: - **Background Tasks:** FastAPI `BackgroundTasks` for long-running operations (e.g., research pipeline). Frontend polls with `refetchInterval`.

head: CLAUDE.md

head: CLAUDE.md > Project Overview
text: bsf (Banshee 3D Framework) is a high-performance, multi-threaded game engine framework written in C++17. The framework uses a plugin-based architecture with support for multiple rendering backends (Vulkan, DirectX 12), physics (PhysX), audio (OpenAudio, FMOD), and includes a C# scripting system.

head: CLAUDE.md > Build System
text: The project uses CMake 4.2 or newer as its build system. Windows builds require Visual Studio 2026 with the v145 toolset. All builds are configured from the repository root.

head: CLAUDE.md > Build System > Build Targets
text: - **bsf** - Framework dynamic library

head: CLAUDE.md > Build System > Build Targets
text: - **UnitTestRunner** - Running unit tests

head: CLAUDE.md > Build System > Debugging
text: When runtime debugging is required (breakpoints, call stacks, variable inspection, crash/assert investigation), use the `clion-debug` skill — it covers connecting to CLion's MCP servers, launching CLion if needed, building, and driving the debugger.

head: CLAUDE.md > Build System > Debugging
text: When running any engine executable unattended (examples, UnitTestRunner, BansheeCookTool), always pass `--debug.DisableErrorDialogs=true`. Without it, Debug-build asserts and aborts pop up interactive dialogs that block the run until a human dismisses them; with it, errors go to stderr and the process fails fast with a proper exit code.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Key Design Patterns
text: - **Component-Based Architecture**: GameObject-like `SceneObject` with attachable `Component` classes

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Key Design Patterns
text: - **Module System**: Core systems are modules (singletons accessed via `GetModuleName()` if provided or `ModuleName::Instance()` otherwise)

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Key Design Patterns
text: - **Handle System**: Type-safe handles (`HSceneObject`, `HRigidbody`, etc.) wrap shared pointers

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Key Design Patterns
text: - **Resource System**: Resources (`Mesh`, `Texture`, `Material`) are loaded/managed centrally

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Key Design Patterns
text: - **Multi-Threading**: Task-based parallelism throughout the engine, internally using fibers rather than threads (See Scheduler)

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Key Design Patterns
text: - **Event System**: Components expose events (e.g., `OnCollisionBegin.Connect(callback)`)

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Key Design Patterns
text: - **Memory allocation**: `B3DNew`/`B3DDelete` instead of `new/delete`, `B3DAllocate/B3DFree` instead of `malloc/free`

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Key Design Patterns
text: - Avoid dynamic memory allocations whenever possible

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Key Design Patterns
text: - Use FrameAllocator for temporary heap allocations

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Key Design Patterns
text: - Re-use temporary containers (e.g. Vector, TArray). Allocate them as class members instead of locally in functions, so their memory can be re-used.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Key Design Patterns
text: - Use TInlineArray when allocating past a certain count is unlikely

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Key Design Patterns
text: - Do not introduce private or internal helper methods with only one caller; inline the code at the call site with a short implementation comment instead.

head: CLAUDE.md > Code Style and Conventions > Line wrapping
text: - Prefer keeping statements, function calls, declarations, and conditions on a single line, even when long.

head: CLAUDE.md > Code Style and Conventions > Line wrapping
text: - Do not enforce a fixed maximum line length.

head: CLAUDE.md > Code Style and Conventions > Naming Conventions
text: - **Classes/Structs**: Capital case, no abbreviations (e.g., `SceneObject`, `Rigidbody`, 'cutRangeCount' vs 'numCutRanges', named index variable in loops, e.g. `elementIndex` vs `i`)

head: CLAUDE.md > Code Style and Conventions > Naming Conventions
text: - **Methods**: Capital case, no abbreviations (e.g., `SetPosition()`, `GetVelocity()`)

head: CLAUDE.md > Code Style and Conventions > Naming Conventions
text: - **Member variables**: Capital case for public fields (e.g., `Spring.Stiffness`), `m` prefix for non-public fields (e.g. `Spring.mInternalData`)

head: CLAUDE.md > Code Style and Conventions > Naming Conventions
text: - **Local variables**: camelCase with full names, no abbreviations (e.g., `rigidbodySceneObject`, not `rbSO`)

head: CLAUDE.md > Code Style and Conventions > Naming Conventions
text: - **Output parameters**: prefix with `out` for any parameter the function writes through — non-const reference, pointer, or array out-param (e.g., `outVariation`, `outRGBA`, `outSource`). This is an engine-wide convention.

head: CLAUDE.md > Code Style and Conventions > Naming Conventions
text: - **Spell the type noun out**: `Parameters` not `Params`, `Information` not `Info`, `Description` not `Desc`; and name a local for the thing it holds or builds, including that noun — `TextureCreateInformation inputTextureCreateInformation;`, `inputTexture` (not `inputInfo`, not bare `input`); `gTextureCompressParameters` (not `gTextureCompressParams`)

head: CLAUDE.md > Code Style and Conventions > Naming Conventions
text: - **Lambdas**: Prefix with `fn`, explicit captures only (e.g., `auto fnProcess = [this, &data](int x) { ... }`)

head: CLAUDE.md > Code Style and Conventions > Naming Conventions
text: - **Handles**: Prefix with `H` (e.g., `HSceneObject`, `HRigidbody`)

head: CLAUDE.md > Code Style and Conventions > Naming Conventions
text: - **Smart pointers**: `TShared<T>` for shared pointers, `TUnique<T>` for unique pointers. `B3DMakeShared` or `B3DMakeSharedFromExisting` to create shared pointer, `B3DMakeUnique` to create unique pointer.

head: CLAUDE.md > Code Style and Conventions > Naming Conventions
text: - **Constants**: `k` prefix (e.g., `Vector3::kZero`, `Quaternion::kIdentity`)

head: CLAUDE.md > Code Style and Conventions > Naming Conventions
text: - **Code documentation**: The codebase consistently uses Doxygen-style documentation

head: CLAUDE.md > Code Style and Conventions > API Patterns
text: - **Logging**: `B3D_LOG(Level, LogCategory, "message {0}", param)` - never use `GetDebug().LogDebug()`

head: CLAUDE.md > Code Style and Conventions > API Patterns
text: - **Construction**: All types must provide constructors; do not use aggregate brace initialization anywhere.

head: CLAUDE.md > Code Style and Conventions > Comments
text: - When writing new implementation comments do not narrate the rationale for an edit or reference what used to be there - that belongs in the commit message, not the source.

head: CLAUDE.md > Code Style and Conventions > Comments
text: - Keep existing implementation comments. If copying or refactoring code, keep the comment if still relevant. This also applies to TODO comments.

head: CLAUDE.md > Code Style and Conventions > Comments
text: - Write Doxygen API documentation on classes/methods/fields. Write smart and concise documentation that does not include implementation details, and also doesn't repeat what is obvious from method/class name or signature, but instead tells you how to use the API.

head: CLAUDE.md > Code Style and Conventions > Comments
text: - Do not mention the caller/user of a method/class when writing documentation. Each method/class should be treated as a black box that may be potentially used for other purpose than the originally intended one.

head: CLAUDE.md > Code Style and Conventions > Comments
text:
- Keep implementation comments to a minimum:
  - You can split up larger code blocks into meaningful sections using an implementation comment
  - You can comment on non-obvious constraints, workarounds for bugs or other things that might be missed without the comment
  - Otherwise use meaningful variable names so the code is self-documenting, avoid abbreviations
  - A short trailing `//` may state a literal's or field's units/meaning (e.g. `outPixelFormat = PF_RG32U; // 64-bit block`, `B3D_UNIFORM_BUFFER_MEMBER(Vector2I, gSize)  // decoded output size in pixels`)

head: CLAUDE.md > Architectural Changes
text: When adding features or refactoring, don't localize a change just to keep it small — if reshaping a higher-level system yields a cleaner API, expand the scope to do it right.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architectural Changes
text: - Don't be afraid to make API or higher-level architectural changes when they make the API cleaner; avoid contorting a new feature to fit an existing API that ends up with code smell.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architectural Changes
text: - Prefer redesigning the API to fit the feature cleanly over bolting the feature onto the side of a system that wasn't shaped for it.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architectural Changes
text: - Clean means easy to use and easy to understand: clear, non-convoluted method names that say what they do.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architectural Changes
text: - Clean means no code duplication: factor shared logic into one place rather than copy-pasting across call sites.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architectural Changes
text: - Clean means symmetry: paired operations match (e.g. `begin`/`end`, `acquire`/`release`, `create`/`destroy`).

head: CLAUDE.md > Answering Questions and Presenting Plans
text: - When answering a question or presenting a plan, be as succinct as possible: give the answer directly, note important gotchas if any, and optionally include a short example. Nothing else.

head: CLAUDE.md > Answering Questions and Presenting Plans
text: - Use as few words as possible — no walls of text, no restating context, no exhaustive option surveys.

head: CLAUDE.md > Planning
text: - When producing an implementation plan, if a big/pivotal decision arises — one the rest of the plan hinges on (e.g. a core data-flow choice, an interface boundary, a correctness assumption that determines whether the whole approach works) — stop and ask before finishing the plan. Do not bake the decision in as an assumption and present a completed plan around it. Surface it early so it can be settled first.

head: CLAUDE.md > Other notes

head: Project Documentation > Building a plugin from this template
text: **This section applies only when working on an actual plugin that was created from this template — not when working on the template repository itself.**

head: Project Documentation > Building a plugin from this template
text: To tell which case you are in, check the git remote: if `origin` points at `dsebastien/obsidian-plugin-template`, you are in the template repo — skip this entire section and leave `TEMPLATE_USAGE.md`, `scripts/init-from-template.ts`, and the `init` script entry alone (they must ship with the template). Otherwise, you are in a downstream plugin.

head: Project Documentation > Building a plugin from this template
text: In a downstream plugin, if `TEMPLATE_USAGE.md` still exists at the repo root, the project has not yet been initialized. Before doing any other work:

head: Project Documentation > Building a plugin from this template
text: 1. Read `TEMPLATE_USAGE.md` end-to-end.

head: Project Documentation > Building a plugin from this template
text: 2. Run `bun install && bun run init` to reset inherited template state (CHANGELOG, versions.json, manifest, package.json).

head: Project Documentation > Building a plugin from this template
text: 3. Complete the manual follow-ups listed in `TEMPLATE_USAGE.md` (plugin class renames, README rewrite, `docs/` user guide, `documentation/` technical docs, funding links).

head: Project Documentation > Building a plugin from this template
text:
4. **Remove the initialization tooling from the downstream plugin once initialization is complete.** Delete:
    - `TEMPLATE_USAGE.md`
    - `scripts/init-from-template.ts` (and its `.spec.ts` if present)
    - The `"init"` entry in `package.json` `scripts`
    These files only belong in uninitialized clones of the template. Leaving them behind is a signal that step 3 isn't actually complete.

head: Project Documentation > Building a plugin from this template
text: Skipping this section (in a downstream plugin) leads to template leakage: bogus version entries in `CHANGELOG.md`, wrong repo URLs in `package.json`, and the `my-plugin` id shipping in the first release.

head: Project Documentation > Bun Runtime
text: Default to using Bun instead of Node.js, with one exception: ESLint runs under Node.

head: Project Documentation > Bun Runtime
text: - `bunfig.toml` sets `[run] bun = false`, so scripts with a `node` shebang (eslint, tsc, prettier, commitlint) run under Node, as the community catalog reviewer's lint does. Under Bun, `node:module` `isBuiltin('bun:test')` is true and `obsidianmd/no-nodejs-modules` misreads every spec's `bun:test` import.

head: Project Documentation > Bun Runtime

head: Project Documentation > Testing
text: **MANDATORY**: run tests with `bun run test`, not bare `bun test`.

head: Project Documentation > Testing
text:
The script adds `--isolate`, which runs each test file in a fresh global object and
module registry. This is a correctness requirement here, not a speed optimization.
`bunfig.toml` preloads `src/test-setup.ts`, which calls `mock.module('obsidian', ...)`.
Module mocks are global and persist across files in a worker, so without `--isolate`
any spec that re-mocks a module silently corrupts every spec that runs after it. The
resulting failures are order-dependent and read as flakiness.

head: Project Documentation > Testing
text:
`--isolate` cannot be set in `bunfig.toml`; it only exists as a CLI flag. That is why
it lives in the `test` script and why every caller (CI, release, agents) must go
through `bun run test`.

head: Project Documentation > Testing > Scaling the test suite
text:
Leave the flags below OFF until a plugin's suite is actually slow. On a small suite
they cost more than they save; measure before adding one.

head: Project Documentation > Testing > Scaling the test suite
text:
| Flag               | Turn it on when                                        | Notes                                                                                                              |
| ------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `--parallel[=N]`   | the suite takes more than a few seconds                | Runs files across worker processes. Implies `--isolate`. Adds per-worker startup, so it is slower on small suites. |
| `--shard=M/N`      | one CI job is the bottleneck AND you have a job matrix | Splitting a fast suite across runners is strictly worse: you pay runner startup N times.                           |
| `--timings=<file>` | using `--parallel` or `--shard`                        | Balances shards by measured duration. Write it with `--update-timings`.                                            |
| `--changed=main`   | the suite is slow and PRs touch a small slice          | Runs only files affected by the diff. Can report "no tests ran" on unrelated PRs.                                  |

head: Project Documentation > Manifest rules (`manifest.json`)
text: - **Never set `minAppVersion` above the latest PUBLIC Obsidian release.** Versions marked "early access" on https://obsidian.md/changelog/ are Catalyst-only; gating on them locks out every regular user (installs and updates are hidden/blocked). The installed `obsidian` typings version is NOT the floor — determine the real floor by typechecking against older typings. Pin the `obsidian` dev dependency to the latest public release (never `latest`, never a Catalyst version); type-only niceties from newer typings (e.g. `override` on `Plugin.settings`, `@since 1.13.0`) are not worth losing public users. Runtime-guarded dual paths (e.g. declarative settings + `display()` fallback) let you adopt new APIs without raising the floor.

head: Project Documentation > Manifest rules (`manifest.json`)
text: - Keep `minAppVersion` accurate when using newer APIs. Common bumps: `1.1.0` (`ButtonComponent.setIcon`/`setTooltip`), `1.4.10` (`AbstractInputSuggest`), `1.5.7` (`Vault.getFileByPath`), `1.7.2` (`Workspace.revealLeaf`).

head: Project Documentation > Manifest rules (`manifest.json`)
text: - Canonical requirements are coded here: https://github.com/obsidianmd/obsidian-releases/blob/master/.github/workflows/validate-plugin-entry.yml

head: Project Documentation > Manifest rules (`manifest.json`) > Community catalog listing rules
text: These rules apply to **`id`**, **`name`**, and **`description`** in `manifest.json` AND are mirrored into `package.json` (`name`, `description`):

head: Project Documentation > Manifest rules (`manifest.json`) > Community catalog listing rules
text: - **`id`**: must not contain the word "obsidian" (catalog trademark rule). The GitHub repo name can keep it; only the manifest `id` is gated. Drop the prefix (`obsidian-time-machine` → `time-machine`).

head: Project Documentation > Manifest rules (`manifest.json`) > Community catalog listing rules
text: - **`name`**: must not contain "Obsidian". Must not be all-uppercase — acronym chains like `CLI REST MCP` trip the check; include at least one lowercase word.

head: Project Documentation > Manifest rules (`manifest.json`) > Community catalog listing rules
text: - **`description`**: must not contain "Obsidian", must not start with the plugin name (the catalog UI already shows it), must end with `.`, `!`, or `?`. These three rules typically fire together — fix in one pass.

head: Project Documentation > Manifest rules (`manifest.json`) > Community catalog listing rules
text: **Draft vs accepted timing for `id`:**

head: Project Documentation > Manifest rules (`manifest.json`) > Community catalog listing rules
text: - While the catalog entry is still in **draft**: free to rename `id`. Do it before acceptance.

head: Project Documentation > Manifest rules (`manifest.json`) > Community catalog listing rules
text: - Once **accepted**: `id` is locked forever (changing it breaks installed users, settings paths, and keyboard shortcuts).

head: Project Documentation > Manifest rules (`manifest.json`) > Community catalog listing rules
text: - **Sticky-draft-slug gotcha**: even in draft, the catalog stores the slug from the _first_ submission and compares every later manifest against it. A rename then triggers `ERROR: The plugin ID in (<new>) does not match the existing plugin ID (<old>)` — contradicting the "must not contain obsidian" rule. Resolution: delete the draft listing in the catalog admin and resubmit fresh under the new id, or open a thread with the catalog maintainers to release the slug.

head: Project Documentation > Commands & settings
text: - Any user-facing commands should be added via `this.addCommand(...)`.

head: Project Documentation > Commands & settings
text: - If the plugin has configuration, provide a settings tab and sensible defaults.

head: Project Documentation > Commands & settings
text: - Persist settings using `this.loadData()` / `this.saveData()`.

head: Project Documentation > Commands & settings
text: - Use stable command IDs; avoid renaming once released.

head: Project Documentation > Commands & settings
text: - The command `name` must not include the plugin name — Obsidian already prefixes commands with the plugin name in the palette. If you need to rebrand, **rename `name`, not `id`** (renaming an id breaks any user-bound keyboard shortcut). Grep `docs/` and `README.md` for old command names when renaming.

head: Project Documentation > Commands & settings
text: - File pickers in settings tabs: never hand-roll. Use `AbstractInputSuggest` for inline autocomplete and `FuzzySuggestModal` for a browse-button modal — both cover keyboard nav, theming, and popout-window correctness for free. Hand-rolled menus accumulate inline-style + `document.createElement` lint warnings fast.

head: Project Documentation > Commands & settings
text: - Replace `window.confirm(...)` with a `Modal` subclass: `confirm()` blocks the UI thread, can't be themed, doesn't play with popout windows, and is forbidden by the scorecard.

head: Project Documentation > Commands & settings
text: - Never give a `PluginSettingTab` subclass a method/property whose name collides with an Obsidian `SettingTab` base member — reserved as of API 1.13.0: `update`, `getSettingDefinitions`, `getControlValue`, `setControlValue`, `settingItems`, `icon` (plus long-standing `display`, `hide`, `containerEl`, `app`). A same-named helper silently **shadows** the framework method; e.g. `addSettingTab()` calls `tab.update()` with no args at registration, so a custom `update(mutator)` receives `undefined` and crashes (`[Immer] The first or second argument to 'produce' must be a function`, or any "expected a function" error). Name helpers distinctively (`mutateSettings`, `renderX`, …), and keep the `obsidian` dev types current so `noImplicitOverride` flags collisions at compile time.

head: Project Documentation > Commands & settings > Declarative settings (Obsidian 1.13+) — mandatory approach and traps
text:
This template declares its settings via `getSettingDefinitions()` (see
`src/app/settings/settings-tab.ts`). Keep that approach. Every rule below cost
a shipped bug the first time it was broken; `settings-guard.spec.ts` enforces
the three statically-catchable ones.

head: Project Documentation > Commands & settings > Declarative settings (Obsidian 1.13+) — mandatory approach and traps
text:
- **`getSettingDefinitions()` REPLACES `display()`.** Non-empty array means
  `display()` is never called. No partial adoption: the whole settings UI is
  declarative or none of it. Requires `minAppVersion` 1.13.0.

head: Project Documentation > Commands & settings > Declarative settings (Obsidian 1.13+) — mandatory approach and traps
text:
- **A `render:` hook renders the ROW.** Write into `setting.settingEl` only
  (drop `setting.infoEl` when the helper draws its own name/desc). Anything
  written outside the row — `group.listEl`, siblings — is the framework's to
  discard: the control is silently absent at runtime. Never call
  `settingEl.remove()`.

head: Project Documentation > Commands & settings > Declarative settings (Obsidian 1.13+) — mandatory approach and traps
text:
- **`update()` re-runs a `render:` hook on the SAME row and resets only its
  name, description and control area.** Obsidian 1.13.7 runs the previous
  cleanup, then `setting.clear()` (empties `controlEl`), `setName` and
  `setDesc` (so anything appended to `descEl` goes too), then the hook.
  Controls added with `addButton`/`addText` are cleared, but anything the hook
  appends elsewhere in the row (a support block, an embedded editor, a status
  block) stays and is appended again: every refresh stacks another copy.
  Render such content into a wrapper and return a cleanup that removes it:
  create `el` with `setting.settingEl.createDiv()`, draw into it, and
  `return () => el.remove()`. Obsidian calls the cleanup before re-running
  the hook. Verified in Obsidian 1.13.7, where fleet
  plugins using this template's Support row went from 1 to 3 copies after
  two `update()` calls; a stacked editor also kept its stale copy on top,
  whose Save wrote an outdated list.

head: Project Documentation > Commands & settings > Declarative settings (Obsidian 1.13+) — mandatory approach and traps
text:
- **The definitions are built only in `update()` and reused on every
  opening.** Anything a definition captures from outside the settings (another
  plugin's state, e.g. which Starter Kit note types exist) is frozen at the
  last `update()`, and plugin `onload` is early: other plugins may not be
  loaded yet. Read such state in a `render:` hook or a `visible:` predicate,
  which run on every render.

head: Project Documentation > Commands & settings > Declarative settings (Obsidian 1.13+) — mandatory approach and traps
text:
- **`defaultValue` is the fallback for a RESOLVER returning undefined/null —
  not for a cleared input.** On numeric controls it turns a cleared field into
  a silent reset to the schema default. Declare none; let a bounds `validate`
  refuse the cleared value inline.

head: Project Documentation > Commands & settings > Declarative settings (Obsidian 1.13+) — mandatory approach and traps
text:
- **A row `action:` fires on the WHOLE row, not on a button.** Destructive
  rows need their own confirmation modal.
  It also draws NO button, so a link row that used to have a CTA silently loses
  it in the port — use a `render:` hook with `addButton` to keep one.

head: Project Documentation > Commands & settings > Declarative settings (Obsidian 1.13+) — mandatory approach and traps
text:
- **A `render:` hook draws into `.setting-item`, which is a flex ROW.** Anything
  that is a vertical stack of full-width rows (the shared support block is the
  canonical case) needs the row put back into block flow, or its heading,
  buttons and badge lay out side by side. `settings-stack` does that.

head: Project Documentation > Commands & settings > Declarative settings (Obsidian 1.13+) — mandatory approach and traps
text:
- **`onDelete` decorates only plain list rows — `type: 'page'` entries get NO
  delete button.** A list of sub-pages silently loses its delete affordance;
  give each page an explicit "Remove" row (a warning-styled button in its own
  row, deleting by stable id). Caught in the first fleet port's vault review.

head: Project Documentation > Commands & settings > Declarative settings (Obsidian 1.13+) — mandatory approach and traps
text:
- **`onDelete(index)` indexes the LIVE list.** The framework re-indexes on
  drag immediately, while a settings refresh waits on persistence. Resolve the
  entity from the live index, never from a render-time snapshot.

head: Project Documentation > Commands & settings > Declarative settings (Obsidian 1.13+) — mandatory approach and traps
text:
- **Persist before committing to memory — AND serialize the writes.**
  `updateSettings` must write to disk first and swap the in-memory settings
  only on success — a rejection rolls the control back to `getControlValue`'s
  answer, which must be the on-disk truth. And writes must queue: two
  overlapping calls that both `produce()` from the same base across the save
  await make the second commit silently drop the first edit. Chain them so
  each mutation derives from the previous committed state (see
  `src/app/plugin.ts`).

head: Project Documentation > Commands & settings > Declarative settings (Obsidian 1.13+) — mandatory approach and traps
text:
- **Never `produce()` from the shared `DEFAULT_SETTINGS`.** Immer
  deep-freezes what `produce` returns, including every subtree it shares with
  its base, so `produce(DEFAULT_SETTINGS, …)` freezes the exported constant
  (nested values too) for the rest of the process. Later code or specs that touch
  it fail with "Attempted to assign to readonly property". The `test` script
  runs `bun test --isolate`, which hides it, so `validate` and CI never see
  it: only the `Object.isFrozen` assertions in `src/app/plugin.spec.ts` do.
  Produce from `createDefaultSettings()`, a deep-fresh object per call: build
  nested arrays and objects as new values, never `{ ...DEFAULT_SETTINGS }`
  (the spread shares them, and they freeze again). Keep `DEFAULT_SETTINGS` for
  reads.

head: Project Documentation > Commands & settings > Declarative settings (Obsidian 1.13+) — mandatory approach and traps
text:
- **`setControlValue` MUST reject on failure.** Resolving tells the framework
  the write landed, so the pane keeps showing a value that was never stored.
  Rejecting rolls the control back to `getControlValue`'s answer.

head: Project Documentation > Commands & settings > Declarative settings (Obsidian 1.13+) — mandatory approach and traps
text:
- **A nullable object cannot be a dot-path control key.** The path walks to
  `null`, the write is refused, and the choice silently does not persist.

head: Project Documentation > Commands & settings > Declarative settings (Obsidian 1.13+) — mandatory approach and traps
text:
- **Free wins:** `SettingDefinitionList` provides drag-to-reorder, delete and
  add natively — delete hand-rolled arrow buttons, do not port them. Declared
  `name`/`desc` are indexed by Obsidian's settings search.

head: Project Documentation > Commands & settings > Declarative settings (Obsidian 1.13+) — mandatory approach and traps
text:
- **Acceptance is a live vault check.** Nothing in CI renders a settings pane.
  Five broken controls once shipped through 2806 passing tests, clean types,
  `--max-warnings 0` and two adversarial reviews. For ANY settings change,
  open the settings pane in a real vault before calling it done — flag it for
  manual verification per the "No UI self-verification" rule.

head: Project Documentation > Versioning & releases
text: - Do not bump `version` in `manifest.json` or edit `versions.json` by hand: `bun run release` does both. `versions.json` gets a new line ONLY when a release raises `minAppVersion`, and that line names the LAST release on the old floor (`"<last release>": "<its minAppVersion>"`), so users left behind by the raise get the newest release that still runs for them. Obsidian reads the file only when the latest manifest's floor is above the user's app, and installs the highest listed release whose floor the app meets. `scripts/version-bump.ts` finds that release as the highest `x.y.z` tag below the new version and fails the release rather than skip the line if it cannot. Every key must be a real published release in `x.y.z` form.

head: Project Documentation > Versioning & releases
text: - Create a GitHub release whose tag exactly matches `manifest.json`'s `version`. Do not use a leading `v`.

head: Project Documentation > Versioning & releases
text: - Attach `manifest.json`, `main.js`, and `styles.css` (if present) to the release as individual assets.

head: Project Documentation > Versioning & releases
text: - After the initial release, follow the process to add/update your plugin in the community catalog as required.

head: Project Documentation > Versioning & releases > Cutting a release
text:
`bun run release` drives the whole thing. It is interactive by default, and takes flags so
it can run unattended — an agent should use those rather than reimplementing the script:

head: Project Documentation > Versioning & releases > Cutting a release
text:
The version is derived from the conventional commits since the last tag
(`bun scripts/calculate-next-version.ts --verbose` shows the analysis). Confirm it before
using `--yes`: a stray `feat!` in the range turns a patch into a major.

head: Project Documentation > Versioning & releases > Cutting a release
text:
**Release notes are written, not generated, whenever users will read them.** The in-app
"What's new" tab and the GitHub release body both show the release's `CHANGELOG.md`
section, which by default is the conventional-changelog list of commit subjects
("fix(build): align with the catalog reviewer's archive") — written for maintainers, not
users. For any release a user should understand (a feature, a visible fix, a major that
bundles earlier minors), write `NEXT_RELEASE.md` at the repo root and commit it before
releasing: what changed for the user, in plain language, with `###` or deeper headings.
A line that reads as a version heading (`### 1.2.0 ...`, even inside a code fence) would
split the section for both readers, and `#`/`##` would outrank the release's own heading:
both are refused. Remember the two surfaces render differently: GitHub autolinks `@user`
(and notifies them) and `#123`, Obsidian renders `[[links]]`. The release uses it as the
section's body under the generated version header, then deletes it in the release commit.
Without it, the generated list is used. `release.sh` validates the file and says which
source the release will use before dispatching. Never hand-edit a GitHub release body
afterwards: that is how the two surfaces came to disagree.

head: Project Documentation > Versioning & releases > Cutting a release
text:
Before releasing: push, then wait for CI to go **green**. The release workflow builds from
what is on `main`, so dispatching while CI is still running means finding out whether the
code was releasable only after the tag exists — and a tag is the one part of this that is
awkward to take back.

head: Project Documentation > Versioning & releases > Cutting a release
text:
**The workflow runs twice, and the first success is not the release.** Run 1 (`prepare`)
bumps the version files, regenerates `CHANGELOG.md`, commits, tags, and re-dispatches
itself at the tag. Run 2 (`publish`) builds, attests and creates the GitHub release. In
between, the tag exists but `gh release view <version>` still reports "release not found",
which reads exactly like a failure and is not one. Wait for the second run.

head: Project Documentation > Versioning & releases > Cutting a release
text:
Afterwards: `git pull --ff-only` to bring the release commit back, then `bun run dev` to
deploy the released build into a vault and confirm the new version number is running.

head: Project Documentation > Security, privacy, and compliance
text: Follow Obsidian's **Developer Policies** and **Plugin Guidelines**. In particular:

head: Project Documentation > Security, privacy, and compliance
text: - Default to local/offline operation. Only make network requests when essential to the feature.

head: Project Documentation > Security, privacy, and compliance
text: - No hidden telemetry. If you collect optional analytics or call third-party services, require explicit opt-in and document clearly in `README.md` and in settings.

head: Project Documentation > Security, privacy, and compliance
text: - Never execute remote code, fetch and eval scripts, or auto-update plugin code outside of normal releases.

head: Project Documentation > Security, privacy, and compliance
text: - Minimize scope: read/write only what's necessary inside the vault. Do not access files outside the vault.

head: Project Documentation > Security, privacy, and compliance
text: - Clearly disclose any external services used, data sent, and risks.

head: Project Documentation > Security, privacy, and compliance
text: - Respect user privacy. Do not collect vault contents, filenames, or personal information unless absolutely necessary and explicitly consented.

head: Project Documentation > Security, privacy, and compliance
text: - Avoid deceptive patterns, ads, or spammy notifications.

head: Project Documentation > Security, privacy, and compliance
text: - Register and clean up all DOM, app, and interval listeners using the provided `register*` helpers so the plugin unloads safely.

head: Project Documentation > UX & copy guidelines (for UI text, commands, settings)

head: Project Documentation > UX & copy guidelines (for UI text, commands, settings)

text: - Keep startup light. Defer heavy work until needed.

head: Project Documentation > Performance
text: - Avoid long-running tasks during `onload`; use lazy initialization.

head: Project Documentation > Performance
text: - Batch disk access and avoid excessive vault scans.

head: Project Documentation > Performance

head: Project Documentation > Coding conventions
text: - **Keep `main.ts` minimal**: Focus only on plugin lifecycle (onload, onunload, addCommand calls). Delegate all feature logic to separate modules.

head: Project Documentation > Coding conventions

head: Project Documentation > Coding conventions

head: Project Documentation > The rule floor is not yours to lower
text:
A commit that loosens a rule instead of fixing the finding is refused. This is
enforced, not advisory: a `pre-commit` hook (`scripts/git-hooks/check-rule-integrity.sh`)
and `bun run rules:check`, which is part of `bun run validate` and therefore runs
in CI too.

head: Project Documentation > The rule floor is not yours to lower
text: Refused outright, in any staged line under `src/` or `scripts/`:

head: Project Documentation > The rule floor is not yours to lower
text: - `eslint-disable`, `eslint-disable-next-line`, `eslint-disable-line`

head: Project Documentation > The rule floor is not yours to lower
text: - `@ts-ignore`, `@ts-nocheck`, `@ts-expect-error`

head: Project Documentation > The rule floor is not yours to lower
text: - `: any`, `as any`, `as unknown as`

head: Project Documentation > The rule floor is not yours to lower
text:
Refused when the RESOLVED configuration gets weaker than `rules-baseline.json`:
a rule downgraded or dropped, `--max-warnings` raised above 0, a TypeScript
strictness switch turned off, or `compilerOptions.types` losing a pin. The
baseline records the _minimum_ severity each rule resolves to across every
source file, so a file-scoped exemption counts as a weakening too.

head: Project Documentation > The rule floor is not yours to lower > Regenerate `bun.lock` with bun 1.3.x, not 1.4.x
text:
The community catalog's automated review runs a bun older than 1.4.0 and cannot
parse `lockfileVersion: 2`. It reports "Unknown lockfile version", ignores the
lockfile, then fails the frozen install — which surfaces on the review page as
two errors ("The bun lockfile is out of date" and "Build verification dependency
installation failed") plus a flood of `no-unsafe-*` warnings, because nothing

head: Project Documentation > The rule floor is not yours to lower > Regenerate `bun.lock` with bun 1.3.x, not 1.4.x
text:
bun 1.4.0 PRESERVES an existing v1 lockfile but writes v2 whenever it generates
one from scratch. So a repo is one `rm bun.lock`, or one dependency change that
forces a regeneration, away from shipping a release the catalog cannot review.
Graph Explorer Base View failed two reviews this way before the cause was found.

head: Project Documentation > The rule floor is not yours to lower > Regenerate `bun.lock` with bun 1.3.x, not 1.4.x

head: Project Documentation > The rule floor is not yours to lower > Regenerate `bun.lock` with bun 1.3.x, not 1.4.x
text:
Both 1.3.x and 1.4.x read a v1 lockfile, so v1 is strictly the safer format.
`bun run rules:check` fails on anything above v1; raise `MAX_LOCKFILE_VERSION`
in `scripts/rules-baseline.ts` once the catalog can read it.

- editing, renaming, or unregistering `scripts/git-hooks/check-rule-integrity.sh`,
  or removing its entry from `.gitconfig`

text: - running `bun run rules:baseline` to make a failing commit pass

head: Project Documentation > The rule floor is not yours to lower > The gate is mandatory. Do not route around it.
text:
That last one is the tempting one, so be explicit about it: regenerating the
baseline is how an _intended, human-approved_ loosening gets recorded. It is not
a way to clear a red check. If the gate fires and you were not already asked to
change the rules, the gate is right and the code is wrong.

head: Project Documentation > The rule floor is not yours to lower > The gate is mandatory. Do not route around it.
text:
A blocked commit is not a problem to solve. It is the answer: fix the finding.
If you believe the rule genuinely does not apply, stop and say so — the decision
to loosen a rule belongs to Sébastien, not to the agent that hit it.

head: Project Documentation > The rule floor is not yours to lower > The gate is mandatory. Do not route around it.
text:
There is no bypass flag, deliberately. If a rule genuinely does not apply to a
file, add a scoped override in `eslint.config.ts` with a written reason, then
run `bun run rules:baseline` in its own commit — the loosening then appears in a
diff a human reads, rather than inside a config nobody re-opens.

head: Project Documentation > The rule floor is not yours to lower > The gate is mandatory. Do not route around it.
text:
The hook is the fast local copy, not the enforcement. `rules:check` runs in
`validate`, in `ci.yml`, and in the release gate, because a pre-commit hook is
advisory the moment someone commits from another machine or a tool writes a
commit directly.

head: Project Documentation > The rule floor is not yours to lower > The gate is mandatory. Do not route around it.
text: Two lessons paid for this gate:

head: Project Documentation > The rule floor is not yours to lower > The gate is mandatory. Do not route around it.
text:
- **A local disable buys nothing.** Five `obsidianmd` rules were once switched
  off with careful rationales; the community catalog reviewer runs its own
  ruleset against the archive and reported every one of them at submission. The
  disable only hid the finding until it was expensive. An _inline_ disable of an
  `obsidianmd` rule is a hard failure there, not a warning.

head: Project Documentation > The rule floor is not yours to lower > The gate is mandatory. Do not route around it.
text:
- **A codemod cannot read.** A `setTimeout` → `setNodeTimer` rewrite made to
  satisfy `prefer-window-timers` swept through template literals holding source
  for a spawned child process, where that alias does not exist — a lint rule
  cannot see inside a string, so nothing flagged it and the suite went red. After
  any mechanical rewrite, check what it changed inside strings and template
  literals, and get the full suite green before committing.

head: Project Documentation > Community catalog review — preventative rules
text: The community-plugin reviewer runs a fixed set of lint rules against every submitted release. Most warnings repeat across plugins and have known idiomatic fixes. **Apply these patterns from day one** — fixing them retroactively is much more expensive than getting them right the first time.

head: Project Documentation > Community catalog review — preventative rules > API conventions (DOM, timers, popouts)
text: - `document` → `activeDocument` (so popout windows hit their own DOM).

head: Project Documentation > Community catalog review — preventative rules > API conventions (DOM, timers, popouts)
text: - Timers — `setTimeout`/`clearTimeout`/`setInterval`/`clearInterval`/`requestAnimationFrame`/`cancelAnimationFrame` → `window.X`. **Not `activeWindow.X`** — the rule complains either way for timers.

head: Project Documentation > Community catalog review — preventative rules > API conventions (DOM, timers, popouts)
text: - Timer handle types: declare as plain `number`, not `ReturnType<typeof setTimeout>`. With `@types/bun` in scope, the overload resolves to Bun's `Timer` and breaks the assignment from `window.setTimeout` (which returns `number`).

head: Project Documentation > Community catalog review — preventative rules > API conventions (DOM, timers, popouts)
text: - `document.createElement(tag)` → `createEl(tag, …)` / `createSpan(…)` / `createDiv(…)`. Prefer parent-bound `el.createEl(…)` when a parent exists; the child is appended automatically.

head: Project Documentation > Community catalog review — preventative rules > API conventions (DOM, timers, popouts)
text: - `globalThis.X` for plugin-injected globals (Excalidraw etc.) → `window.X`.

head: Project Documentation > Community catalog review — preventative rules > API conventions (DOM, timers, popouts)
text: - `processFrontMatter` callback param type: `(frontmatter: Record<string, unknown>) => …` — Obsidian's default is `any` and trips unsafe-access rules.

head: Project Documentation > Community catalog review — preventative rules > API conventions (DOM, timers, popouts)
text: - External SDKs that need a custom `fetch`: inject a `requestUrl`-based adapter via the SDK's `fetch` option (most SDKs that need a custom fetch — Replicate, OpenAI, etc. — expose one). Never `node-fetch`, never `globalThis.fetch = require('node-fetch')`. The adapter wraps `requestUrl` in a `fetch`-shaped function and refuses non-string/ArrayBuffer bodies; no streaming, no AbortSignal, no FormData. Adequate for plain GET/POST polling.

head: Project Documentation > Community catalog review — preventative rules > Lint / TypeScript rules
text: - `eslint-disable @typescript-eslint/no-explicit-any` is **forbidden** — the reviewer treats both the violation and the disable as an **error** (blocks the scorecard). Type properly instead: `typeof Chart` for dynamically-imported classes, widen your custom interface rather than `as any`, narrow `unknown` at the call site.

head: Project Documentation > Community catalog review — preventative rules > Lint / TypeScript rules
text: - Every other `eslint-disable-next-line <rule>` requires a `-- reason` description.

head: Project Documentation > Community catalog review — preventative rules > Lint / TypeScript rules
text: - **`obsidianmd/ui/sentence-case`: `brands` REPLACES the plugin's defaults, it does not extend them.** The rule reads `options?.brands ?? DEFAULT_BRANDS`, so listing only this plugin's own names drops every built-in brand (`Obsidian`, `Git`, `Markdown`, `GitHub`, `Windows`, …). The catalog reviewer runs the plugin's own ruleset and keeps enforcing all of them, so the effect is findings you never see locally — not findings that go away. Always spread `DEFAULT_BRANDS` first. Never add an ordinary UI word (`Settings`) as a brand: it makes every lowercase occurrence of that word a violation. `acronyms` replaces `DEFAULT_ACRONYMS` the same way: when a plugin passes it, spread `DEFAULT_ACRONYMS` (deep import from `eslint-plugin-obsidianmd/dist/lib/rules/ui/acronyms.js`) first.

head: Project Documentation > Community catalog review — preventative rules > Lint / TypeScript rules
text: - `new Array(n)` leaks `any[]` — write `new Array<T>(n)` or `Array.from({ length: n }, () => …)`. `Array.from` is cleaner when each slot needs a fresh sub-array.

head: Project Documentation > Community catalog review — preventative rules > Lint / TypeScript rules
text: - `Object.values(union)` returns `any[]` for union types — annotate the local as `unknown[]` and narrow at use.

head: Project Documentation > Community catalog review — preventative rules > Lint / TypeScript rules
text: - Drop redundant `as T` casts after `instanceof T` narrowing.

head: Project Documentation > Community catalog review — preventative rules > Lint / TypeScript rules
text: - Switch over an enum: case labels reference enum members (`TimeGranularity.Daily`), not raw string literals.

head: Project Documentation > Community catalog review — preventative rules > Lint / TypeScript rules
text: - `.catch((error: unknown) => …)`: coerce to `Error` before rethrowing — `error instanceof Error ? error : new Error(String(error))`.

head: Project Documentation > Community catalog review — preventative rules > Lint / TypeScript rules
text: - Async function passed to a void-returning callback: wrap in `void (async () => { … })()`, or widen the callback type to `() => void | Promise<void>` for helpers you own.

head: Project Documentation > Community catalog review — preventative rules > Lint / TypeScript rules
text: - "Legacy" ≠ "@deprecated": types that migration code intentionally keeps reading (V1 on-disk shapes etc.) are **legacy**, not deprecated. Drop the `@deprecated` tag and document them as legacy formats — the tag will otherwise fire the no-deprecated rule on every legitimate consumer.

head: Project Documentation > Community catalog review — preventative rules > CSS rules
text: - **Rules that have to beat Obsidian's own must be unlayered.** Unlayered CSS wins over layered CSS regardless of specificity, and Obsidian's app styles are unlayered — so a rule inside `@layer components` loses to `.setting-item { display: flex }` however many times you double the class. If you wrap this stylesheet in `@layer`, keep the settings overrides outside it. Verify with `getComputedStyle` against a rendered pane; the build, types, linter and tests are all green with a rule that does nothing.

head: Project Documentation > Community catalog review — preventative rules > CSS rules
text: - No hand-written `!important`. Bump specificity with a doubled-class selector (`.foo.foo`) — that goes from 0,1,0 to 0,2,0 and beats most Obsidian defaults (`.setting-item-control button` 0,1,1; `.modal-container .modal` 0,2,0).

head: Project Documentation > Community catalog review — preventative rules > CSS rules
text: - Before removing `!important`, identify what the rule is fighting and verify in a live vault with `getComputedStyle()`. Inline styles always win — keep `!important` only when the source it beats is itself inline.

head: Project Documentation > Community catalog review — preventative rules > CSS rules
text: - When `!important` is genuinely load-bearing (visibility toggles like `.lt-hidden` are the canonical example), restore it and add a `/* stylelint-disable-next-line declaration-no-important -- reason: … */` comment. The reviewer accepts descriptive disables.

head: Project Documentation > Community catalog review — preventative rules > CSS rules
text: - Collapse mirrored 4-value shorthands: `8px 0 12px 0` → `8px 0 12px`.

head: Project Documentation > Community catalog review — preventative rules > CSS rules
text: - `obsidianmd/no-static-styles-assignment` only flags **literal** RHS — dynamic style assignments (template literals with expressions, ternaries, variable RHS) can stay inline. Move only the static ones to a CSS class.

head: Project Documentation > Community catalog review — preventative rules > Logging
text: - The reviewer flags every `console.*` call in shipped code. The template's `src/utils/log.ts` ships with its `console.*` lines commented out — re-enable only behind a `debugModeEnabled` settings toggle when you actually need verbose logs.

head: Project Documentation > Community catalog review — preventative rules > Logging
text: - Route stray `console.error(...)` from catch blocks through `log(msg, 'error', err)` so the suppression stays centralized.

head: Project Documentation > Community catalog review — preventative rules > Build-time inlining
text: - **CHANGELOG.md reaches the "What's new" view through a bundler `define`, not an import.** `import changelog from '../../CHANGELOG.md' with { type: 'text' }` is not resolvable on every Bun version, and the community catalog reviewer builds with one where it is not: the build fails there while succeeding locally. `scripts/build.ts` reads the file and substitutes `__PLUGIN_CHANGELOG__`; `src/app/whats-new.ts` declares the binding inline (not in a `.d.ts`, so `no-undef` sees it) and `typeof`-guards it for the test and dev runtimes, where nothing substitutes.

head: Project Documentation > Community catalog review — preventative rules > Build-time inlining
text: - The curated notes (`NEXT_RELEASE.md`) reach the tab through the same path: `scripts/generate-changelog.ts` writes them into the new CHANGELOG.md section (`applyCuratedNotes`), and the release body is cut from CHANGELOG.md by the tab's own parser (`--release-body`, written to a file for `body_path`, never through a heredoc step output), so the tab and the GitHub release body always carry the same text.

head: Project Documentation > Community catalog review — preventative rules > Build-time inlining
text: - Keep CHANGELOG.md out of `.gitattributes` `export-ignore` regardless — the archive build still needs it to produce non-empty release notes.

head: Project Documentation > Community catalog review — preventative rules > Release workflow
text: - Two-phase by design: a `prepare` job (dispatch on a branch) bumps versions, generates the changelog, commits, tags the release commit (lightweight tag), then re-dispatches the workflow at the tag; the `publish` job (dispatch at the tag, or a bare tag push) builds, attests, and releases at `github.sha == tag commit`. Never build/attest before tagging — the provenance attestation must be bound to the commit the release tag points to, or the community-catalog review rejects the release.

head: Project Documentation > Community catalog review — preventative rules > Release workflow
text: - Attach only `main.js`, `manifest.json`, and `styles.css` (if present) — never a zip. The CI release workflow in this template already does this; don't add zip-upload steps back.

head: Project Documentation > Community catalog review — preventative rules > Release workflow
text: - Build in CI; don't post-edit `main.js`.

head: Project Documentation > Community catalog review — preventative rules > Release workflow
text: - `bun-version-file: package.json` (already wired) keeps Bun pinned across CI and release. Update `packageManager` in `package.json` to bump.

head: Project Documentation > Community catalog review — preventative rules > Release workflow
text: - `actions/attest-build-provenance@v3` (already wired) attaches provenance to release artifacts.
