head: Repository Guidelines > Coding Style & Naming Conventions
text: Follow existing style: two-space indentation and single quotes in JavaScript; four-space indentation in Python. No repository-wide formatter or linter is configured. Use kebab-case Markdown filenames, relative document links, and GitHub LaTeX (`$...$`, `$$...$$`). Add new documents to `README.md` and `llms.txt`.

head: Repository Guidelines > Coding Style & Naming Conventions
text: Keep both `owm_to_mermaid.mjs` copies synchronized. OWM coordinates are `[visibility, evolution]`, each within `[0,1]`; dependencies must satisfy `visibility(source) >= visibility(target)`. Distinguish canonical Wardley concepts from this repository's proposed heuristics.

head: Repository Guidelines > Testing Guidelines
text: Hook tests use `node:test` and strict assertions; follow the `*.test.mjs` naming pattern with descriptive test names. No numeric coverage threshold is configured. Revalidate maps after layout changes and inspect rendered diagrams. Check placement changes against the 25-map benchmark, following `BENCHMARK-METHODOLOGY.md`; map generation must remain blind to reference maps. Comparators overwrite committed summaries; review regenerated diffs deliberately.

head: Repository Guidelines > Commit & Pull Request Guidelines
text: History mixes imperative subjects (`Add`, `Update`, `Patch`) with prefixes such as `feat:` and `docs:`. Use concise, scoped subjects. PRs should explain the change and rationale, link relevant issues, and report validation performed. Include rendered examples for visual changes and benchmark comparisons for placement or grading changes.

head: CLAUDE.md
text: Guidance for Claude Code when working in this repository.

head: CLAUDE.md > Never read secrets from config files
text: **This is the highest-priority rule in this file. It overrides convenience, debugging, and "I just need to see the shape of it."**

head: CLAUDE.md > Never read secrets from config files
text: Real network config files in this repo may still contain live credentials: SSH root passwords (`provisioning_config.ssh_auth.password`), Wi-Fi PSKs (`key` on `wifi-iface` sections), PPPoE credentials (`username`/`password` on `interface` sections), and DDNS/VPN tokens. Prefer `{ "$secret": "wifi/home" }` refs (resolved from the macOS keychain at load) so a grep of the file is not a leak.

head: CLAUDE.md > Never read secrets from config files
text: Do **not** open, `cat`, `grep`, print, or otherwise pull the contents of:

head: CLAUDE.md > Never read secrets from config files
text: - `*.config.json` at the repo root (e.g. `stellenberg.config.json`) — gitignored, mode `0600`, real.

head: CLAUDE.md > Never read secrets from config files
text: - Anything under `configs/` — gitignored, and a separate nested git repo of the user's live network configs.

head: CLAUDE.md > Never read secrets from config files
text: - Any file the user points at as "my config" / "my network config", wherever it lives.

head: CLAUDE.md > Never read secrets from config files
text: If you need to understand config *structure*, use the committed fixtures instead — they contain only placeholder secrets:

head: CLAUDE.md > Never read secrets from config files
text: - `sampleConfigs/basic.json`

head: CLAUDE.md > Never read secrets from config files
text: - `src/tests/main/config.json`, `src/tests/main/config2.json`

head: CLAUDE.md > Never read secrets from config files
text: - `README.md` (documents every top-level key with examples)

head: CLAUDE.md > Never read secrets from config files
text: If a task genuinely cannot proceed without something in a real config file, stop and ask the user to paste the specific non-secret value. Never dump the file to find it.

head: CLAUDE.md > Never read secrets from config files
text: Corollaries: don't echo a secret you happened to encounter, don't write one into a test fixture, commit message, log line, or scratch file, and don't add code that logs `ssh_auth` or wireless `key` values. Do not resolve `$secret` refs or pass `--show-secrets` just to inspect values. Do not dump UCI `wireless`/`network` password fields off a live device either — after provision those values live in UCI because OpenWrt needs them.

head: CLAUDE.md > Never provision without being asked
text: `provision` connects over SSH to real routers and access points and rewrites their UCI config. A bad config can drop the network or lock the user out of a device mid-run.

head: CLAUDE.md > Never provision without being asked
text: - Never run `npm run provision`, `build-images` (non-dry-run), or the built binary against real devices unless the user explicitly asks in that message.

head: CLAUDE.md > Never provision without being asked
text: - `print-uci-commands` is read-only *on the device*, but it still opens an SSH connection to introspect it (see "Device schemas are introspected live"). Treat it as a network action, not a local one.

head: CLAUDE.md > Never provision without being asked
text: - The only fully offline commands are `npm test`, `npm run build`, and `build-images --dry-run` (which only reaches out to the OpenWrt ASU API for profile resolution, and tolerates that failing).

head: CLAUDE.md > What this project is
text: A CLI that takes one UCI-like JSON file describing an entire network — every device, its packages, firmware version, UCI config and arbitrary files — and provisions it to OpenWrt devices over SSH. The JSON is conditionally composed with `.if` / `.overrides` keys so a single file drives routers, switches and dumb APs of different models.

head: CLAUDE.md > What this project is
text: Published to GitHub Releases as standalone binaries (macOS/Linux/Windows) via `@yao-pkg/pkg`.

head: CLAUDE.md > Open work
text: Tracked in `TODO.md` at the repo root. Add to it what is found and deferred, and remove an item in the commit that finishes it.

head: CLAUDE.md > Commands
text: Node 24 (`.node-version`), TypeScript 6, CommonJS. `ts-node --transpile-only` for the dev scripts, so type errors do **not** surface there — run `npm run build` to typecheck.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture
text: The pipeline, in dependency order:

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture
text: 1. **`bin/index.ts`** → **`src/cli.ts`** — `bin/index.ts` (Node) and `bin/qjs.ts` (QuickJS) are only entry points: each builds its platform (see "The platform boundary") and calls `run({ argv, platform })`. The CLI lives in `src/cli.ts`, as command specs parsed by the small `src/args.ts` (no commander). It reads the config file via `loadOncConfig`: `parseConfigJson` (`src/parseJson.ts`: JSONC — comments and trailing commas allowed — via `jsonc-parser`, with `file:line:col` errors that read the same on every engine; device output goes through the strict `parseJson`), resolve `{ "$secret": "name" }` from the macOS keychain (`src/resolveSecrets.ts`), then `parseSchema(oncConfigSchema, ...)`. `print-uci-commands` and `build-images --dry-run` redact resolved values unless `--show-secrets`.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture
text: 2. **`src/oncConfigSchema.ts`** — zod schema for the *input* JSON ("ONC config"): `version`, `devices`, `package_profiles`, `files`, `configs_to_not_reset`, `config`. `.strict()` throughout, so unknown keys are hard errors by design.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture
text: 3. **`src/getDeviceSchema.ts`** — builds a `DeviceSchema` (ports, radios, CPU port, firmware version) for each device.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture
text: 4. **`src/resolveOncConfig.ts`** — collapses `.if` / `.overrides` for one device. `conditionMatches` evaluates conditions against `device.tag.*`, `device.hostname`, `device.ipaddr`, `device.model_id`, `device.version`, `device.sw_config`, parsed by `src/condition.ts` (a small recursive-descent parser: `==`, `!=`, `in [...]`, `AND`/`OR`/`NOT` and their `&&`/`||`/`!` spellings, parentheses, quoted strings with escapes). A tag the device does not set is absent (`==` false, `!=` true) rather than an error, since every device shares the conditions; an unknown built-in name still throws, to catch typos.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture
text: 5. **`src/getOpenWrtConfig.ts`** — the interesting one. Turns abstractions into concrete UCI: expands `@cpu_port`, resolves `"*"` / `"*t"` port wildcards to actual unused physical ports (at most one device section per device may use `"*"`: only explicit lists count as uses, so two would each claim every free port), maps `bridge-vlan` (DSA) vs `switch_vlan` (legacy swconfig) depending on `deviceSchema.sw_config`, assigns `.name`s, injects the hostname, and expands `wifi-iface` across radios by band.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture
text: 6. **`src/getOpenWrtState.ts`** — adds packages to install/uninstall, which config sections to reset, and resolved `files`.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture
text: 7. **`src/getUciCommands.ts`** + **`src/getDeviceScript.ts`** + **`src/uci.ts`** — emit the scripts, in three parts that `provision` runs separately. **Prepare** (`getPrepareCommands`): discard every pending UCI change (clean start, see below) → package install/removal → `reload_config` (baseline refresh, see below). **Stage** (`getStageCommands`, built from the device's config as read *after* prepare): one `uci batch` that deletes every section `configs_to_not_reset` does not keep, by exact name, then sets every declared section → file writes (each with its optional `run_after`). **Finalise** (`getFinaliseCommands`): `uci commit` per changed config → `reload_config`. Then each `run_after_reload`, over the *reconnected* session: `reload_config` is what can sever the link, and once dropbear exits the next marker `printf` in `execScript` takes SIGPIPE and kills the script, so a hook after the reload in that same script would be silently dropped on exactly the runs that reshape networking. `getDeviceScript` concatenates all of it for the dry run (see "The wipe").

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture
text: 8. **`src/execScript.ts`** — runs the whole command list as one script: it is written to a `0600` file in `/tmp` over stdin (`cat >`), then run as `sh <file> < /dev/null`. Do not "simplify" this into a single joined exec string: dropbear rejects exec requests over ~9 KB and drops the connection on larger ones, while a real provision script is comfortably past that. Nor pipe it straight into `sh`: commands that read stdin then swallow the rest of the script. `set -e` plus a marker echoed after each command preserves per-command failure granularity.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture
text: 9. **`src/devicePhases.ts`** + **`src/provisionNetwork.ts`** — provisioning as explicit phases over a `DeviceRun` record: `planDevice` (verify the board id, read state, warn about removals and discarded changes) → `armRollback` → `configureDevice` (prepare, read the config, stage, read back and verify) → `ensureTimeToConfirm` → `commitDevice` → `confirmDevice` → `disarmDevice` → `runPostReloadHooks`, plus the ways out: `revertStaged` (nothing committed), `rollBackNow` and `waitForRecovery`. Each phase returns an updated record or throws a `ProvisionFailure` saying whether the device's change was committed. `provisionNetwork` runs them across every device as **one change** (see "Several devices, one change"); a single device is N = 1. Files are written *before* `uci commit` so a write failure leaves the revert effective. Every question asked of a device is a typed probe in **`src/deviceProbes.ts`** (see "Device probes").

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > The intent layer and the web UI
text: An *intent file* (`{"schema": 1, ...}`, `src/intent/schema.ts`) describes the network in the user's terms: site, devices (name + role), internet, the home network, Wi-Fi, DNS. It holds decisions only, **never device facts** (model, ports, radios, version): those are read from the devices at provision time. `compileIntent` (`src/intent/compile.ts`) is pure: each module in `src/intent/features/` returns a fragment of low-level config and they are merged in order. Anything device-specific is left to the engine as a condition (`.if device.model_id == ...`) or a placeholder (`"*"` ports, `@wan_port`, `@cpu_port`). `loadOncConfig` compiles an intent file transparently, so every command takes one; `compile` prints the result. There is no escape hatch: a setting the intent cannot express does not exist, and because of the wipe, the features plus their defaults must produce a complete working device. The intent file has its own version (`schema`); `src/intent/migrations.ts` upgrades older files one version at a time when read (the CLI, the API, the provision check and the diff all migrate), and a save writes the current version. Bumping the format means adding a migration, never breaking an old file.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > The intent layer and the web UI
text: Networks: one untagged main network (bridge VLAN 1, the one devices are managed over) and any number on their own VLANs, all carried on every port (main untagged, others tagged), on DSA (`bridge-vlan`) and swconfig (`switch_vlan` + `br-lan.N`) alike. Each has a hidden stable `id` (Wi-Fi refers to it; it names the UCI interface and DHCP section) and a purpose, which only sets up its firewall zone when the network is created (`zoneForPurpose`, applied by `withNetworkZone` in `src/intent/edits.ts`) and presets Wi-Fi client isolation.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > The intent layer and the web UI
text: The firewall (`src/intent/firewall.ts`, compiled one to one by `features/firewall.ts`) is OpenWrt's model as LuCI shows it: the target user is an OpenWrt / UniFi-console user, so keep its concepts and structure, polished, rather than inventing abstractions. Defaults; zones (WAN among them, covering the internet interfaces; each with input/output/forward, masquerading, MSS clamping, covered networks; an unnamed zone is known by its networks' names); forwardings; traffic rules in order, OpenWrt's stock ones and a restricted zone's DHCP/DNS/NTP/ICMPv6 allowances included as ordinary rules (source a zone or `"*"`; destination a zone, `"router"` for fw4 input, or `"*"`; protocols a list, `all` for any: fw4's default when unset is tcp+udp); and port forwards (fw4 `redirect`, into the zone of the target's network). Every network is in exactly one zone; deleting a zone removes the forwardings and rules naming it, as LuCI does. The UI mirrors LuCI's Network › Firewall: General settings (defaults above the zones table, "zone ⇒ forwardings"), Port forwards, Traffic rules; the zone page is LuCI's zone editor.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > The intent layer and the web UI
text: The web UI edits the intent file and nothing else. `src/server/handlers.ts` is the whole backend (GET/PUT `/api/intent` plus the built UI's static files), transport-free: `onc ui` serves it with Node on a Mac (loopback, Host/Origin-checked against DNS rebinding), `onc cgi` answers one request under uhttpd on a router (QuickJS cannot listen on a socket). A save is validated by the intent schema and by compiling, then written atomically with mode `0600` (it holds the Wi-Fi passwords). **The API has no authentication yet: do not expose `cgi` on a router** (see `TODO.md`).

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > The intent layer and the web UI
text: `ui/` is React + Mantine + React Query + React Hook Form + React Router, built by `scripts/build-ui.js` (esbuild) into `dist/ui`. Layers: `data/` (the only HTTP code, as React Query hooks), `kit/` (presentation: `SettingsPage`, `Section`, `SettingRow`, `DataTable`, `ConfirmButton`, `LogView`), `form/` (fields bound to the intent by name, e.g. `<TextField name="site.name" />`, validated with the same zod schema as the server; `ListPage` turns a `defineList` spec into a table page, per-item pages and a `new` page; the new page edits a copy of the draft with the item appended, through the same editor, and only its Add puts the item into the draft), `provision/` (the header button and its panel), and `pages/`, which stay declarative: which settings, in what order, labelled how. Inputs should make invalid values impossible, not just rejected: dropdowns and structured fields (`SubnetField`, `DurationField`) over free text, with every rule in the shared schema so the server enforces it too; the draft is validated on load, so problems already in a file show at once. URLs are relative and routing is a hash router, so the same build works at `/` and under `/cgi-bin/onc/`. Every API write must carry `X-ONC: 1` (CSRF). `src/intent/timezones.ts` and `countries.ts` are generated by `scripts/gen-timezones.js`.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > The intent layer and the web UI
text: The provision panel diffs the draft against the last provisioned intent with `src/intent/diff.ts`, labelled by `src/intent/fields.ts` (secrets only ever read "Changed"). A provision runs as `selfCommand() provision <snapshot>` in the background, its state in `<intent>.state/` (`src/server/provisionJob.ts`); a successful run makes the snapshot `live.json`. The API refuses to provision a draft that does not validate and compile.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > The platform boundary
text: Nothing in `src/` outside `src/platforms/` may import a Node built-in or a Node-only package (`node-ssh`), or touch `process` — a test enforces it (`platformBoundary.test.ts`). The goal is one bundle that runs under Node on a workstation and under QuickJS on an OpenWrt device. All runtime access goes through a `Platform` (`src/platform.ts`): files, `sha256`, HTTP, local processes, `connect` (returns a `Session`, shaped like node-ssh's `execCommand`/`dispose`), env, sleep and exit. There is no global: the entry point builds one (`nodePlatform` or `qjsPlatform`) and passes it down, and each function takes only what it uses, typed `Pick<Platform, ...>` (or just a `sleep`), so a test can hand in a fake. Tests pass `nodePlatform` explicitly.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Running under QuickJS
text: `npm run bundle` builds `dist/qjs/openwrt-configurator.mjs` from `bin/qjs.ts` with the options in `scripts/bundle.js`, which the parity test reuses; run it with `qjs --module`. Bundles prefer packages' ESM builds (`mainFields: module, main`): jsonc-parser's UMD `main` does a dynamic `require` QuickJS cannot satisfy. The QuickJS platform is `src/platforms/qjs/`: `process.ts` (temp-file stdio, spawn), `files.ts` (files and hashing), `http.ts` (curl), `ssh.ts` (transports), `runtime.ts` (typed `os`), assembled in `index.ts`. Things that differ from Node and are easy to trip over:

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Running under QuickJS
text: - **QuickJS has only `console.log`**, no `setTimeout`, `Buffer` or `TextEncoder`/`TextDecoder`. `qjsGlobals.ts` (imported first by every QuickJS entry) polyfills `console.warn`/`error` to stderr; the boundary test bans the rest outside `platforms/` (`src/utf8.ts` covers the UTF-8 needs).

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Running under QuickJS
text: - **`@types/node` owns the module name `"os"`**, so QuickJS's `os` is typed as the global `QuickJsOs` interface in `quickjs.d.ts` and cast on import.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Running under QuickJS
text: - **SSH is a spawned client per command**: `dbclient` when present (OpenWrt), else OpenSSH. A password reaches OpenSSH through a generated `SSH_ASKPASS` helper and dbclient through `DROPBEAR_PASSWORD`, never argv. Host keys are checked; see "Host keys".

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Running under QuickJS
text: - **Exit status comes from a marker, not the client.** Each remote command is wrapped as `( cmd ) ; printf '__ONC_EXIT__%s' $? >&2`, because both clients reuse the remote exit codes for their own failures (OpenSSH 255, dbclient 1). No marker means the command never finished, reported as `code: null` just like node-ssh's dropped channel.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Running under QuickJS
text: - **Local mode**: when the target host is one of this machine's addresses, commands run through `sh -c` with the same wrapping, so a device can provision itself. Its session is marked `local`, and commit-confirm then needs more than a reconnect, since a local session never drops: `reachableSession` also requires the device's own address to answer SSH (`sshAnswersCommand`, busybox `nc` killed after 2 s, looking for dropbear's `SSH-` banner). That catches a lost address or dropbear no longer listening; it cannot catch a firewall or cabling change that only affects other hosts. Run a local provision under `setsid`: if it is started from an SSH session that the reload drops, it dies and the watchdog rolls back.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Running under QuickJS
text: - **Secrets** come from the macOS keychain on macOS and from `/etc/onc/secrets.json` (`{ "name": "value" }`, must be `0600`; `ONC_SECRETS_FILE` overrides) elsewhere. Its parse errors deliberately carry no excerpt.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Running under QuickJS
text: - HTTP uses `curl`; sha256 uses `sha256sum` or `shasum`.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Packaging
text: A pushed tag runs `.github/workflows/release.yml`. Besides the `pkg` binaries it attaches the QuickJS bundle, then:

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Packaging
text: - **OpenWrt feed** — `packaging/openwrt/build.sh` builds `packaging/openwrt/openwrt-configurator/` (`PKGARCH:=all`, `DEPENDS:=+quickjs`) in the `openwrt/sdk:x86-64-v25.12.5` image and signs the index with the `OPENWRT_FEED_KEY` secret (an EC P-256 PEM). The feed and its public key are published to GitHub Pages under `/openwrt/`. The key must never change: devices trust the feed by it. The SDK does not sign the `.apk` itself; apk verifies it through the signed index's hash, like OpenWrt's own feeds. Without a key the script generates a throwaway one, fine for local testing only. The SDK warns that `quickjs` "does not exist" (it lacks the packages feed); the dependency is still recorded.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Packaging
text: - **Homebrew** — `packaging/homebrew/render.sh` fills `openwrt-configurator.rb.in` with the release URL and sha256, and the workflow pushes it to `jasrusable/homebrew-tap` over SSH with a write deploy key on that repo (the `HOMEBREW_TAP_DEPLOY_KEY` secret). The formula's test checks `--version` against the tag, which is why the workflow also refuses a tag that disagrees with `package.json` and `src/cli.ts`.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Packaging
text: To test the package without a device, install it into `openwrt/rootfs:x86-64-v25.12.5` from a `file://` feed.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Host keys
text: Trust on first use, everywhere. A device's key is recorded the first time and a different key is refused (`hostKeyChangedMessage` says which line to delete after a reflash). Node (ssh2's `hostVerifier`) and OpenSSH (`StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new`, `HashKnownHosts=no`) share `~/.config/openwrt-configurator/known_hosts` (`ONC_KNOWN_HOSTS` overrides) in plain OpenSSH format; `src/knownHosts.ts` holds the pure logic. Once a host's key type is known, Node negotiates only that type, so a server cannot sidestep the check by offering another — `checkHostKey` treats an unseen type for a known host as changed. On a device, `dbclient` keeps its own `~/.ssh/known_hosts` (single `-y`: accepts new, refuses changed).

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Several devices, one change
text: `provisionNetwork` makes a run all-or-nothing: plan every device (nothing changes), arm every device's watchdog (snapshots only), configure and commit each, then confirm **all** of them before disarming any. The window is `--confirm-timeout` × number of devices, and the commit of any device is refused if the earliest deadline leaves too little time to confirm. On a failure in configure or commit, devices already committed are rolled back immediately (`rollBackNow`: the watchdog sleeps in the background with its pid in `sleepPidFile`, so killing that sleep makes it run its restore now) and untouched ones are disarmed. If a device cannot be reached to confirm, the others are rolled back now and it rolls itself back at its deadline. Order matters, since changing a device can cut the path to others: devices are provisioned in config order except that the workstation's default gateway (`src/gateway.ts`) and the device running the tool (a `local` session) go last (`provisioningOrder`). The rig's `network` job checks a lockout on one device rolls back both.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Commit-confirm
text: Because committing `network`/`firewall` can sever the connection doing the provisioning, `provision` snapshots state, starts a detached `setsid` watchdog, commits, then reconnects (retrying, since `reload_config` briefly drops the network) and touches its confirm flag to disarm it. If the tool cannot get back in, the device rolls back and reboots itself. `--no-confirm` disables it; `--confirm-timeout` changes the 90 s window (minimum 60: the window is timed from arming, so it must cover configuring *and* leave 30 s to confirm). `ONC_TEST_MIN_CONFIRM_WINDOW` (seconds, at least 10) lowers that 30 s for tests and prints a warning; never use it against real devices.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Commit-confirm
text: **Confirming waits for services to settle.** `reload_config` only signals services; procd restarts them afterwards. Reconnecting straight after the commit raced that: on the test rig, a config that dropped dropbear's section was confirmed while the old dropbear was still listening, then locked the device out a second later. So `reconnectSettled` reconnects, waits on the device until procd's service table (`ubus call service list`, which carries every instance's pid and parameters) has been unchanged for three seconds — procd runs reload triggers after `PROCD_RELOAD_DELAY`, 1 s — then reconnects *again* and confirms over that fresh session. The wait is capped at 20 s and by the window.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Commit-confirm
text: What the rollback covers, best to worst:

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Commit-confirm
text:
| | Rewound? |
|---|---|
| `/etc/config` | Yes — snapshotted and restored wholesale |
| Managed files that existed before | Yes — archived with `tar`, restored |
| Managed files this run creates | Yes — deleted |
| Packages this run installs | Yes — `apk del` needs no network |
| Packages this run removes | Usually — staged beforehand, see below |

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Commit-confirm
text: **Package staging.** Before removing anything — while the link is still up — `provision` runs `apk fetch` over the whole `apk del --simulate --rdepends` cascade into the rollback directory. A rollback then reinstalls with `apk add --allow-untrusted --repositories-file /dev/null`, which resolves with **no repositories configured at all** (verified on-device), so it works with the network down.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Commit-confirm
text: Package changes are undone in reverse: newly installed packages are removed *first*, then removed ones reinstalled, because the two can conflict (`wpad-mbedtls` and `wpad-basic-mbedtls` do).

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Commit-confirm
text: Fast-moving feeds drop old builds, so where the exact installed version is no longer published `apk fetch` takes the newest available — LuCI especially. A rollback therefore restores a working package set, not necessarily byte-identical versions. The `firewall4` cascade is 21 packages / 380 KB / ~3s on the test device.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Commit-confirm
text: `provision` prints the full removal cascade before acting: on a stock image, removing `firewall4` takes 21 packages with it, `uhttpd` and all of LuCI included, because `luci-light` depends on `luci-app-firewall`.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Commit-confirm
text: Rollback paths are per-run (`/tmp/onc-*-<runId>`). With fixed paths, a second provision inside the confirm window would clear the flag that had already disarmed an earlier watchdog, which would then wake and restore a stale snapshot over a healthy device.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Commit-confirm
text: `at` and `nohup` are **not** present on a stock OpenWrt image — `setsid` is, and a process started that way outlives the SSH session. Note that killing the CLI between arming and confirming will let the watchdog fire.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Commit-confirm
text: `src/getBuildPlan.ts` + `src/buildImage.ts` are a separate branch off step 2: they resolve version/packages/LAN/timezone into an ASU (firmware-selector) build request with a generated UCI-defaults bootstrap script, poll the build, and download + sha256-verify the sysupgrade image.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > How changes actually get applied
text: `uci commit` writes `/etc/config`; `reload_config` is what makes services re-read it. It diffs `uci show <pkg>` against `/var/run/config.md5` using `md5sum -c`, and fires a `config.change` ubus event per changed package. Services pick that up via `procd_add_reload_trigger`. All five first-class packages are covered: netifd registers `network` **and** `wireless` (and `wifi reload` is literally `ubus call network reload`, so wireless needs no special handling), dnsmasq registers `dhcp`/`system`, firewall4 registers `firewall`, and `/etc/init.d/system` registers `system`.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > How changes actually get applied
text: **`md5sum -c` never checks a file missing from the baseline.** The baseline is written only by `/etc/init.d/boot` and by `reload_config` itself — installing a package does not refresh it, since `default_postinst` runs `<init> enable/start` but never `reload_config`. So a config file that first appears during a provision would get no reload event at all on that run: the service would start on its shipped defaults and keep them until a reboot, while `uci show` reported the intended config. That is why the script runs `reload_config` once after the package step and **before** any staging (`baselineRefreshCommands`). It must stay before staging — `reload_config` compares `uci show`, which includes uncommitted deltas, so refreshing it later would record this run's own changes as the baseline and the closing reload would fire nothing.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > How changes actually get applied
text: Corollary: don't use a `files` entry to create something under `/etc/config`. Files are written after staging, so a config created that way misses the baseline refresh. Drive UCI through `config` instead.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Each run starts from committed state, and commits by name
text: The tool owns the device's config, so before staging anything the script discards **every** pending UCI change on the device, whoever made it (`revertPendingCommands`; the package list comes from `uci changes` on the device). The same command is the abort path and the watchdog's revert. It has to be everything: a run that dies before it can revert leaves deltas in `/tmp/.uci` that the watchdog's `/etc/config` restore does not touch; `default_postinst` ends with a bare `uci commit` for any package shipping `/etc/uci-defaults`, so a package install mid-run would commit whatever was staged anywhere; and a rollback's own `reload_config` reads deltas on top of the restored files. It must run before the packages step. `provision` first prints what it is discarding, as per-package counts only (`summarisePendingChanges`) — staged values can be secrets.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Each run starts from committed state, and commits by name
text: LuCI's unsaved changes are **not** affected: rpcd stages them per session under `/var/run/rpcd/uci-<session>`, which plain `uci changes`/`uci revert` never see (verified on 25.12.5; the rig checks it).

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Each run starts from committed state, and commits by name
text: The commit stays `uci commit <pkg>` per changed config (`changedConfigs`: configs with a section to wipe, plus configs the run declares sections in) rather than a bare `uci commit`, so it never commits anything it did not stage.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > The wipe
text: The config file is the whole truth: every run leaves each device's UCI config exactly as declared, whatever it held before, except what `configs_to_not_reset` keeps (`<config>.*`, or `<config>.<section type>` — types, not section names). So `configureDevice`:

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > The wipe
text: 1. runs the prepare step — packages are what change config behind our back (postinst, uci-defaults), and they can bring whole new configs and section types;

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > The wipe
text: 2. reads every config with the `uciConfigs` probe (one `uci export` per `/etc/config` file, staged changes included; a full `uci export` silently skips a config it cannot parse, so per-file it can name it) and parses it in `src/uci.ts`, quote-aware — a multi-line value can contain a line reading `config x`;

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > The wipe
text: 3. stages the wipe and the declared config in one batch (anonymous sections are deleted as `@type[0]`, once each, after the named ones);

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > The wipe
text: 4. reads it back and **verifies** (`verifyConfigs`): every config not kept must hold exactly the declared sections, in order, with exactly the declared options, lists as lists. A declared section of a kept type is merged, so only its options are checked. Any difference reverts with nothing committed; messages name sections and options, never values.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > The wipe
text: The wipe used to be computed at plan time from section *types* and deleted with shell loops: sections a package added mid-run survived it, a staged deletion hid a type from it, and a device value could inject into the script. Verification is what makes the guarantee checked rather than reasoned. An unreadable config that is not kept stops the run. A keep entry naming a config the device lacks is warned about (typos there lock you out). `uci set` of an empty value deletes the option, so `declaredConfigs` leaves empty values and empty lists out. The dry run reads the config before packages are installed, so it does not show their sections being wiped.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > The wipe
text: Both are guarded with `if [ -f /etc/config/<pkg> ]`: `uci commit` and `uci revert` both exit 1 on a config that is not present (verified on 25.12.5) and the script runs under `set -e`, so one absent config would otherwise abort the provision — or stop a rollback's remaining reverts partway.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > The wipe
text: `getFinaliseCommands(state)` is derived from state rather than being a constant, so `planDevice` must use it (not a fixed length) to split the configure phase from the finalise phase.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Dropbear does not kill your command
text: When the connection drops, dropbear does **not** signal the running command — its only `kill()` is for an explicit client signal request, there is no `setsid`/`setpgid`, and a non-pty exec has no controlling terminal. OpenWrt defaults are `SSHKeepAlive:300`, `IdleTimeout:0`, so it may not even notice a blackholed peer for five minutes. Measured on 25.12.5: a remote loop writing only to a file finished 12/12 iterations after its client was killed; an identical loop writing to stdout died at 3/12.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Dropbear does not kill your command
text: Two consequences. The commit step is safe — `reload_config` writes nothing to stdout, so it runs to completion even if committing severs the link. But the per-command marker in `execScript` means the configure phase dies by SIGPIPE within about one command of a *clean* disconnect, and on a blackholed network an abandoned script can keep executing for up to `SSHKeepAlive` while the watchdog is already restoring `/etc/config`.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Two parallel schema hierarchies
text: Under `src/configSchemas/<package>/`, every UCI section has **two** zod schemas:

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Two parallel schema hierarchies
text: - `networkInterfaceSchema` — the strict *output* shape, used by `openWrtConfigSchema` to validate what gets turned into `uci` commands.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Two parallel schema hierarchies
text: - `oncNetworkInterfaceSchema` — the *input* shape: same fields, but `.partial()` and extended with `.if` / `.overrides` / `.name`.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Two parallel schema hierarchies
text: The `index.ts` in each package folder wires them up with helpers from `src/utils.ts` (`sectionSchema`, `oncSectionSchema`, `configSchema`, `makeOncConfigSchema`, `getExtensionObject`).

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Two parallel schema hierarchies
text: **Adding support for a new UCI option means editing both schemas.** Adding a whole new section type also means adding it to that package's `index.ts`. What gets wiped does not depend on these schemas: it is read from the device (see "The wipe").

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Device probes
text: Everything the tool asks a device is a `Probe<T>` in `src/deviceProbes.ts`: a command plus the parse of its result — board.json, radios, every config (`uciConfigs`), the release, installed packages, the managed-files manifest, the removal cascade, pending changes, the staged-package count, whether an address answers SSH, the services settling, and disarming the watchdog. `runProbes(session, {...})` sends several in one round trip (each in a subshell, outputs split on a `__ONC_PROBE__<status>` marker line), which matters under QuickJS where every round trip is a new SSH process. **node-ssh trims command output and the QuickJS transports do not**, so the marker split must not depend on leading or trailing newlines (a test covers it). Parsers are tested against recorded output, without SSH. The script protocol (`execScript`'s markers) and the transport's `__ONC_EXIT__` are separate: they wrap commands rather than ask questions.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Quoting
text: Every value from the config that reaches a shell or `uci batch` goes through `shellQuote` (`src/shell.ts`): UCI values and list items, file paths, modes, package names. `uci batch` accepts the same `'\''` form as sh (verified on 25.12.5); before this, any value containing `'` aborted the provision. UCI *names* cannot be quoted, so `getUciCommands` rejects a package, section type or option name that is not a plain word; package names, file modes and paths are validated by the schema. `shell.test.ts` runs hostile strings through a real `sh`, and the rig sets a value with quotes and `$(...)` on every client path.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Device schemas are introspected live
text: `getDeviceSchema` normally SSHes into the device and derives everything from it:

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Device schemas are introspected live
text: - `/etc/board.json` → ports, and whether the device is legacy swconfig (`.switch` present) or DSA.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Device schemas are introspected live
text: - `ubus call uci get '{"config":"wireless","type":"wifi-device"}'` → radios (band, path, type).

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Device schemas are introspected live
text: - `/etc/openwrt_release` → `DISTRIB_RELEASE`.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Device schemas are introspected live
text: The checked-in `deviceSchemas/*.json` files are only used when `getDeviceSchema` is given `local` (a file reader, e.g. `nodePlatform`) — that path exists for the tests. Two are old (21.02 EdgeRouter X and Archer C50); `friendlyarm,nanopi-r6s` and `zyxel,nwa50ax-pro` were captured from the user's own devices with `capture-device-schema <config>` (read-only, like `print-uci-commands`; a schema holds port names, radio band/type/path and the version — no option values). Don't assume it's the normal path.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Managed files
text: `files` entries are written via a quoted heredoc (not `base64` — busybox on small-flash builds often lacks the applet). The set of written paths is recorded in `/etc/onc/managed_files` on the device, so a file removed from the config is `rm -f`'d on the next provision. `run_after` runs immediately after the write.

head: CLAUDE.md > Tests
text: `ava` with `ts-node/register/transpile-only`, in `src/tests/main/`. Note ava's default glob picks up **everything** under a `tests/` directory, so `network2.ts` is a test file despite the missing `.test` suffix.

head: CLAUDE.md > Tests
text: Most tests are golden-ish: load `config.json` / `config2.json`, build the OpenWrt config against a local device schema, and assert on the resulting structure. `files.test.ts`, `uci.test.ts` and `resolveSecrets.test.ts` are focused unit tests. All are offline — no test touches the network or the keychain (lookups are injected).

head: CLAUDE.md > Tests
text: `qjsParity.test.ts` runs the same work under Node and QuickJS and requires identical results: 11 CLI invocations (stdout, stderr and exit code), a report of everything the pipeline derives from the fixtures (`src/tests/helpers/parityReport.ts`), and the session layer over the local `sh` transport. It bundles with esbuild on the fly (the QuickJS side with `scripts/bundle.js`, exactly as shipped) and is skipped where `qjs` is not installed (`brew install quickjs`). Shared test code goes under `src/tests/helpers/`, which ava does not treat as test files. A platform difference users can see, such as a file error's wording, should be normalised in the platforms rather than tolerated here.

head: CLAUDE.md > Tests
text: `hardware.test.ts` covers the hardware abstraction one rule at a time with small made-up device schemas (`*`/`*t` ports, `@cpu_port`, `bridge-vlan` and `switch_vlan`, radio fan-out by band, distinct names for two radios in one band); `hardwareSnapshots.test.ts` snapshots the sample config's UCI commands on the two captured real devices, so a change to that logic shows up as a snapshot diff (`npx ava --update-snapshots` when intended). `provisionNetwork.test.ts` drives the phases against `src/tests/helpers/fakeDevice.ts` — a device that speaks the tool's protocol, keeps a small UCI model it applies the staged `uci batch` to (so verification reads back what the batch really did), and records what happens to it — on a virtual clock (the run takes `now` and `sleep`), so failure paths are tested without Docker.

head: CLAUDE.md > Tests
text: CI (`.github/workflows/test.yml`, on push to `main` and on pull requests; the release workflow calls it as its gate) runs the tests, `npm run typecheck`, and the rig. It builds `qjs` through the `setup-quickjs` composite action (`scripts/install-quickjs.sh`) — exactly the version OpenWrt 25.12 ships, hash-pinned — and the parity test *fails* rather than skips when `CI` is set and `qjs` is missing. ava's timeout is 2 min: the parity tests run processes synchronously and are slow on emulated or loaded runners.

head: CLAUDE.md > Tests
text: **Testing provision without a real device.** `scripts/rig-test.sh` automates all of this and runs in CI: each SSH client path gets its own device and controller, in parallel; the router path (`dbclient`) gets every scenario, the others those where their client behaves differently. It sets `ONC_TEST_MIN_CONFIRM_WINDOW=15` with `--confirm-timeout 30` so rollbacks do not wait out the real window — no shorter, or the settle step's reserve for the final reconnect leaves it no time and it is skipped, which is exactly the check the wipe scenario exercises. On Apple Silicon it uses the native `armsr-armv8` rootfs, which is labelled `linux/aarch64_generic` so it must run with no `--platform`. `openwrt/rootfs:x86-64-v25.12.5` boots fully under Docker with `--privileged ... /sbin/init` (procd, ubusd, netifd, dropbear, a real `board.json` with model `orbstack,virt` under OrbStack). netifd moves eth0 into `br-lan` at 192.168.1.1, so set `network.lan` to the container's Docker address on `eth0` directly. OrbStack does not route the Mac to container IPs, so run the tool from a second container on the same network: another OpenWrt rootfs with `apk add quickjs` (dbclient path; delete `/usr/bin/dbclient` and `apk add openssh-client` for the OpenSSH path), or `node:24-alpine` with `NODE_PATH` at the repo's `node_modules`. A config that does not declare `dropbear` must list it in `configs_to_not_reset`, or the declarative reset deletes its section and the rig locks itself out — which is how the settle bug above was found. Wait for `board.json` (generated late in boot), not just for dropbear and netifd, which are up almost at once.

head: CLAUDE.md > Gotchas
text: - **The CLI version is duplicated.** `package.json` `version` and the `version` in the spec in `src/cli.ts` must be bumped together.

head: CLAUDE.md > Gotchas
text: - **Releases are tag-driven.** `.github/workflows/release.yml` fires on a pushed `X.Y.Z` or `vX.Y.Z` tag, runs `test.yml` (tests, typecheck, rig) as a gate, checks the tag against the version, then publishes the binaries, the bundle, the OpenWrt feed and the Homebrew formula (see "Packaging").

head: CLAUDE.md > Gotchas
text: - **`print-uci-commands` builds against the live SSH session**, the same as `provision`. It used to call `getDeviceScript({ state })` with no session, so package diffing never ran: every package the config named was printed as an install and every removal as a removal, regardless of what was on the device. That reported a 21-package `apk del` cascade for packages that were not installed at all. Keep the session open until the script is built, or the dry run stops matching what a provision would do. Resolved `$secret` values are redacted in the printed script; `--show-secrets` turns that off — don't pass it unless the user asks.

head: CLAUDE.md > Gotchas
text: - **`$secret` refs are resolved once at load** (`loadOncConfig`), before schema parse. The rest of the pipeline still sees plaintext strings. `secrets set` prompts for a value and stores it; there is no `get`.

head: CLAUDE.md > Gotchas
text: - **`npm start` is dead.** It points at `./src/index.ts`, which does not exist.

head: CLAUDE.md > Gotchas
text: - **`src/config.json` is a stray scratch config**, not used by the tests or the CLI.

head: CLAUDE.md > Gotchas
text: - **`images/` is gitignored** — built sysupgrade images bake hostnames and LAN IPs into the artifact.

head: CLAUDE.md > Gotchas
text: - **`uci batch` exits 0 even when an operation fails**, reporting the error only on stderr. `getDeviceScript` therefore captures stderr and fails the step if it is non-empty. Don't switch that back to checking the exit code. Only `set`/`add_list` go through the batch — the reset loops stay outside it, because a delete of a missing section is expected there rather than an error.

head: CLAUDE.md > Gotchas
text: - **`getInstalledPackages` uses `apk info`**, which prints bare names. It previously parsed `apk list --installed` by splitting on the last `-`, which mangled 86% of names (`curl-8.19.0-r2` → `curl-8.19.0`) so nothing ever matched: removals were silently dropped and installs re-ran every provision.

head: CLAUDE.md > Gotchas
text: - **Code style:** heavy functional composition — `reduce`/spread over mutation, arrow-function exports, object-destructured named parameters (`({ oncConfig, deviceConfig })`). Match it. Comments are sparse and explain *why*, usually a device-level quirk worth preserving.

head: Gooey Engineering Style
text:
Gooey is designed for safety, performance, and developer experience, in that order.
Readability is necessary, but it is a means to those goals rather than the goal itself.

head: Gooey Engineering Style
text:
These are engineering rules, not suggestions. `MUST`, `MUST NOT`, `SHOULD`, and `MAY`
have their usual normative meanings. When a rule cannot be followed, document why at the
call site and obtain explicit agreement before merging the exception.

head: Gooey Engineering Style
text:
Simplicity is not the first attempt. It is the result of understanding the problem, sketching
alternatives, and finding one design that advances safety, performance, and usability at the
same time. Spend design effort before implementation, while change is still cheap.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 1. Zero Technical Debt
text:
Solve discovered problems correctly now. Do not defer known correctness risks, unbounded
work, allocation jitter, latency spikes, or accidental exponential complexity. A second pass
may never happen.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 1. Zero Technical Debt
text:
New code MUST leave its area more correct than it found it. Do not hide debt behind TODOs,
follow-up issues, comments, feature flags, or "temporary" abstractions. Missing features are
acceptable. Unsound foundations are not.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 2. Static Memory Allocation
text: All Gooey-owned memory MUST be allocated during initialization. After initialization:

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 2. Static Memory Allocation
text: - No heap allocation is permitted.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 2. Static Memory Allocation
text: - No object may be freed and replaced.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 2. Static Memory Allocation
text: - No lazy initialization is permitted.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 2. Static Memory Allocation
text: - No cache miss may allocate.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 2. Static Memory Allocation
text: - No render, layout, input, accessibility, animation, asset, or callback path may allocate.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 2. Static Memory Allocation
text: - Shutdown MAY free resources only after event and frame processing have stopped.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 2. Static Memory Allocation
text: The initialization boundary is explicit:

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 2. Static Memory Allocation
text: - Native initialization ends immediately before entering the event loop.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 2. Static Memory Allocation
text: - Web initialization ends immediately before the first frame can run.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 2. Static Memory Allocation
text: - Application `on_init` work is part of initialization.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 2. Static Memory Allocation
text: - Work completed after either boundary MUST consume storage reserved before the boundary.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 2. Static Memory Allocation
text:
This rule applies to application state, framework state, worker queues, decoded assets,
staging buffers, GPU resources, and bookkeeping. An OS or driver implementation may allocate
internally, but Gooey MUST NOT request avoidable dynamic storage from it after initialization.
Window resize, device recovery, asynchronous completion, and cache eviction are not implicit
exceptions; their storage and work MUST be bounded in the design.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 2. Static Memory Allocation
text:
Use fixed-capacity arrays, slot maps, object pools, arenas, slabs, and ring buffers. Allocate
or reserve their complete backing storage at startup. Runtime operations claim and release
slots; they do not allocate and free backing memory.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 2. Static Memory Allocation
text:
Pool exhaustion is a capacity-planning error. It MUST fail fast with the pool name, configured
capacity, requested count, and relevant frame or operation. It MUST NOT silently drop work,
grow, evict unrelated data, or fall back to a general-purpose allocator.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 2. Static Memory Allocation > Application resource budgets
text:
Gooey applications MUST declare one complete resource budget at the canonical `gooey.App`
entry point. The intended public model is a comptime `ResourceLimits` value or named comptime
profile because `gooey.App` already accepts comptime configuration.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 2. Static Memory Allocation > Application resource budgets
text: The resource budget MUST include every application-dependent capacity, including:

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 2. Static Memory Allocation > Application resource budgets
text: - Windows and maximum framebuffer dimensions.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 2. Static Memory Allocation > Application resource budgets
text: - Widgets, elements, entities, and component-tree depth.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 2. Static Memory Allocation > Application resource budgets
text: - Layout nodes, clips, render commands, vertices, indices, and draw batches.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 2. Static Memory Allocation > Application resource budgets
text: - Glyphs, atlas pages, images, SVG data, and upload staging bytes.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 2. Static Memory Allocation > Application resource budgets
text: - Input events, callbacks, timers, animations, and accessibility announcements.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 2. Static Memory Allocation > Application resource budgets
text: - Async requests, completions, failures, and worker-queue entries.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 2. Static Memory Allocation > Application resource budgets
text: - Per-frame work limits for every incremental subsystem.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 2. Static Memory Allocation > Application resource budgets
text:
Each subsystem MUST have an absolute framework ceiling. The application-selected limit MUST
be less than or equal to that ceiling. Relationships between limits MUST be checked at
comptime. Runtime-only platform constraints MUST be checked during initialization.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 2. Static Memory Allocation > Application resource budgets
text:
Capacity values MUST NOT be scattered through hidden subsystem defaults. A subsystem may use
a named default profile for examples, but production applications MUST select a profile or
provide explicit limits. The budget is part of the application's operational contract.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 2. Static Memory Allocation > Application resource budgets
text:
Where capacity changes a type's size, specialize the type at comptime. Where platform APIs
require runtime sizes, allocate the exact bounded storage during initialization. Pass the
validated budget downward; do not let leaf subsystems independently invent capacities.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 2. Static Memory Allocation > Application resource budgets
text:
Until the unified `ResourceLimits` API exists, new subsystem capacities MUST follow this model
locally and MUST be structured so they can be moved into the app budget without redesign.
Do not describe an unavailable API as implemented.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 2. Static Memory Allocation > Application resource budgets
text:
A debug allocation guard SHOULD mark the lifecycle as `initializing`, `running`, or
`deinitializing` and assert that Gooey allocator calls occur only in the permitted phases.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 3. Assertions
text:
Assertions detect programmer errors. Operating errors are expected and MUST be returned or
handled. Corrupt program state is unexpected and MUST stop execution.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 3. Assertions
text:
The codebase MUST average at least two meaningful assertions per function. Non-trivial
functions SHOULD assert at least two independent properties. Do not add tautologies merely to
meet a count; strengthen the mental model instead.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 3. Assertions
text: - Every function argument not already proven by its type.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 3. Assertions
text: - Preconditions before state is read or mutated.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 3. Assertions
text: - Invariants while state transitions occur.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 3. Assertions
text: - Postconditions and return values before returning.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 3. Assertions
text: - Counts before indexing and capacities before writing.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 3. Assertions
text: - Enum, tag, alignment, ownership, and lifecycle assumptions.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 3. Assertions
text: - Relationships between compile-time constants and important type sizes.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 3. Assertions
text:
Pair assertions across boundaries. Assert data before writing it to a queue, file, GPU buffer,
or platform API, and assert it independently when reading or completing the operation.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 3. Assertions
text: Split compound assertions:

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 3. Assertions
text:
Do not write `assert(offset <= length and size <= length - offset)`. Separate assertions make
the failed property precise. Use a single-line implication when appropriate:

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 3. Assertions
text:
A blatantly true assertion MAY replace a comment when it enforces a critical and surprising
relationship. Assertions are executable documentation, but they are not a substitute for
understanding or tests.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 4. Put a Limit on Everything
text:
Every loop, queue, stack, buffer, retry, callback list, state machine, and unit of work per
frame MUST have a hard upper bound. Use explicit names with units:

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 4. Put a Limit on Everything
text:
Loops MUST make their bound visible in the loop condition or assert it in the body. An
intentional event loop that does not terminate MUST assert or structurally prove that each
iteration performs bounded work.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 4. Put a Limit on Everything
text:
Do not convert a bounded queue into unbounded latency. Bound both storage and the number of
items processed per frame. Define overload behavior explicitly and fail fast when preserving
correctness is impossible.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 5. Function Shape
text:
Functions have a hard limit of 70 physical lines, including assertions and comments but
excluding the signature. Do not evade the limit with dense formatting.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 5. Function Shape
text: When splitting functions:

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 5. Function Shape
text: - Keep control flow in the parent.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 5. Function Shape
text: - Push `if` and `switch` upward.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 5. Function Shape
text: - Push loops and pure computation downward.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 5. Function Shape
text: - Keep state mutation centralized.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 5. Function Shape
text: - Make leaf functions pure where possible.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 5. Function Shape
text: - Prefer a few arguments and a simple return value.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 5. Function Shape
text: - Move complex nested types to top-level declarations.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 5. Function Shape
text:
A helper split MUST represent a coherent responsibility. Do not create fragments named
`part1`, `continued`, or `helper` merely to satisfy the line count.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 6. Explicit Control Flow
text: - Recursion is forbidden. Use a fixed-capacity explicit stack.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 6. Explicit Control Flow
text: - Suspending functions and hidden coroutine control flow are forbidden.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 6. Explicit Control Flow
text: - Functions MUST run to completion while their preconditions remain true.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 6. Explicit Control Flow
text: - Abstractions MUST justify their safety and performance cost.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 6. Explicit Control Flow
text: - Dynamic dispatch MUST be bounded and justified.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 6. Explicit Control Flow
text: - Hidden callbacks and reentrancy MUST be avoided.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 6. Explicit Control Flow
text:
Split compound conditions into nested branches when separate facts are being decided. Write
complex `else if` chains as explicit `else { if (...) { ... } else { ... } }` trees. Consider
both the positive and negative space of every branch.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 6. Explicit Control Flow
text:
Add braces unless the complete `if` statement fits on one line. This is defense in depth
against edits that accidentally change control flow.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 7. Performance Sketches
text:
Before implementation, write a back-of-the-envelope sketch for network, disk, memory, CPU,
and GPU where applicable. Cover both bandwidth and latency. State:

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 7. Performance Sketches
text: - Maximum operations and bytes per frame.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 7. Performance Sketches
text: - Maximum resident and transient memory.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 7. Performance Sketches
text: - Maximum queue depth and completion rate.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 7. Performance Sketches
text: - Expected cache behavior and data locality.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 7. Performance Sketches
text: - Worst-case work, not only average work.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 7. Performance Sketches
text: - The configured limit that enforces each estimate.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 7. Performance Sketches
text:
For Gooey, include vertices, indices, draw commands, texture uploads, glyph lookups, layout
nodes, event batches, accessibility updates, and asset completions as applicable.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 7. Performance Sketches
text:
Optimize network, disk, memory, and CPU in that order after accounting for frequency. A fast
operation repeated often can dominate a slower operation performed rarely.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 8. Batching and Planes
text:
Do not react directly to external events. Capture them into bounded queues and let Gooey run
at its own pace. Batch network, disk, memory, CPU, and GPU accesses.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 8. Batching and Planes
text:
Separate the control plane from the data plane. Assert heavily when constructing and
validating batches. Keep the hot data-plane loop compact, predictable, and free of allocation,
branching, pointer chasing, and redundant computation.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 9. Naming
text: - Use `snake_case` for functions, variables, fields, and filenames.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 9. Naming
text: - Use proper acronym capitalization in type names, such as `VSRState`, not `VsrState`.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 9. Naming
text: - Do not abbreviate names except primitive integer parameters in sorting or matrix code.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 9. Naming
text: - Put units and qualifiers last, ordered from most to least significant.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 9. Naming
text: - Prefer `latency_ms_max` to `max_latency_ms`.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 9. Naming
text: - Prefer `source` and `target` to `src` and `dest`.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 9. Naming
text: - Choose related names of similar length when this improves visual symmetry.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 9. Naming
text: - Infuse allocator names with ownership, such as `gpa`, `arena`, or `frame_arena`.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 9. Naming
text: - Do not overload a domain term with a second meaning.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 9. Naming
text: - Prefer nouns that compose outside code, such as `pipeline` rather than `preparing`.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 9. Naming
text: - Use long-form script flags, such as `--force`, except for interactive convenience.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 9. Naming
text:
When one function owns a helper or callback, prefix the helper with the caller's name, such as
`read_sector` and `read_sector_callback`. Callbacks go last in parameter lists.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 9. Naming
text:
Use an `options: struct` when arguments can be confused. A function taking two values of the
same integer type MUST use named options. Nullable arguments MUST be named so `null` is clear
at the call site.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 9. Naming
text:
Thread singleton dependencies through constructors positionally from most general to most
specific when their distinct types make confusion impossible.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 9. Naming
text:
Order files top-down by importance. Put `main` first. In structs, place fields first, then
nested types, then methods. Move a nested type to top level when it is complex. When semantic
order is not stronger, use alphabetical or big-endian naming order.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 9. Naming
text: Follow the Zig style guide for everything not overridden here.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 10. Shrink Scope
text:
Declare variables at the smallest possible scope. Calculate and validate values close to use
to prevent place-of-check-to-place-of-use bugs. Do not retain aliases or duplicate derived
state that can become inconsistent.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 10. Shrink Scope
text: Prefer simpler signatures and return types. As a default ordering:

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 10. Shrink Scope
Gooey Engineering Style > 10. Shrink Scope
text:
Complex return types add branches at every caller and spread through the call graph. Return
only information the caller must act upon.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 11. Positive and Negative Space
text: State invariants positively:

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 11. Positive and Negative Space
text:
Prefer `index < count` over negated or reversed forms such as `index >= count`. For every valid
state, identify and handle or assert the invalid states. Boundary transitions are where the
most valuable bugs are found.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 12. Dependencies
text:
Gooey has zero third-party package dependencies. The Zig toolchain, Zig standard library, and
required platform APIs such as CoreText, Metal, Wayland, Vulkan, and browser APIs are allowed.
Do not add a package when the functionality can be implemented and maintained locally.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 12. Dependencies
text:
Any proposed exception MUST document supply-chain risk, supported platforms, binary size,
initialization behavior, runtime allocation behavior, failure modes, and removal cost. An
exception requires explicit approval before code is written.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 13. In-Place Initialization
text:
Construct large or immovable values in place with an out pointer. In-place initialization is
viral: if one field requires a stable address, initialize its containing object in place too.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 13. In-Place Initialization
text: Pass an argument larger than 16 bytes as `*const` unless copying is intentional and documented.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 13. In-Place Initialization
text:
For small structs, an in-place initializer MAY use `self.* = .{ ... }`. For large structs,
initialize field by field because a struct literal can create a stack temporary.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 13. In-Place Initialization
text:
Initialization functions MUST establish and assert every field's state. Partially initialized
objects MUST NOT escape. Use `errdefer` to unwind every successfully acquired resource.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 14. WASM Stack Budget
text: WASM has a 1 MiB stack beginning at address 1,048,576 and growing downward.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 14. WASM Stack Budget
text: - Heap-allocate structs larger than 50 KiB during initialization.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 14. WASM Stack Budget
text: - Initialize those structs in place.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 14. WASM Stack Budget
text: - Mark their initializer `noinline` to prevent frame accumulation in `ReleaseSmall`.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 14. WASM Stack Budget
text: - Do not use large struct literals or return large structs by value.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 14. WASM Stack Budget
text: - Add compile-time size assertions for large foundational types.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 14. WASM Stack Budget
text:
Known approximate sizes include `TextSystem` at 1.7 MiB, `WebRenderer` at 1.15 MiB, `Gooey` at
400 KiB, and `Tree` at 350 KiB. Update these figures when layouts materially change.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 14. WASM Stack Budget
text:
For stack diagnosis, use the existing `verbose_init_logging` switches in the relevant Gooey,
accessibility, or web bridge implementation.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 15. Explicitly Sized Types
text:
Use explicitly sized integers such as `u8`, `u16`, `u32`, and `u64`. Use `usize` only when
interfacing with Zig APIs, pointer arithmetic, or slice indexing that requires it. Convert to
and from explicitly sized domain types at the boundary, with checked casts and assertions.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 15. Explicitly Sized Types
text:
Explicit sizes make overflow, memory layout, serialization, native behavior, and WASM behavior
predictable.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 16. Explain Why and How
text:
Code alone is not documentation. Comments MUST explain rationale, invariants, constraints, or
methodology rather than narrating syntax.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 16. Explain Why and How
text:
Comments are sentences: one space after `//`, an initial capital, and a final full stop. A
colon is appropriate when introducing code. End-of-line comments MAY be short phrases.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 16. Explain Why and How
text:
Tests MUST begin with a short explanation of their goal and methodology when the test body does
not make both immediately obvious. Performance-sensitive code MUST show its resource sketch or
link to the design that contains it.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 17. Handle Every Error
text:
Every error MUST be returned, transformed, logged and handled, or explicitly classified as an
impossible programmer error with a nearby proof. Do not silently discard errors. Do not use
`catch unreachable` without documenting and asserting why the error is impossible.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 17. Handle Every Error
text:
Test error paths. Incorrect handling of non-fatal errors causes catastrophic failures more
often than the original operation does.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 18. Off-by-One Discipline
text: Treat indexes, counts, sizes, offsets, and capacities as distinct conceptual types.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 18. Off-by-One Discipline
text: - Index to count: add one.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 18. Off-by-One Discipline
text: - Count to byte size: multiply by the unit size.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 18. Off-by-One Discipline
text: - Offset plus size: prove the addition cannot overflow before comparing with capacity.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 18. Off-by-One Discipline
text: - Inclusive to exclusive bounds: perform and check the conversion explicitly.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 18. Off-by-One Discipline
text:
Use `@divExact`, `@divFloor`, or an explicit ceiling-division helper. Do not use `/` where the
rounding contract matters. Names MUST include the relevant unit or qualifier.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 19. Explicit Options
text:
Pass library options explicitly at call sites. Do not rely on defaults when a choice affects
correctness, performance, compatibility, or generated code.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 19. Explicit Options
text:
Named defaults are acceptable only when the default itself is the reviewed policy and its name
communicates that policy.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 20. Hot Loops
text:
Extract hot loops into standalone functions with primitive arguments and no `self`. Load
needed fields before the call so the compiler and reader do not need to prove repeated pointer
accesses are stable.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 20. Hot Loops
text:
Hot loops MUST NOT allocate, perform virtual dispatch, grow buffers, acquire contended locks,
or hide bounds checks inside abstractions. Keep loop bounds and memory strides explicit.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 21. Buffer Bleeds
text:
A partially written buffer can leak stale or sensitive bytes and break deterministic output.
Zero every unused byte, including alignment padding, unused GPU ranges, serialization padding,
and pooled storage returned to a different logical owner.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 21. Buffer Bleeds
text: Assert the used range when writing and again before submission or transmission.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 22. Resource Grouping
text:
Place a blank line before resource allocation and after its matching `defer` or `errdefer` so
ownership and cleanup are visually obvious:

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 22. Resource Grouping
text: Keep acquisition and cleanup together. Do not separate them with unrelated work.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 23. Compiler Warnings
text:
Enable the compiler's strictest practical diagnostics from the first day. Every warning is a
bug report. Fix the cause; do not suppress the warning.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 24. Testing
text:
Build a precise mental model before writing the implementation. Encode that model in types,
assertions, comments, and tests. Fuzzing and simulation find contradictions in the model; they
do not prove the absence of bugs.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 24. Testing
text: - Minimum, maximum, empty, full, and one-past-the-boundary cases.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 24. Testing
text: - Valid input becoming invalid at each boundary.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 24. Testing
text: - Capacity exhaustion and overload behavior.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 24. Testing
text: - Every error return and partial-initialization cleanup path.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 24. Testing
text: - Integer overflow, truncation, and rounding boundaries.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 24. Testing
text: - Repeated reuse of pooled slots and zeroed padding.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 24. Testing
text: - Deterministic output where determinism is promised.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 24. Testing
text:
A capacity test MUST fill the resource exactly, verify the last valid operation, attempt one
additional operation, and verify the documented failure mode.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 25. Formatting
text: - Run `zig fmt` on every changed Zig file.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 25. Formatting
text: - Use four spaces of indentation.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 25. Formatting
text: - Hard-limit every source and documentation line to 100 columns.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 25. Formatting
text: - Use the available width; do not create needlessly narrow code.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 25. Formatting
text: - Add trailing commas and let `zig fmt` wrap declarations, calls, and literals.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 25. Formatting
text: - Nothing important may be hidden behind a horizontal scrollbar.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 25. Formatting
text: Formatting rules are mechanical and MUST be enforced by tooling where possible.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 26. Tooling
text:
Prefer the standardized tool already used by the repository. Every additional tool adds
installation, portability, security, and maintenance cost.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 26. Tooling
text:
Prefer Zig programs to shell scripts for repository automation. Zig scripts are cross-platform,
type-checked, and keep the team's toolbox small. A shell script is acceptable only when it is
trivial, portable, and demonstrably clearer.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 26. Tooling
text:
Do not add a formatter, task runner, code generator, or package manager when the Zig toolchain
can perform the job adequately.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 27. Review Checklist
text: Before considering work complete, verify:

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 27. Review Checklist
text: 1. Safety, performance, and developer experience were considered in that order.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 27. Review Checklist
text: 2. Every resource and unit of work has a documented hard bound.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 27. Review Checklist
text: 3. All Gooey-owned memory is reserved before the initialization boundary.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 27. Review Checklist
text: 4. Runtime paths cannot allocate, grow capacity, or lazily initialize.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 27. Review Checklist
text: 5. Arguments, invariants, boundaries, and postconditions are asserted.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 27. Review Checklist
text: 6. Positive and negative spaces, capacity exhaustion, and errors are tested.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 27. Review Checklist
text: 7. Functions and lines obey the 70-line and 100-column limits.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 27. Review Checklist
text: 8. Names expose units, ownership, and domain meaning.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 27. Review Checklist
text: 9. Errors and partial initialization are handled completely.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 27. Review Checklist
text: 10. The performance sketch fits within the declared app resource budget.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 27. Review Checklist
text: 11. `zig fmt`, focused tests, and relevant broader validation pass.

head: Gooey Engineering Style > 27. Review Checklist
text: 12. Comments and the change description explain why the design is correct.

text: This repository uses a light AgentPMO integration: skills, existing CI, CodeQL, and staged Dependabot updates. Use the installed skills in `.agents/skills/` for relevant tasks. head: RestClient.Net — Agent Instructions > Commands
text: Use .NET 8 and 9 runtimes for the repository's targets. Run focused tests while iterating, then the relevant CI checks. Preserve the existing assertions and regression coverage. Generated sample code is regenerated by the existing build targets.

head: RestClient.Net — Agent Instructions > Website
text: The Eleventy site uses local layouts and a shared `.prose` class for docs, API references, and blog posts. Total shipped CSS must remain at or below **2,500 raw UTF-8 bytes**, including every stylesheet. Do not bypass the budget with inline styles, external CSS, or JavaScript that injects CSS. `npm run build` enforces the budget and checks generated links and metadata.

head: RestClient.Net — Agent Instructions > Website
text: API reference pages are exported from C# declarations and XML comments by `Website/tools/ApiDocs/`; edit the source rather than generated `Website/src/api/reference/` files. Run `npm run test:unit`, `npm run build`, and `npm test` in `Website/`. The deployment workflow also verifies the GitHub Pages path prefix. See `Website/README.md`.

head: RestClient.Net — Agent Instructions > Git and CI
text: Use a feature branch and a PR to `main`; derive the PR title and description from the diff with `origin/main`. Follow the user's authorization for committing, pushing, and merging. Monitor the latest PR commit's checks and resolve failures before merging. Do not add AI co-author trailers.

head: RestClient.Net — Agent Instructions > Git and CI
text: Dependabot updates accumulate on `dependabot-upgrades`; ordinary CI and CodeQL run on the consolidation PR to `main`, not on each bot bump. Never publish packages or create release tags as part of an ordinary PR.

head: RestClient.Net — Agent Instructions > Git and CI
text: When a release is authorized, use `.github/workflows/publish-restclient.yml`. It builds and tests both packages, publishes and verifies `Exhaustion` first, then publishes `RestClient.Net` and verifies a fresh NuGet consumer. `ExhaustionVersion` in `Directory.Build.props` is shared by the analyzer and all references. See `scripts/README.md` for package verification and immutable-version rules.

head: RestClient.Net — Agent Instructions > Integration-test isolation
text: The Nuclia integration fixture starts Docker Compose and removes its project's containers and volumes. If the host already has services, use an isolated `COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME` and Compose configuration with non-conflicting ports before running it. Keep the heap-limited child processes in the Exhaustion regression tests intact.
