text: 19. Never develop on the shared main checkout. Every development task runs in its own git worktree on its own dedicated branch, and you MUST confirm the base branch with the operator before creating the worktree/branch — never assume `main` or the currently checked-out branch. A `git checkout` in the shared checkout silently destroys other sessions' uncommitted work. Tear down only the worktrees/branches you created (by name, never `fix/*`/`feat/*` wildcards), leave other sessions' worktrees untouched, and end on the branch you started on (the active `release/vX.Y.Z`, never `main`). See Git Workflow → "Worktree isolation".

head: OmniRoute agent guide > Hard Rules
text: 20. PII redaction/sanitization is **opt-in — never on by default**. OmniRoute proxies for self-hosted/local LLMs where the operator owns the data, so mutating request/response payloads by default would silently corrupt legitimate traffic. The two data-mutating PII feature flags **MUST** keep `defaultValue: "false"` in `src/shared/constants/featureFlagDefinitions.ts`: `PII_REDACTION_ENABLED` (request-side) and `PII_RESPONSE_SANITIZATION` (response + streaming). All three application points — `src/lib/guardrails/piiMasker.ts` (request guardrail), `src/lib/piiSanitizer.ts` (response), `src/lib/streamingPiiTransform.ts` (SSE) — are gated on these flags; with both off the `pii-masker` guardrail still runs but never mutates payloads (data passes through untouched). Flipping either default to `"true"` requires explicit operator approval. The regression guard is `tests/unit/pii-opt-in-default.test.ts` (asserts both definition defaults + behavioral pass-through). Opt-in is per-operator via env or the settings/DB override (`src/lib/db/featureFlags.ts`), never a silent default. See `docs/security/GUARDRAILS.md`.

head: OmniRoute agent guide > Hard Rules
text: 21. **Release-freeze — the FROZEN release branch belongs to the release captain; development does NOT stop (parallel-cycle model, 2026-07-04).** `/generate-release` opens a marker issue labeled `release-freeze` at the start of reconciliation (Phase 0a), **immediately cuts the next cycle's branch `release/vX+1` from the frozen tip (Phase 0a.0b — bump + living release PR + re-home of open PRs)**, and closes the freeze once the release PR squash-merges to `main`. Before merging **any** PR, every campaign workflow (`/review-prs`, `/review-group-prs`, `/merge-prs`, `/triage-fix-bugs`, `/implement-fix-bugs`, `/triage-features`, `/implement-features`, `/green-prs`, `/port-upstream-*`) **MUST** check `gh issue list --repo diegosouzapw/OmniRoute --label release-freeze --state open` — if a freeze is active: **NEVER merge into the frozen `release/vX.Y.Z` named in the freeze title**; instead resolve the ACTIVE development branch (the **highest** `release/v*` by semver — normally `release/vX+1`, announced in a freeze-issue comment) and **retarget the PR there** (`gh pr edit <N> --base release/vX+1`, then VERIFY with `gh pr view <N> --json baseRefName` — the edit fails silently) and merge normally. **HOLD only when the highest release/v\* branch IS the frozen one** (the short window before 0a.0b completes, or a pre-parallel-cycle release) — in that case leave the PR ready and open, tell the operator, and resume when the next branch appears or the freeze lifts. The just-shipped fixes reach `release/vX+1` via the Phase 5 sync-back (`scripts/release/sync-next-cycle.mjs`); do not try to sync mid-release. This is a **coordination signal, not a permission lock**: the release captain and the campaign sessions share the `diegosouzapw` identity, so a GitHub branch-protection lock cannot distinguish them — only this honored marker prevents the mid-release commit races that forced full CHANGELOG re-reconciliation in v3.8.40/v3.8.41 (a parallel campaign advanced `release/vX.Y.Z` by 34 commits mid-run). The release captain's own reconciliation/cycle-open pushes are exempt — they _are_ the release. Fixes that must land during a freeze (a homologation finding) follow the post-merge read-only rule: land on `main` first via `fix/release-vX.Y.Z-*`. **⛔ ONLY `/generate-release` may raise a release-freeze, and ONLY at its Phase 0a (start of generating a new version) — lifted at Phase 12c after the squash-merge to `main`.** No campaign, session, or agent may open a `release-freeze` marker at any other time — a freeze is **never** a mid-development coordination tool. If a session ever believes a freeze is genuinely, unavoidably necessary outside the `/generate-release` flow, it **MUST first ask the operator (`diegosouzapw`) in chat, explicitly alert "estou criando um freeze" and get an explicit yes** — never open, extend, or re-open a `release-freeze` autonomously. Conversely, do **not** close/lift an active `/generate-release` freeze to unblock campaign merges: it protects the captain's single clean CI run and auto-lifts at Phase 12c — closing it early re-triggers the exact commit race it prevents. Verify a freeze is legitimate before acting on it: an open `release-freeze` whose title/body references an **OPEN** release PR (`gh pr view <N> --json state`) is the authorized captain freeze — hold, don't touch. (Cycle-model proposal: `_tasks/finished/release-flow/2026-07-04_proposta-ciclo-paralelo-v2.md`.)

head: OmniRoute agent guide > Hard Rules
text:
22. **Cross-session safety — this repo is worked by MANY parallel sessions/agents at once; never step on another's in-flight work.** Two absolute bans, both recurring incidents (this rule exists because they keep happening):
    - **(a) Never `git stash` / `git stash pop` — ANYWHERE in this repo, including inside an isolated worktree, and including inside any subagent you dispatch.** `git stash` operates on the **shared repository object store**, not the per-worktree working tree — so a stash pushed or popped in one session can silently clobber or resurrect another parallel session's uncommitted changes. This is not hypothetical: 2026-07-02 a `#5923` quotaCache change leaked into the unrelated `#2296` worktree via a global `stash pop`, and the same class reincided through a **subagent**. To compare working changes against a base ref **without** stashing, use `git show <ref>:<path>` or `git diff <ref> -- <path>`; to confirm a typecheck/lint error is pre-existing on the base, inspect the base ref directly (`git show origin/release/vX.Y.Z:<path>`) — never stash your tree away to "get it clean". **Put this ban verbatim in the prompt of every subagent that touches git** (agents don't inherit this file's context — the recurrence was a subagent).
    - **(b) Never merge, push, rebase, or force-push a PR / branch / worktree that another session is actively working.** An open PR whose head is a live fix worktree in `.claude/worktrees/` you did **not** create (e.g. `fix-5852`/`fix-5923` carrying fresh commits, even when they share your `diegosouzapw` identity), or any branch another session owns, is **off-limits — HOLD**, and let the owning session merge it. **Before** merging or pushing to any PR you did not create _this_ session, run `git worktree list` to check for a matching in-flight worktree and re-check `gh pr view <N> --json state,headRefOid`. Only the owning session merges its own in-flight PR; mid-flight merges race the owner and re-trigger the exact commit/CHANGELOG races Rule #19 and Rule #21 guard against. (Reinforces Rule #19.)

head: ExifReader - Agent Guide > Coding Style
text: Enforced by ESLint (`eslint.config.mjs`). Key rules:

head: ExifReader - Agent Guide > Coding Style
text: - ES modules (`import`/`export`), no CommonJS in `src/`

head: ExifReader - Agent Guide > Coding Style
text: - 4-space indent, single quotes, semicolons always

head: ExifReader - Agent Guide > Coding Style
text: - `const`/`let` only (no `var`), `prefer-const`, strict equality (`===`)

head: ExifReader - Agent Guide > Coding Style
text: - `object-shorthand`, no `console`, no TODO/FIXME comments

head: ExifReader - Agent Guide > Coding Style
text: - No curly-brace spacing: `{a, b}` not `{ a, b }`

head: ExifReader - Agent Guide > Coding Style
text: - Arrow parens always: `(x) => x`

head: ExifReader - Agent Guide > Coding Style
text: - Space before anonymous function paren, not named: `function foo()` vs `function ()`

head: ExifReader - Agent Guide > Coding Style
text: - kebab-case filenames, camelCase variables/functions, PascalCase constructors/class-like exports

head: ExifReader - Agent Guide > Coding Style
text: - Place functions in the order they are used. That means the definition of a function is placed after the location from where it is called.

head: ExifReader - Agent Guide > Coding Style
text: Every `.js` and `.ts` file in `src/`, `bin/` and `test/`, and `exif-reader.d.ts`, starts with the MPL 2.0 license header, after the shebang line if there is one. The linter does not check it, so copy the three-line version from an existing file such as `src/tags.js`.

head: ExifReader - Agent Guide > Older runtime support (src/ only)
text:
The browserslist target includes IE10 and other older runtimes. The
build pipeline transpiles down to a low ECMAScript baseline, and a few
modern constructs balloon the output. Avoid them in `src/`:

head: ExifReader - Agent Guide > Older runtime support (src/ only)
text:
- **No `async`/`await` keywords.** They transpile to a regenerator
  runtime that adds significant bundle size. Use explicit promise
  chains (`Promise.resolve(...).then(...)`) instead.

head: ExifReader - Agent Guide > Older runtime support (src/ only)
text:
- **No object spread (`{...obj, key: value}`) and no `Object.assign`.**
  Use `objectAssign(target, ...sources)` from `src/utils.js` instead.
  Example: `const next = objectAssign({}, options, {async: true});`.

head: ExifReader - Agent Guide > Older runtime support (src/ only)
text:
`test/`, `bin/`, and `webpack.config.js` run only in modern Node on
maintainer machines, so they may use any modern syntax.

head: ExifReader - Agent Guide > Comments
text: Prefer self-explaining code (clear names, small functions) over comments. Add a comment only when the code cannot be made obvious on its own, for example a non-trivial spec reference, a workaround for a known quirk, or a subtle invariant.

head: ExifReader - Agent Guide > Comments
text: When a comment is warranted, keep it short and to the point. One or two lines is usually enough.

head: ExifReader - Agent Guide > Comments
text: When an exported function warrants documentation, use JSDoc (not a plain comment) to describe its contract: parameters and return shape. Keep it concise and skip restating what the signature already says.

head: ExifReader - Agent Guide > Type Definitions
text: This is **not** a TypeScript project, but `exif-reader.d.ts` provides types for consumers. When adding or changing public API surface (new tags, options, return types):

head: ExifReader - Agent Guide > Type Definitions
text: 1. Update `exif-reader.d.ts`

head: ExifReader - Agent Guide > Type Definitions
text: 2. Update `test/types/exif-reader.ts` with type-level tests (including `@ts-expect-error` for invalid usage)

head: ExifReader - Agent Guide > Type Definitions
text: 3. Verify with `npm run test:types`

head: ExifReader - Agent Guide > Tests
text: Every source file has a corresponding `test/unit/*-spec.js`. New code needs tests. Coverage thresholds are enforced (via `c8`, configured in `package.json`).

head: ExifReader - Agent Guide > Tests
text: Unit tests run as native ES modules with no transpilation. Develop on Node 24.7+ to be able to run the full suite: the integration and build test suites parse JPEG XL fixtures that need its Brotli support, and they `require()` the ES module source which needs at least 22.12. Relative imports in test files must carry explicit `.js` extensions, and named imports from `src/` modules must actually exist (most `src/` modules only have a default export).

head: ExifReader - Agent Guide > Tests
text: There is no module-mocking library, and none should be introduced. To isolate a module from its dependencies:

head: ExifReader - Agent Guide > Tests
text: - Swap properties on a shared default-export object (`Constants`, `TagNames`, module API objects like `Tags` or `ImageHeader`, or `globalThis`) with `swapProperties` from `test-utils.js`, and call the returned restore function in `afterEach`.

head: ExifReader - Agent Guide > Tests
text: - Where the dependency is a named function import (immutable binding), do not mock it. Craft real binary input with `getDataView` so the real function runs, or test one level up through the module's public API.

head: ExifReader - Agent Guide > Tests
text: Use `npm run test` to run the unit tests and make use of `describe.only` and `it.only` for focused testing.

head: ExifReader - Agent Guide > Tests
text: Mocha defaults to the quiet `dot` reporter locally (`spec` on CI), configured in `.mocharc.cjs`; failures always print in full. Set `EXIFREADER_MOCHA_REPORTER=spec` for per-test output.

head: ExifReader - Agent Guide > Tests > TDD: red-green-refactor
text: Write code test-first. For each new behavior:

head: ExifReader - Agent Guide > Tests > TDD: red-green-refactor
text: 1. **Red** — write the smallest failing test that captures the next bit of behavior. Run it and watch it fail for the expected reason (missing function, wrong return, etc.).

head: ExifReader - Agent Guide > Tests > TDD: red-green-refactor
text: 2. **Green** — write the smallest change in `src/` that makes the test pass. Resist adding anything the test doesn't demand.

head: ExifReader - Agent Guide > Tests > TDD: red-green-refactor
text: 3. **Refactor** — with tests green, tidy names, extract helpers, remove duplication. Re-run the suite after each change.

head: ExifReader - Agent Guide > Tests > TDD: red-green-refactor
text: Cycle one behavior at a time, not one feature. A feature like "parse iloc constructionMethod 1" is many cycles (parse the idat box; resolve a single-extent cm-1 offset; handle a missing idat box; etc.), each one a red-green-refactor turn.

head: ExifReader - Agent Guide > Changelog

Use the [Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/en/1.1.0/) format with the appropriate change type: `Added`, `Changed`, `Deprecated`, `Removed`, `Fixed`, or `Security`.

head: ExifReader - Agent Guide > Changelog
text: After updating, read through the whole `Unreleased` section again. Each change type must appear at most once, in the Keep a Changelog order above, with all its entries under that one heading. Duplicate headings (a second `Security`, for example) have slipped in several times.

head: Repository Guidelines > Project structure
text: **Vendor API SDK** means the GraphQL-facing library (`pipefy`) used by both MCP and CLI, distinct from app glue or generic shared helpers. MCP and CLI depend on it and never import each other.

head: Repository Guidelines > Import namespace migration: `pipefy_sdk` → `pipefy`
text:
The SDK distribution is named `pipefy`, but its import module is still `pipefy_sdk`. The
import module is being renamed to `pipefy` gradually, so the distribution and import names
converge. New code should target `pipefy`; existing `pipefy_sdk` imports are migrated in
small batches rather than one sweep.

head: Repository Guidelines > Import namespace migration: `pipefy_sdk` → `pipefy`
text:
The mechanism that lets both paths work during the transition is a `sys.modules` alias. The
real code lives at the new location and the old name is aliased to the *same module object*,
so `import pipefy_sdk` keeps resolving. Once code moves under a `pipefy/` package:

head: Repository Guidelines > Import namespace migration: `pipefy_sdk` → `pipefy`
text:
- Do NOT shim with `from pipefy import *`. That re-imports and creates two copies of every
  class under two names, which breaks `isinstance` checks and module-level singletons. The
  `sys.modules` alias preserves a single module identity; use it.

head: Repository Guidelines > Import namespace migration: `pipefy_sdk` → `pipefy`
text:
- Migrate call sites incrementally. New code imports `pipefy`; touch old `pipefy_sdk` imports
  as you pass through their files.

head: Repository Guidelines > Import namespace migration: `pipefy_sdk` → `pipefy`
text:
- Add a lint/grep guard so new `pipefy_sdk` imports fail once the migration starts, so the old
  surface only ever shrinks.

head: Repository Guidelines > Import namespace migration: `pipefy_sdk` → `pipefy`
text:
- On completion: remove the shim, repoint the ruff banned-api paths (`pipefy_sdk.services`,
  `pipefy_sdk.queries` → `pipefy.services`/`.queries`), move `__version__` into
  `pipefy/__init__.py`, and rename the directory `packages/sdk` → `packages/pipefy`.

head: Repository Guidelines > Coding style
text: - Python 3.11+ with `from __future__ import annotations` on every module.

head: Repository Guidelines > Coding style
text: - Built-in generics (`list[str]`, `dict[str, Any]`), union syntax (`str | None`).

head: Repository Guidelines > Coding style
text: - `ruff` enforces formatting and import sorting — run before committing.

head: Repository Guidelines > Coding style > Type validation at boundaries, not inside
text: Static typing is the contract for internal code; do not re-check it at runtime. A parameter annotated `value: str` is trusted by every internal caller, and a type checker, not a hand-written `isinstance` guard, is the right place to enforce it. Adding runtime type guards inside internal functions reinvents dynamic typing by hand and sets the wrong norm: do it once and it becomes the expectation everywhere.

head: Repository Guidelines > Coding style > Type validation at boundaries, not inside
text: Runtime type checks belong only at a trust boundary, where untyped or external data crosses into typed code and static analysis cannot follow:

head: Repository Guidelines > Coding style > Type validation at boundaries, not inside
text: - The MCP tool signature is the boundary. `MCPServer` builds a pydantic model per tool from the signature, so a scalar arg declared `color: str` is coerced and rejected there. SDK planners called behind it (for example `normalize_label_color`) trust the type and must not guard it again.

head: Repository Guidelines > Coding style > Type validation at boundaries, not inside
text: - The CLI command signature is the same kind of boundary. Typer parses and coerces options against their annotations (a `color: str` option in `pipefy_cli` is the rejection point), and the same SDK planners run behind it, so the MCP and CLI surfaces validate at the edge and trust the type underneath identically.

head: Repository Guidelines > Coding style > Type validation at boundaries, not inside
text: - A `dict`-typed tool arg (for example `filter: dict | None`) validates the container but not its nested values. Validating that nested, un-schema'd structure (the job of `validate_report_cards_filter`) is legitimate boundary work, not defensive noise.

head: Repository Guidelines > Coding style > Type validation at boundaries, not inside
text: When a type-related failure looks plausible, the fix is a type checker in CI, not a per-function guard.

head: Repository Guidelines > Coding style > Parse, don't validate
text: The boundary check should return a type that carries its result, not a bool or a bare raise that the interior re-derives. Validation that only raises throws away what it learned: the value flows on with its original loose type, so every downstream caller re-checks or re-normalizes it. Parsing turns loose input into a precise type once, and that type carries the proof, so the interior is total.

head: Repository Guidelines > Coding style > Parse, don't validate
text: - pydantic-settings models are the parse step for env vars: raw `os.environ` strings in, a typed `PipefySettings` / `AuthSettings` out, illegal values rejected at construction. Normalize there (strip, `rstrip('/')`, lowercase) so no consumer re-normalizes the same field later.

head: Repository Guidelines > Coding style > Parse, don't validate
text: - Prefer a closed sum type over a bag of optionals when inputs are mutually exclusive or co-dependent. `pipefy_auth.resolve_pipefy_auth` returns a `ResolvedAuth` (`StaticTokenAuth | ServiceAccountAuth | StoredSessionAuth`), so the winning credential tier is kept in the type; `build_httpx_auth` is then total over it, with no `None` branch and no fallthrough. Recovering the decision after the fact (an `isinstance` reverse lookup that maps a built `httpx.Auth` back to its tier name) is the anti-pattern this replaces.

head: Repository Guidelines > Coding style > Parse, don't validate
text: - Make illegal states unrepresentable instead of checking for them downstream. A cross-field rule such as "verify_audience requires audience" is a sum type wearing two fields; co-dependent credentials are one optional value, not two independent optionals that a helper later re-assembles.

head: Repository Guidelines > Coding style > Parse, don't validate
text: A function that accepts the parsed type may assume the guarantee and must not re-check it. This pairs with the boundary rule above: that one says where to validate, this one says what the check should hand back.

head: Repository Guidelines > Coding style > Parsed types are self-guaranteeing
text: A parsed type rejects invalid construction itself; it does not rely on the pipeline that usually builds it. Its constructor enforces every invariant it claims, so holding an instance is proof it is valid and a hand-written instance cannot be invalid. The domain name is the guarantee, not the resolver that happens to produce it.

head: Repository Guidelines > Coding style > Parsed types are self-guaranteeing
text: - A recurring (value + invariant) pair earns a dedicated leaf type rather than a bare `str`, so every field holding one inherits the guarantee instead of re-checking it. A one-off invariant stays with its owner.

head: Repository Guidelines > Coding style > Parsed types are self-guaranteeing
text: - When validity depends on a policy, carry the policy as part of the value so the constructor has the context to judge it.

head: Repository Guidelines > Coding style > Parsed types are self-guaranteeing
text: - A runtime-erased alias does not qualify: it disappears at runtime, so an invalid value still constructs. Reach for a type whose constructor actually runs.

head: Repository Guidelines > Coding style > Parsed types are self-guaranteeing
text: - Settings models stay pure data readers. A cross-field rule fails fast at construction, not through a projection method a consumer must remember to call, which makes the parse optional and invites a silent `None`.

head: Repository Guidelines > Coding style > Composition: the per-app runtime
text: Parsed types are decisions and cost no I/O to build. Effects (keychain reads, network, building clients or verifiers) live in a per-application runtime built once at startup: the single place raw settings become domain types and wired resources. Downstream depends on the runtime or the types it holds, never on raw settings or an ad-hoc resolve. The runtime lives in the app package; shared packages export parsed types and resolvers, not app wiring or effects. Whether an app wires eagerly (fail fast at boot) or keeps effectful members lazy is a per-app choice.

head: Repository Guidelines > Coding style > Composition: the per-app runtime
text: The layer model this sits inside (domain, adapter, composition root), the rule that domain types do not carry framework or SDK types, and where an alternative constructor lives (classmethod on the type versus free factory in the adapter) are in [`docs/architecture.md`](docs/architecture.md). Intra-package layering is enforced by import-linter in `packages/mcp`; the inter-package direction is enforced by ruff `TID251`.

head: AGENTS.md
text: Fullsend is a platform for fully autonomous agentic development for Git-hosted organizations (GitHub, GitLab, Forgejo). It contains design documents organized by problem domain (`docs/`) and a Go CLI (`cmd/fullsend/`) that manages forge setup and org configuration. See [fullsend.sh](https://fullsend.sh) for the full documentation site.

head: AGENTS.md > How to work in this repo
text: - Problem documents (`docs/problems/`) should present multiple options with trade-offs, not prescribe single solutions.

head: AGENTS.md > How to work in this repo
text: - Each problem document has an "Open questions" section — this is where unresolved issues live.

head: AGENTS.md > How to work in this repo
text: - When adding new problem areas, create a new file in `docs/problems/`. The documentation site auto-discovers files in this directory.

head: AGENTS.md > How to work in this repo
text: - For each existing problem doc that a new problem doc links to, add a reciprocal contextual backlink at the passage that motivated the outbound link in the same PR. Then run `grep -rn '<concept>' docs/problems/`, searching adjacent terms and synonyms as well as the new doc's title words, to find related passages the new doc does not already link to; wherever an existing doc *substantively discusses* the concept (not merely mentions it in passing), add a single contextual backlink at that passage, not a link at every match. This keeps cross-referencing bidirectional so readers can discover the new doc from its related contexts. When the new doc is organization-specific (`docs/problems/applied/<org-name>/`), frame any backlink you add to a core problem doc as an explicit org-specific pointer, so core docs stay organization-agnostic (see the organization-agnostic rule below).

head: AGENTS.md > How to work in this repo
text: - The security threat model (threat priority: external injection > insider > drift > supply chain) should inform all other documents.

head: AGENTS.md > How to work in this repo
text: - Keep core problem documents organization-agnostic. Organization-specific details belong in `docs/problems/applied/<org-name>/`.

head: AGENTS.md > How to work in this repo
text: - The target audience for problem documents is any contributor community considering autonomous agents — keep language accessible and avoid presuming solutions.

head: AGENTS.md > How to work in this repo
text: - Always stage your changes before running `make lint` and fix any failures. Pre-commit only checks staged files — without staging first, it stashes your work and finds nothing to lint.

head: AGENTS.md > How to work in this repo
text: - When invoking the fullsend CLI from this checkout, **prefer** `go run ./cmd/fullsend …` from the repo root. Do **not** use a `fullsend` binary from mise, `$PATH`, `go install`, or another checkout — those often lag this tree. A stale CLI once rewrote hosted-mint `ALLOWED_ROLES` during enrollment (dropping `e2e`/`fix`) and broke e2e. Details: [Go Code](docs/contributing/go-code.md#running-the-fullsend-cli).

head: AGENTS.md > How to work in this repo
text: - You **must** read and follow [COMMITS.md](COMMITS.md) when writing or reviewing commit messages and PR titles. Getting the prefix right is not optional — GoReleaser uses PR titles to build release notes. Breaking changes **must** carry the `!` suffix in both commit messages and PR titles; a missing `!` is an important-severity review finding.

head: AGENTS.md > How to work in this repo
text: - This repository requires a [Developer Certificate of Origin (DCO)](https://developercertificate.org/). Human-proposed commits **must** be signed off: use `git commit -s` (or add `Signed-off-by: Your Name <email>` as a trailer). Human-driven agent sessions (e.g., using Claude Code locally) should also sign off — the human directing the session is the one certifying the DCO. **Autonomous agent commits are exempt** and must never supply the DCO with `-s` or with `Signed-off-by`. These agents commit using the GitHub App's bot identity, which the [Probot DCO app](https://github.com/apps/dco) auto-skips.

head: AGENTS.md > How to work in this repo
text: - **Go coverage gate:** When changing Go production code (files under `cmd/` or `internal/` that are not `_test.go`), you **must** verify approximate patch coverage meets the 80% target (75% enforced floor) from [`.codecov.yml`](.codecov.yml) before considering verification done. `make go-test` passing alone is not sufficient — it does not enforce Codecov thresholds. See [Verifying patch coverage locally](docs/contributing/go-code.md#verifying-patch-coverage-locally) for the exact commands. If coverage is below threshold, add tests for uncovered new/changed lines and re-check within the same run.

head: AGENTS.md > How to work in this repo
text: - **Forge abstraction:** All forge operations (GitHub API calls, setting repository variables, PR comments, etc.) **must** go through `forge.Client` — never shell out to `gh` CLI or make direct API calls outside `internal/forge/github/`. If `forge.Client` lacks a method you need, add one to the interface. See [Forge Abstraction](docs/contributing/forge-abstraction.md) for the full rules.

head: AGENTS.md > How to work in this repo
text: - Never commit secrets (tokens, API keys, PEM keys, gcloud credentials) or sensitive data (GCP project names, service account identifiers, Model Armor template names, internal hostnames). Use environment variables with no defaults for sensitive values.

head: AGENTS.md > How to work in this repo
text: - **Experiments issues:** Work on experiment source (the `experiments/` submodule, which tracks [`fullsend-ai/experiments`](https://github.com/fullsend-ai/experiments)) is filed in that repository. Submodule integration (`.gitmodules`, CODEOWNERS, Renovate bumps, docs-site wiring) and fullsend product work stay in this tracker. When the right tracker is unclear, file here and link the experiments issue tracker in the body. See [CONTRIBUTING.md § Where to file experiments-related issues](CONTRIBUTING.md#where-to-file-experiments-related-issues).

head: AGENTS.md > How to work in this repo
text: - When adding a new doc under `docs/`, check `docs/.vitepress/config.ts` sidebar config. head: AGENTS.md > How to work in this repo

head: AGENTS.md > Blink in 60 seconds
text:
Blink is a native macOS spatial note-taking app. It is not a document library
with detachable windows: **the note is the window, and the desktop is the
workspace**.

head: AGENTS.md > Blink in 60 seconds
text: The human loop is capture → place → recall:

head: AGENTS.md > Blink in 60 seconds
text:
1. Create or find a note from the menubar popover, command palette, or global
   new-note hotkey.

head: AGENTS.md > Blink in 60 seconds
text:
2. The note opens as its one floating `NSPanel`; reopening it focuses that panel
   rather than creating a duplicate.

head: AGENTS.md > Blink in 60 seconds
text:
3. Move, resize, shade, or focus panels to arrange a working set. Blink restores
   each note to the same place.

head: AGENTS.md > Blink in 60 seconds
text:
4. Edit and read in the same panel. The menubar popover and command palette are
   launchers, not alternate document windows.

head: AGENTS.md > Blink in 60 seconds
text:
Blink is an `LSUIElement` menubar-only app: floating note panels + menubar
popover + command palette, with no Dock icon and no main/library window. The v1
Tauri app remains at tag `v1-final`; port lessons and behavior, never its code.

head: AGENTS.md > Blink in 60 seconds
text:
When operating Blink rather than changing its code, use the `blink` CLI for
notes and edit `config.json` for behavior/appearance. Drive the GUI only when a
task specifically requires the live visual surface.

head: AGENTS.md > State model
text:
The markdown files are the durable truth for notes. Runtime note state
converges through one path:

head: AGENTS.md > State model
text:
- Notes live at `~/Library/Application Support/Blink/Notes/<id>.md`, where `id`
  is a unique title-derived slug. Body and metadata travel together in each
  markdown file; metadata is YAML frontmatter. Unknown frontmatter must survive
  round trips verbatim. UUIDv5 identity is derived only for v1 compatibility.

head: AGENTS.md > State model
text:
- `NoteStore` owns note mutations and the in-memory index. `AppModel` mirrors it
  for UI surfaces; it is not a second store.

head: AGENTS.md > State model
text:
- `PanelManager` owns live windows, pending editor text, one-panel-per-note
  identity, geometry, and save flushing. Do not bypass it for panel lifecycle.

head: AGENTS.md > State model
text:
- Exact per-device panel frames (`NSWindow` frame autosave), the open-panel set,
  and each note's read/edit mode live in `UserDefaults`. Portable
  `blink.slot` frontmatter is placement intent; the autosaved frame is the
  device-specific position. `NotePanel` suspends frame autosave while physics
  owns a drag/fling/shade and persists the unshaded resting frame once settled.

head: AGENTS.md > State model
text:
- External writers are first-class. The directory watcher calls
  `NoteStore.reconcile()`, producing the same notifications as in-app edits.

head: AGENTS.md > State model
text:
- `config.json` owns behavior and appearance and hot-applies independently of
  note state. `BLINK_HOME` overrides the file-backed root (notes, config, and
  attachments) for tests/agents; it does not redirect `UserDefaults`. The Mac
  peer host is disabled whenever `BLINK_HOME` is set so sandbox notes can never
  inherit the production device identity or trust list.

text: 2. This file's hard requirements are non-regression constraints.

3. `docs/cli.md`, `docs/config.md`, `docs/workspaces.md`, and `docs/release.md`

text:
4. `docs/placement.md` is mixed-status: the grid primitive is shipped; its
   live-plane collision, scene, and tidy semantics are proposed.

head: AGENTS.md > Source-of-truth order
text:
5. `docs/v2-plan.md`, `docs/v2-ui-map.md`, and
   `docs/notes-representation.md` are local, untracked design references absent
   from a fresh clone. They contain intent and history and may lag the code.

head: AGENTS.md > Source-of-truth order

6. `docs/agent-api.md` and `docs/agent-integration.md` are proposals, not
   implemented surfaces.

  `bun dev` → `localhost:3060/studio`).

text:
- The CLI operates on the same files as the app:
  `blink ls/cat/new/present/type/write/search/rm/path/workspace`; see
  `docs/cli.md`.

head: AGENTS.md > Source-of-truth order
AGENTS.md > Source-of-truth order
text:
- `blink workspace` defines a named treatment in `config.json`; membership is
  one `blink.workspace` frontmatter key. See `docs/workspaces.md`. Brands are
  generic treatments—never hardcode a specific product identity into Blink.

head: AGENTS.md > Where changes belong
text:
- `Sources/BlinkApp` — AppDelegate/status item/popover, command palette,
  AppModel, PanelManager, NotePanel, read-only SourcePanel companions, config hot
  reload, and the note/source web bridges.

head: AGENTS.md > Where changes belong
text:
- `Sources/BlinkCore` — pure Swift with no AppKit: note model and identity,
  frontmatter, atomic file storage, NoteStore, treatments, workspaces, and grid
  math / panel physics. Portable `blink.companions` source references and their
  contained, device-local root resolution also live here.

head: AGENTS.md > Where changes belong
text:
- `Sources/BlinkCLI` — `swift-argument-parser` CLI over BlinkCore. `BlinkPaths`
  keeps the app and CLI on the same locations.

head: AGENTS.md > Where changes belong
text:
- `Sources/BlinkPeer` — encrypted Multipeer Connectivity discovery, pairing,
  and snapshot transport shared by macOS and iOS. Bonjour advertises presence;
  new devices request explicit Mac approval inside an encrypted session, and
  remembered device access remains revocable from the Mac. Both sides keep
  their private identity and trust material in non-synchronizing Keychain
  storage, never preferences; the iOS seed and note cache do not travel in
  device backups.

head: AGENTS.md > Where changes belong
text:
- `apps/ios` — XcodeGen source for the read-only, offline-first iPhone/iPad
  companion. It consumes the local BlinkCore and BlinkPeer package products.

head: AGENTS.md > Where changes belong
text:
- `Tests/BlinkCoreTests` — narrow tests for storage, frontmatter, identity,
  workspaces, grid placement, and panel physics; run the matching suite for
  domain changes.

head: AGENTS.md > Where changes belong
text:
- `web/editor` — vanilla CodeMirror 6 (no React), bundled into
  `dist/editor.html` for note panels and `dist/source-viewer.html` for read-only
  source panels. Load-bearing note bridge contract:
  `ready` / user-only `contentChanged` / `saveRequested` → native;
  `setContent` / `getContent` / `focus` ← native. The source bridge has no
  getter, change message, save request, or native write callback.

head: AGENTS.md > Where changes belong
text:
- Generic panel or web-bridge primitives should be shaped for eventual
  HudsonKit upstreaming once proven here.

head: AGENTS.md > Hard requirements (inherited from v1 bugs)
text:
- Flush pending saves on note-switch, panel-close, and quit. Never trust a
  debounce alone.

head: AGENTS.md > Hard requirements (inherited from v1 bugs)
text: - All note writes are atomic: temp file + `fsync` + rename.

head: AGENTS.md > Hard requirements (inherited from v1 bugs)
text:
- Note metadata lives in the markdown file's frontmatter, never only in a side
  index. Preserve foreign frontmatter verbatim.

head: AGENTS.md > Hard requirements (inherited from v1 bugs)
text: - One panel per note—opening an open note focuses it.

head: AGENTS.md > Hard requirements (inherited from v1 bugs)
text:
- Panel geometry persists per note and restores exactly; never scramble a
  layout.

head: AGENTS.md > Hard requirements (inherited from v1 bugs)
text:
- Note mutations flow through `NoteStore` → notifications → `AppModel`; never
  mutate one UI surface as the source of truth.

head: AGENTS.md > Hard requirements (inherited from v1 bugs)
text:
- `contentChanged` fires on user edits only. Programmatic `setContent` must
  never echo (the v1 cross-note corruption bug).

head: AGENTS.md > Conventions
text:
- `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md` mirror the same instructions (apart from their
  title); keep them in sync.

head: AGENTS.md > Conventions
text:
- For larger initiatives/features, survey the ecosystem first: check HudsonKit
  (`../hudson/packages/native/apple/HudsonKit`) for reusable primitives and
  lattices / talkie / scout (`../lattices`, `../talkie`, `../openscout`) for
  proven patterns. Small widgets/tweaks do not need the survey.

head: AGENTS.md > Conventions
text: - Log prefix `[BLINK]` via HudLogger (HudsonObservability).

head: AGENTS.md > Conventions
text:
- Hyper = ⌃⌥⇧⌘. Global hotkeys use Carbon `RegisterEventHotKey` and do not
  require Accessibility permission.

head: AGENTS.md > Conventions
text: - User-visible name is "Blink".

head: AGENTS.md > Conventions
text:
- GUI verification: LSUIElement apps are invisible to System Events' "visible
  processes." Activate Blink before synthesized keystrokes, and use `AXRaise`
  for restored panels.

head: jupyter.nvim
text: A Neovim plugin that reproduces the Jupyter Notebook experience inside the editor.

head: jupyter.nvim > Goal
text: Provide an interactive code execution experience equivalent to Jupyter Notebook from within Neovim, while preserving the editor's native strengths (text editing, Treesitter, LSP integration). Users can run code, get completions, and inspect symbols against a live Jupyter kernel without leaving Neovim.

head: jupyter.nvim > Overall Strategy: Two Lua Modules in One Repository
text: The implementation lives in a single repository but is split into **two Lua modules**, separated by responsibility:

head: jupyter.nvim > Overall Strategy: Two Lua Modules in One Repository
text:
1. **`jupyter_core`** (`lua/jupyter_core/`) — the API module.
   - Backed by a Python remote plugin (`rplugin/python3/`) that wraps `jupyter_client` and speaks RPC to Neovim.
   - Exposes a higher-level, typed Lua abstraction (`Kernel`, `Output`, `KernelSpec`, …) over the raw RPC.
   - Knows nothing about cells, buffers, virtual text, or the percent format. Pure Jupyter-domain abstraction.
   - Reusable in principle: another plugin could `require("jupyter_core")` directly for Jupyter access.

head: jupyter.nvim > Overall Strategy: Two Lua Modules in One Repository
text:
2. **`jupyter`** (`lua/jupyter/`) — the editor module.
   - Depends on `jupyter_core`.
   - Owns everything editor-facing: cell detection, navigation, virtual-text display, completion sources, hover, format conversion, commands, keymaps.

head: jupyter.nvim > Overall Strategy: Two Lua Modules in One Repository
text: Boundary rule: `jupyter_core` must contain no editor concepts (no buffers, no extmarks, no Treesitter), and `jupyter` must not speak the Jupyter protocol directly — it always goes through `jupyter_core`'s Lua interface.

head: jupyter.nvim > Supported File Formats
text:
- **Phase 1 (initial):** Python, Julia, and R source files using the
  percent format (`# %%`).
  - Edited and saved as ordinary `.py` / `.jl` / `.R` files.
  - Cell markers are the same across all three languages — `#` is the
    line-comment character in each, so Jupytext's `# %%` convention
    works uniformly.
  - Cell boundaries are detected via Treesitter; one query lives at
    `queries/<lang>/jupyter.scm` per supported language.

head: jupyter.nvim > Supported File Formats
text:
- **Phase 2 (later):** automatic round-trip conversion with `.ipynb`.
  - On load: `.ipynb` → percent format expanded into the buffer.
  - On save: percent format → `.ipynb`.
  - Metadata and execution outputs are preserved on the `.ipynb` side.

head: jupyter.nvim > Feature Requirements > 1. Cell Detection (Treesitter)
text: - A Treesitter query detects `# %%` markers and extracts code-block ranges.

head: jupyter.nvim > Feature Requirements > 1. Cell Detection (Treesitter)
text:
- One query per supported language lives at `queries/<lang>/jupyter.scm`
  (Phase 1: `python`, `julia`, `r`). The Lua side maps the buffer's
  filetype to the matching language before fetching the query.

head: jupyter.nvim > Feature Requirements > 1. Cell Detection (Treesitter)
text: - Cell type (code / markdown) is distinguished by the marker variant (`# %%` vs `# %% [markdown]`).

head: jupyter.nvim > Feature Requirements > 2. Cell Execution
text: - Send the cell under the cursor to the Jupyter kernel.

head: jupyter.nvim > Feature Requirements > 2. Cell Execution
text:
- Display results **without modifying file contents**, using virtual text (extmarks) only.
  - Floating windows and split windows are explicitly out of scope for output display.

head: jupyter.nvim > Feature Requirements > 2. Cell Execution
text: - Execution status (busy / idle / error) is also surfaced as an indicator via virtual text.

head: jupyter.nvim > Feature Requirements > 2. Cell Execution
text: - **(Future)** Format outputs based on their MIME / content-type as needed — e.g. render `text/plain` as plain virtual text, format `application/json` for readability, surface `text/html` or `image/*` in some lightweight inline form. Phase 1 ships plain-text rendering only.

head: jupyter.nvim > Feature Requirements > 3. Cell Navigation and Creation
text: - Move to the next / previous cell (`next_cell`, `prev_cell`).

head: jupyter.nvim > Feature Requirements > 3. Cell Navigation and Creation
text: - Insert a new cell above / below the cursor (`insert_cell_above`, `insert_cell_below`).

head: jupyter.nvim > Feature Requirements > 3. Cell Navigation and Creation
text: - Delete / merge / split cells.

head: jupyter.nvim > Feature Requirements > 3. Cell Navigation and Creation
text: - Text object / visual selection that covers a whole cell.

head: jupyter.nvim > Feature Requirements > 4. Completion & Hover (virtual LSP)
text:
- A single in-process LSP server, registered via `vim.lsp.start` with a Lua `cmd` function, exposes:
  - `textDocument/completion` backed by the kernel's `complete_request`.
  - `textDocument/hover` backed by the kernel's `inspect_request`.

head: jupyter.nvim > Feature Requirements > 4. Completion & Hover (virtual LSP)
text: - Any LSP-aware client (Neovim built-in, nvim-cmp, blink.cmp, …) gets kernel-backed completions and docs through their generic LSP source — **no plugin-specific adapter is needed**.

head: jupyter.nvim > Feature Requirements > 4. Completion & Hover (virtual LSP)
text: - Position encoding is declared as `utf-8` so LSP positions and Jupyter's byte-based `cursor_pos` use the same unit.

head: jupyter.nvim > Feature Requirements > 4. Completion & Hover (virtual LSP)
text: - Aim to surface completions that pure static analysis (LSP) cannot — e.g. dynamic attributes, DataFrame column names, runtime-defined symbols.

head: jupyter.nvim > Feature Requirements > 5. (Future) Enhanced Cell Visualization
text: - Use virtual text to decorate cell boundaries, execution counters, timestamps, etc.

head: jupyter.nvim > Feature Requirements > 5. (Future) Enhanced Cell Visualization
text: - Folding / highlighting for readability.

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > Development Setup > Version Management
text: The `.version` file and git tags are managed by [bump](https://github.com/perbu/bump). It's installed as a Go tool dependency.

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > Development Setup > Version Management
text: **Release order matters.** Edit and commit `CHANGELOG.md` **before** running `bump`. `bump` tags the commit it creates, and the Docker publish workflow (`.github/workflows/docker.yml`) only publishes when the latest commit on `main` carries the version tag. A changelog commit landing *after* the bump leaves the tag stranded on a non-head commit, and CI's tag check fails silently — image and Helm chart never get pushed.

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > Development Setup > Version Management
text: **Verify the changelog is in sync with `git log` before bumping.** Run `git log --oneline <last-tag>..HEAD` and walk every commit — not just the headline fix. It's easy to land a release that captures the obvious bug fix but quietly omits unrelated `feat`/`fix`/`chore` commits that piggybacked on the same cycle (e.g. v0.21.2 shipped a `LOG_LEVEL` feature, a `DefaultKeepCount` bump, and a chaperone startup-race fix that none of the changelog entries mentioned). Each functional commit in the range should map to a bullet, or you should be able to justify why it doesn't belong (pure refactor, internal-only, etc.).

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > Architecture > Data Flow
text:
1. **Operator** watches Gateway/HTTPRoute resources
   - Generates `routing.json` (host → service mappings) and stores in ConfigMap
   - Generates ghost preamble VCL and merges with user VCL
   - Creates Varnish listeners from Gateway listeners (one per unique port)

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > Architecture > Data Flow
text:
2. **Chaperone** runs as wrapper for varnishd
   - Starts varnishd via vrun package with named listeners from `VARNISH_LISTEN`
   - Watches `routing.json` + EndpointSlices
   - Merges them into `ghost.json` (host → actual pod IPs)
   - Triggers ghost reload via HTTP endpoint

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > Architecture > Data Flow
text:
3. **Ghost VMOD** handles all routing inside Varnish
   - Reads `ghost.json` on reload
   - Routes requests by hostname to weighted backend groups
   - Filters routes by `local.socket` for listener-aware routing
   - Sets `X-Gateway-Listener` header on requests for user VCL

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > Architecture > Multi-Listener Architecture
text:
Each Gateway listener maps to a Varnish `-a` socket named `{proto}-{port}` (e.g., `http-80`, `https-443`).
Multiple Gateway listeners on the same port collapse into a single Varnish socket — hostname
isolation is handled by ghost's existing vhost routing.

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > Architecture > Multi-Listener Architecture
text:
**Container ports = listener ports**: No port translation. Listener port 3000 means Varnish
binds to `:3000` inside the container. Listener changes trigger a pod restart (via infra hash).

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > Architecture > Multi-Listener Architecture
text: **Listener naming convention**: `{proto}-{port}` encodes both protocol and port:

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > Architecture > Multi-Listener Architecture
text: - `http-80` — HTTP on port 80

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > Architecture > Multi-Listener Architecture
text: - `https-443` — HTTPS on port 443

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > Architecture > Multi-Listener Architecture
text: - `http-3000` — HTTP on port 3000

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > Architecture > Multi-Listener Architecture
text:
Ghost uses `local.socket()` to get the Varnish socket name and filters routes accordingly.
The `listeners` field in routing.json/ghost.json contains socket names that a route applies to.
An empty `listeners` list means the route matches on all listeners.

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > Architecture > Multi-Listener Architecture
text: **Request headers**: Ghost sets two headers on every request for use in user VCL:

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > Architecture > Multi-Listener Architecture
text: - `X-Gateway-Listener` — Varnish socket name (e.g., `http-80`)

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > Architecture > Multi-Listener Architecture
text: - `X-Gateway-Route` — HTTPRoute namespace/name (e.g., `default/my-route`)

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > Architecture > Multi-Listener Architecture
text: These propagate to the backend and are available in user VCL:

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > Architecture > Multi-Listener Architecture
text:
**VCL caveat**: User VCL applies globally across all listeners. There is no per-listener or
per-route VCL. Users who need listener-specific behavior should branch on these headers.

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > Architecture > Controller Architecture Principles
text: **Separation of Concerns**

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > Architecture > Controller Architecture Principles
text: The Gateway and HTTPRoute controllers have clearly defined responsibilities:

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > Architecture > Controller Architecture Principles
text: **Gateway Controller** (infrastructure owner):

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > Architecture > Controller Architecture Principles
text:
- Responsibilities:
  - Generate ghost preamble VCL
  - Fetch and merge user VCL from GatewayClassParameters
  - Create and update ConfigMap with `main.vcl`
  - Manage Deployment, Service, RBAC resources
  - Resolve Service shape (Type, annotations, labels, LB class, source ranges, traffic policy) from `GatewayClassParameters.spec.service`, overlaid with `Gateway.spec.infrastructure.{labels,annotations}`
  - Compute infrastructure hash for pod restart detection

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > Architecture > Controller Architecture Principles
text:
- Watches:
  - Gateway resources (primary)
  - GatewayClassParameters (for varnishdExtraArgs, logging, user VCL ref)
  - User VCL ConfigMaps (referenced by GatewayClassParameters)

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > Architecture > Controller Architecture Principles
text: - Owns: Deployment, Service, ConfigMap, Secret, ServiceAccount, Role, RoleBinding

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > Architecture > Controller Architecture Principles
text: **HTTPRoute Controller** (routing owner):

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > Architecture > Controller Architecture Principles
text:
- Responsibilities:
  - Generate routing.json from HTTPRoutes
  - Update ConfigMap with `routing.json` ONLY (preserves main.vcl)
  - Update Gateway listener AttachedRoutes counts

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > Architecture > Controller Architecture Principles
text:
- Watches:
  - HTTPRoute resources (primary)
  - Gateway resources (for parent references)

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > Architecture > Controller Architecture Principles
text: - Owns: routing.json field in ConfigMap (shared ownership)

text: - Logging configuration change

text: - Listener changes (port additions/removals, protocol changes)

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > Architecture > Controller Architecture Principles
text: - **Trigger**: Annotation change causes Kubernetes to perform rolling restart

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > Architecture > Controller Architecture Principles
text: **Hot Reload** (config changes):

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > Architecture > Controller Architecture Principles
text: - User VCL changes → varnishadm reload (no pod restart)

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > Architecture > Controller Architecture Principles
text: - Routing changes → ghost HTTP reload (no pod restart)

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > Architecture > Controller Architecture Principles
text: - **Detection**: Chaperone watches ConfigMap via Kubernetes informers with content-based deduplication

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > Architecture > Controller Architecture Principles
text: - **Trigger**: In-process reload, zero downtime

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > Architecture > Controller Architecture Principles
text: **ConfigMap Shared Ownership Pattern**

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > Architecture > Controller Architecture Principles
text: The Gateway's ConfigMap (`{gateway-name}-vcl`) uses shared ownership:

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > Architecture > Controller Architecture Principles
text: **Rule**: Each controller updates only its owned fields, preserves others.

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > Architecture > Two Reload Paths
text: - **VCL changes** (user VCL updates): varnishadm hot-reload

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > Architecture > Two Reload Paths
text: - **Backend/routing changes**: ghost HTTP reload (`/.varnish-ghost/reload`)

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > Architecture > Cache Invalidation
text:
VarnishCacheInvalidation is a one-shot CRD for purging/banning cached objects across all gateway pods.
Supports multiple paths per resource for batch invalidation.

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > Architecture > Cache Invalidation
text: 1. User creates a VarnishCacheInvalidation CR with type (Purge/Ban), hostname, paths, and gatewayRef

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > Architecture > Cache Invalidation
text: 2. Each chaperone pod watches VarnishCacheInvalidation resources via dynamic client

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > Architecture > Cache Invalidation
text: 3. Chaperone sends HTTP requests to local Varnish for each path: PURGE or BAN method

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > Architecture > Cache Invalidation
text: 4. VCL preamble handles the method: `return(purge)` for PURGE, `std.ban()` for BAN

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > Architecture > Cache Invalidation
text: 5. Chaperone writes per-pod result (with per-path detail) to `status.podResults`

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > Architecture > Cache Invalidation
text: 6. Phase transitions: Pending → InProgress → Complete (all pods succeed) or Failed

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > Architecture > Cache Invalidation
text: 7. Operator GC deletes completed CRs after TTL (default 1h)

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > Architecture > Cache Invalidation
text: - **PURGE**: Exact URL removal. Chaperone sends `PURGE /path` with `Host: hostname`. Varnish looks up and removes the single cached object.

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > Architecture > Cache Invalidation
text: - **BAN**: Regex pattern invalidation. Chaperone sends `BAN /pattern` with `Host: hostname`. Uses ban lurker-friendly expressions (`obj.http.x-cache-host`, `obj.http.x-cache-url`) for efficient background cleanup.

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > Architecture > Cache Invalidation
text: The VCL preamble stores `x-cache-host` and `x-cache-url` on cached objects in `vcl_backend_response` and strips them in `vcl_deliver`. These enable efficient ban lurker matching.

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > Architecture > Ghost ↔ VCL Communication
text:
Ghost should use the Varnish C API directly whenever possible instead of setting internal
request headers for VCL to interpret. Headers are a last resort for values that must cross
VCL subroutine boundaries (e.g., `vcl_recv` → `vcl_backend_response`).

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > Architecture > Ghost ↔ VCL Communication
text: **Use header + postamble for VCL flow control:**

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > Architecture > Ghost ↔ VCL Communication
text:
- `X-Ghost-Pass` header — signals pass mode; the postamble `vcl_recv` (appended after
  user VCL) checks this header and calls `return(pass)`. This ensures user VCL runs
  before the pass decision takes effect. Do NOT use `ctx.set_pass()` as it terminates
  VCL execution immediately, preventing user VCL from running.

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > Architecture > Ghost ↔ VCL Communication
text:
**Use headers only for cross-subroutine bridging** (values set in `vcl_recv` that must
reach `vcl_backend_response` via `bereq`):

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > Architecture > Ghost ↔ VCL Communication
text: - `X-Ghost-Default-TTL` / `X-Ghost-Forced-TTL` — TTL control

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > Architecture > Ghost ↔ VCL Communication
text: - `X-Ghost-Grace` / `X-Ghost-Keep` — stale serving parameters

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > Architecture > Ghost ↔ VCL Communication
text: - `X-Ghost-Cache-Key-Extra` — additional hash data

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > Architecture > Ghost ↔ VCL Communication
text:
**Default cache behavior**: Without a VarnishCachePolicy, ghost sets `pass` on all
routes — behaving as a plain reverse proxy with no caching, consistent with Gateway API
expectations.

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > VCL Merging Strategy
text:
VCL allows multiple definitions of the same subroutine - they get concatenated at compile time. We use this
to avoid parsing user VCL:

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > VCL Merging Strategy
text: 1. Generated VCL includes: ghost import, `vcl_init` (ghost.init, router creation), `vcl_recv` (ghost.recv), `vcl_backend_fetch` (router.backend)

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > VCL Merging Strategy
text: 2. User VCL is appended after the generated VCL

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > VCL Merging Strategy
text: 3. If user defines the same subroutines, their code runs *after* the gateway code

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > VCL Merging Strategy
text: Users who need pre-routing logic (URL normalization, etc.) should define their own `vcl_recv`.

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > VCL Merging Strategy
text: **Important:** Avoid generating `vcl_synth` and `vcl_backend_error` in the gateway VCL:

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > VCL Merging Strategy
text: - These subroutines are commonly customized by users for error handling and synthetic responses

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > VCL Merging Strategy
text: - If our generated VCL includes `return` statements in these subroutines, user VCL won't run (VCL execution stops at first return)

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > VCL Merging Strategy
text: - This creates unexpected conflicts where user customizations are silently ignored

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > VCL Merging Strategy
text: - Instead, handle errors and special cases in `vcl_recv` before backend selection, or provide VMOD methods users can call explicitly

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > VCL Merging Strategy > Synthetic Response Pattern for VMODs
text: When the ghost VMOD needs to generate synthetic responses (e.g., 404 for unknown vhosts), we use the **synthetic backend pattern** instead of VCL error handlers:

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > VCL Merging Strategy > Synthetic Response Pattern for VMODs
text: 1. **Create a synthetic backend** - A struct implementing `VclBackend` trait that generates responses programmatically

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > VCL Merging Strategy > Synthetic Response Pattern for VMODs
text: 2. **Populate beresp in get_response()** - Set status, headers, and body content directly

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > VCL Merging Strategy > Synthetic Response Pattern for VMODs
text: 3. **Return from director** - The director returns the synthetic backend instead of `None`

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > VCL Merging Strategy > Synthetic Response Pattern for VMODs
Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > VCL Merging Strategy > Synthetic Response Pattern for VMODs
text: - No VCL generation needed for error handling

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > VCL Merging Strategy > Synthetic Response Pattern for VMODs
text: - Zero conflict with user VCL

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > VCL Merging Strategy > Synthetic Response Pattern for VMODs
text: - Responses generated entirely within the VMOD

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > VCL Merging Strategy > Synthetic Response Pattern for VMODs
text: - User can still customize via `vcl_backend_response` or `vcl_deliver` if needed

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > VCL Merging Strategy > Synthetic Response Pattern for VMODs
text: **See:** `ghost/src/not_found_backend.rs` for the implementation

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > File Formats > routing.json (operator output, stored in ConfigMap)
text: Generated by operator from HTTPRoutes. Maps hostnames to routes with match criteria:

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > File Formats > routing.json (operator output, stored in ConfigMap)
text:
The `listeners` field contains Varnish socket names (`{proto}-{port}`) that this route
applies to. Empty or absent means the route matches on all listeners.

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > File Formats > ghost.json (chaperone output, consumed by ghost VMOD)
text: Generated by chaperone by merging routing.json with EndpointSlice discoveries.

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > File Formats > ghost.json (chaperone output, consumed by ghost VMOD)
text:
Uses **backend groups** for correct weighted traffic distribution. Weights belong to the
service group, not individual pods. Selection is two-level: (1) pick a group by weight,
(2) pick a random pod within the group. This ensures traffic split matches configured
weights regardless of replica counts.

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > File Formats > ghost.json (chaperone output, consumed by ghost VMOD)
text:
If a group has no backends (service has no ready endpoints), requests selecting that group
return 500. Traffic is **not** redistributed to other groups — this matches the Gateway API
spec behavior (consistent with Envoy Gateway).

| `GATEWAY_IMAGE` | `ghcr.io/varnish/gateway-chaperone:latest` | Combined varnish+ghost+chaperone image (the "gateway data plane") |

The operator manages all GatewayClasses with `controllerName: varnish-software.com/gateway`.
Multiple GatewayClasses can coexist, each with different GatewayClassParameters (different VCL, varnishd args, etc.).

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > Deployment > Helm (Recommended)
text: The easiest way to install Varnish Gateway is using the Helm chart from the OCI registry:

head: Varnish Gateway Operator - Development Guide > Deployment > Helm (Recommended)
text: **Important:** Always use the published OCI chart, not `./charts/varnish-gateway`. The local chart has `appVersion: 0.0.0-dev` placeholder values — CI substitutes the real version at publish time. Using the local chart will deploy with wrong image tags.

head: AGENTS.md
text:
Wallaby is a family of Rails engine gems that autocomplete resourceful
controllers and views for an ORM (ActiveRecord) to build admin interfaces.

head: AGENTS.md > Repository layout
text:
Monorepo of five gems plus the documentation site. Dependency direction
(low → high):

head: AGENTS.md > Repository layout
text:
| Gem | Path | Role |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `wallaby-view` | `wallaby-view/` | Plain view/rendering helpers, no Rails app |
| `wallaby-core` | `wallaby-core/` | Core: decorators, servicers, paginators, providers |
| `wallaby-active_record` | `wallaby-active_record/` | ActiveRecord adaptor for `wallaby-core` |
| `wallaby` | `wallaby/` | Rails engine (`app/`), assets, generators, JS |
| `wallaby-cop` | `wallaby-cop/` | Shared RuboCop config, standalone |

head: AGENTS.md > Repository layout
text: Supporting structure at the repository root:

head: AGENTS.md > Repository layout
text:
| Area | Path | Role |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Documentation site | `docs/`, `index.md`, `_config.yml` | just-the-docs (Jekyll) site covering the whole project; home page is `index.md`, pages under `docs/` |
| Docs deployment | `.github/workflows/pages.yml` | Builds the Jekyll site and deploys to GitHub Pages on pushes to `main` (also `workflow_dispatch`) |
| CI (lint) | `.github/workflows/pr-build.yml` | RuboCop only, on changed files (does not run specs) |
| Test harness | `spec/` | Host dummy app at `spec/dummy`; `spec/support/` holds helpers/shared examples |
| Version matrix | `.gemfiles/` | `Gemfile.rails-8.0` / `Gemfile.rails-8.1` for the CI matrix; do not pin Ruby |
| Agent files | `.opencode/` | Skills for running specs and releasing gems (see [Skills](#skills)) |

head: AGENTS.md > Repository layout
text:
- `wallaby-core` is the bulk of the logic under `lib/wallaby/`; the `wallaby`
  gem is mostly the mountable engine in `app/` plus `lib/wallaby/generators/`.

head: AGENTS.md > Repository layout
text:
- Gem versions are independent. `wallaby`'s gemspec comment
  (`This will determine wallaby-core's version`) means the dependency
  constraints in the gemspecs must stay in sync when releasing.

head: AGENTS.md > Repository layout

  `remote_theme: just-the-docs/just-the-docs` (fetched at build time), not
  `theme: just-the-docs`. Jekyll build artifacts (`.jekyll-cache/`, `_site/`)
  are gitignored.

head: AGENTS.md > Toolchain

- Ruby: root `Gemfile` pins `ruby '4.0.7'`; gems require `>= 3.3.0`.
  The `.gemfiles/*` matrix gemfiles do **not** pin a Ruby version.

head: AGENTS.md > Toolchain

head: AGENTS.md > Toolchain

head: AGENTS.md > Docker
text:
`Dockerfile`, `docker-compose.yml` and `docker/entrypoint.sh` provide a
self-contained dev environment (Ruby 4.0.7, Node/Yarn, Postgres 18, MySQL 9) so
the suite and the dummy app can run without a local toolchain. SQLite is
file-based and needs no service.

head: AGENTS.md > Docker
text:
- Gems are installed into the `bundle` named volume; the entrypoint runs
  `bundle install` on first boot and whenever the Gemfile changes.

head: AGENTS.md > Docker
text:
- The `app` service defaults to `RAILS_ENV=test`, like CI. To boot the dummy app
  (the service publishes `${APP_PORT:-3000}`), override the environment:
  ```shell
  docker compose exec -e RAILS_ENV=development app bin/rails db:schema:load
  docker compose exec -e RAILS_ENV=development app bin/rails server -b 0.0.0.0
  ```

head: AGENTS.md > Docker
text:
- Database ports are intentionally not published, so the stack does not clash
  with a local Postgres/MySQL. Publish them per service if a host client needs
  access. `postgres:18` mounts its data at `/var/lib/postgresql` (not `.../data`).

head: AGENTS.md > Docker
text:
- Node 20 / Yarn 1 are in the image for the `wallaby` gem's asset build, kept in
  the `node_modules` volume:
  ```shell
  docker compose exec app bash -lc 'cd wallaby && yarn install'
  docker compose exec app bash -lc 'cd wallaby && yarn build:js && yarn build:scss'
  ```

head: AGENTS.md > Docker
text:
- `db:seed` populates demo data for the dummy app (products, categories, orders,
  blogs with Active Storage images). It downloads placeholder images from
  `picsum.photos`, so it needs network access.

head: AGENTS.md > Docker
text:
- `ostruct` and `puma` were added as development dependencies so the dummy app
  boots on Ruby 4.0 (`massa` requires `ostruct`, which is no longer a default
  gem) and so `bin/rails server` has a server gem. The specs need neither.

head: AGENTS.md > Testing
text:
- Specs boot the **host dummy app** at `spec/dummy`, not the gems in isolation.
  `spec/rails_helper.rb` requires `dummy/config/environment`.

head: AGENTS.md > Testing
text:
- `DB` selects the adapter the specs run against (default `postgresql`):
  ```shell
  DB=postgresql POSTGRES_USER=postgres POSTGRES_PASSWORD=password bundle exec rspec
  DB=mysql MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=password bundle exec rspec
  DB=sqlite bundle exec rspec
  ```
  Schemas live in `spec/dummy/db/{sqlite,postgresql,mysql}_schema.rb` and all
  three carry the shared tables. `AllPostgresType` is pinned to the `postgresql`
  connection (like `AllMysqlType`/`AllSqliteType`), so its PostgreSQL-only
  columns work regardless of which adapter `DB` selects.

head: AGENTS.md > Testing
text:
- **All three databases must be running**, regardless of `DB`. The dummy app
  overrides `db:test:load_schema` and `db:test:purge` in
  `spec/dummy/lib/tasks/database.rake` to loop over `postgresql`, `mysql` and
  `sqlite`; the purge task also touches every configured connection. `DB=sqlite`
  therefore does **not** avoid needing Postgres and MySQL. CI supplies Postgres
  and MySQL services for this reason.

head: AGENTS.md > Testing
text:
- Coverage: `simplecov` enforces `SimpleCov.minimum_coverage 100` in
  `spec/rails_helper.rb`. Adding untested code fails the suite. Set `DEEP=1`
  to switch to `deep-cover` instead.

head: AGENTS.md > Testing
text:
- CI (`.github/workflows/pr-build.yml`) runs **RuboCop only**, and only on
  changed files. It does not run the test suite. A green CI does not mean the
  specs pass — run them yourself.

head: AGENTS.md > Conventions
text: - Every Ruby file starts with `# frozen_string_literal: true`.

head: AGENTS.md > Conventions
text:
- RuboCop config is inherited from the local `wallaby-cop` gem
  (`gitlab-styles` + `rubocop-rails` + `rubocop-rspec`, `Layout/LineLength`
  max 120). Spec files are excluded from several cops — see `.rubocop.yml`.

head: AGENTS.md > Conventions
text:
- Follow Keep a Changelog + SemVer. Each gem has its own `CHANGELOG.md` with an
  `## [Unreleased]` section; add entries there.

head: AGENTS.md > Conventions
text:
- Test support lives in `spec/support/` (helpers, metadata, shared examples,
  custom spec types), auto-required by `rails_helper.rb`.

head: AGENTS.md > Gotchas
text:
- **Docs live in this repo.** The documentation site (just-the-docs/Jekyll) is
  built from the root `_config.yml` and the markdown under `docs/`. The
  `docs/*.md` links in `wallaby/README.md` point at these local files. When
  adding or updating documentation, edit the markdown in `docs/` and add Jekyll
  build artifacts (`.jekyll-cache/`, `_site/`) to `.gitignore`, not the repo.

head: AGENTS.md > Gotchas
text:
- `wallaby-cop`'s version constant is in `lib/wallaby-cop.rb`
  (`Wallaby::Cop::VERSION`), not a `version.rb`.

head: AGENTS.md > Gotchas
text:
- `wallaby` has a separate JS/asset build (`package.json`, `yarn.lock`);
  `node_modules/` is gitignored.

head: AGENTS.md > Gotchas
text: - RuboCop command in CI uses `--force-exclusion` against `git diff` output.

head: AGENTS.md > Gotchas
text:
- **`csv` must stay declared.** It is not a default gem since Ruby 3.4, but
  `wallaby-core` and `wallaby` `require 'csv'` at runtime, so each gemspec
  declares it. Do not remove those dependencies.

head: AGENTS.md > Gotchas
text:
- Building Ruby 4.0.7 locally on macOS needs `MACOSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET` set to
  the Homebrew libraries' target (e.g. `26.0`); the default in some shell setups
  is lower, and `ld` warnings then make Ruby's configure probes report false
  negatives.

head: CLAUDE.md — chromium.swt > What this repo is
text:
`chromium.swt` is **the Java product** of Equo Chromium: the OSGi bundle `com.equo.chromium`.
It embeds a Chromium browser (CEF, via a vendored JCEF) into Java apps under **four toolkit
modes** — SWT, Swing, Standalone (CEF owns the window), and Windowless (offscreen). The public
SWT API deliberately mirrors `org.eclipse.swt.browser.Browser` so it's a drop-in replacement.

head: CLAUDE.md — chromium.swt > What this repo is
text:
This repo is **not built standalone** — it's orchestrated from the sibling `../chromium.build`
(`./gradlew buildP2Repo`, needs **JDK 11+**; Tycho/Maven). See `../chromium.build/CLAUDE.md`.

head: CLAUDE.md — chromium.swt > What this repo is
text:
> **Per-version branches.** Each CEF/Chromium version lives on its own branch (`80`, `116`,
> `124`, `128`, `138`, `144`, …). They share the same structure; only versions and a few
> feature flags differ. **Check out the branch matching the version you're working on** — don't
> assume `build`/`master` is "latest". `src/version.properties` + `Engine.CEFVERSION` tell you
> which version the checkout is.

head: CLAUDE.md — chromium.swt > Source layout
text:
Exported packages (MANIFEST): `com.equo.chromium`, `.swt`, `.utils`, `.events`. Everything
under `internal` / `swt.internal` is implementation detail.

head: CLAUDE.md — chromium.swt > Core architecture — how the pieces connect
text:
**`ChromiumBrowser`** (`com.equo.chromium`) is the main public interface, with static factory
methods: `swt(composite, style)`, `swing(container, layout, url)`, `standalone(url, …)`,
`windowless(url, …)`, plus lifecycle (`earlyInit`, `startBrowsers`), `getAllBrowsers`,
`clearCookies`. Every factory calls `IndependentBrowser.checkToolkit(BrowserType)` —
**only one toolkit may be initialized per process**; mixing throws `UnsupportedOperationException`.

head: CLAUDE.md — chromium.swt > Core architecture — how the pieces connect
text:
**`IndependentBrowser`** (`internal`, abstract, implements `ChromiumBrowser`) — the
**toolkit-agnostic core**. It owns the `CefClient` and all CEF handlers (lifespan, request,
display, load, find, print, download), the event `Subscriber`, the JS↔Java message routers, and
implements navigation, `executeJavaScript`, screenshots, DevTools, `printToPdf`, storage. The
three windowed/offscreen toolkits subclass it directly:

head: CLAUDE.md — chromium.swt > Core architecture — how the pieces connect
text:
- **`Standalone`** → `ChromiumBrowserStandalone`. CEF creates its **own native OS window**; adds
  window management (fullscreen, icon, title, size/position, move/resize, maximize/minimize) and
  optional Client-Side Decoration that injects a `window.equo.*` JS API via a message router.

head: CLAUDE.md — chromium.swt > Core architecture — how the pieces connect
text:
- **`SwingBrowser`** → embeds CEF's UI component into an **AWT/Swing `Container`**; Swing file
  dialog (`JFileChooser`), JS dialogs (`JOptionPane`), clipboard routers, Mac keyboard shortcuts.

head: CLAUDE.md — chromium.swt > Core architecture — how the pieces connect
text: - **`Windowless`** → **offscreen/headless** browser (`CefBrowserWl`).

head: CLAUDE.md — chromium.swt > Core architecture — how the pieces connect
text: **SWT path is different** (it's a real SWT widget, not a subclass of IndependentBrowser):

head: CLAUDE.md — chromium.swt > Core architecture — how the pieces connect
text:
`Chromium` ([Chromium.java](com.equo.chromium/src/com/equo/chromium/swt/internal/Chromium.java))
is the heavy SWT/JNI bridge: wires every CEF handler to SWT, manages the SWT widget, focus,
keyboard, drag-and-drop, context menus, downloads, popups, cookies, `setUrl`/`setText`.
**`extraApi()`** lazily builds the inner **`ExtraApi`** — the adapter that exposes the SWT
browser through the same toolkit-agnostic `ChromiumBrowser` API (so SWT reuses
`IndependentBrowser`'s navigation/JS/DevTools/etc. instead of duplicating them). `ChromiumBrowser.swt(...)`
returns `new Browser(...).getWebBrowser()` → that `ExtraApi`.

head: CLAUDE.md — chromium.swt > Core architecture — how the pieces connect
text:
**`Engine`** (`internal`) — static **CEF lifecycle manager**. `loadLib()` loads the native libs
from the `chromium-<CEFVERSION>` folder (e.g. `chromium-7204` on the 138 branch) via
`SystemBootstrap` + `CefApp.startup`. Provides `initCEF(BrowserType)`, `createClient()`,
`startCefLoop()`, scheme-handler registration, and the `SecurityManager`. The config surface is
**`chromium.*` JVM system properties** (e.g. `-Dchromium.remote_debugging_port`,
`-Dchromium.multi_threaded_message_loop`, `-Dchromium.headless`, `-Dchromium.cache_path`,
`-Dchromium.args`, `-Dchromium.ssl`, proxy props…).

head: CLAUDE.md — chromium.swt > Events & extension points
text:
- **Events:** the `events` package + `Subscriber`/`ISubscriber` pub-sub. Call `subscribe()` on
  any browser, then register listeners for `EventType`s (load, title, console, download,
  before-browse, before-popup, fullscreen, …).

head: CLAUDE.md — chromium.swt > Events & extension points
text:
- **spi** (`swt/internal/spi`): custom **scheme/protocol handlers**, **`CommunicationManager` +
  `CommRouterHandler`** (the JS↔Java bridge via CEF message routers), **`ScriptExtension`**
  (inject JS extensions), **`SecurityManager`**, and resource-request middleware.

head: CLAUDE.md — chromium.swt > Conventions & gotchas
text:
- **Match the branch to the CEF version.** Cross-version edits belong on each version's branch;
  `Engine.CEFVERSION` / `version.properties` are the source of truth for the checkout.

head: CLAUDE.md — chromium.swt > Conventions & gotchas
text:
- **Never hand-edit `cef/org/cef/`** — it's regenerated from `../java-cef` by
  `chromium.build`'s `copyJCefJava`. Edit `../java-cef` instead. Same for the vendored
  `com/github/cliftonlabs/json_simple`.

head: CLAUDE.md — chromium.swt > Conventions & gotchas
text: - **One toolkit per process** — `IndependentBrowser.checkToolkit` enforces it.

head: CLAUDE.md — chromium.swt > Conventions & gotchas
text: - Code uses SWT internals (`@SuppressWarnings("restriction")`, `org.eclipse.swt.internal.*`).

head: CLAUDE.md — chromium.swt > Conventions & gotchas
text:
- The native lib is `equochro` (Equo's JCEF rebrand), loaded from the `com.equo.chromium.cef.*`
  fragment, not bundled here.

head: CLAUDE.md — chromium.swt > Conventions & gotchas
text: - Build/run through `../chromium.build` (P2 repo + samples), not Maven in isolation.
