head: Bauplan > Looking up documentation
text: **CLI:** The `bauplan` CLI is also self-documenting:

head: Bauplan > Looking up documentation
text: - `bauplan --help` — lists all available commands

head: Bauplan > Looking up documentation
text: - `bauplan <command> --help` — shows arguments and options for a specific command (e.g., `bauplan query --help`, `bauplan branch --help`)

head: Bauplan > Looking up documentation > Embedded data documentation
text: In Bauplan, table-level and column-level documentation is accessible by the CLI and Python SDK. This documentation can hold any text the user would like, but it is best to use as a **semantic layer** that describes the intent and context of tables and columns to ensure correct usage of the data. It is stored in Iceberg and versioned per data branch, so a table documented on one branch may be bare on another.

head: Bauplan > Looking up documentation > Embedded data documentation
text: **With the CLI.** When the `bauplan table get ...` command is used, table-level documentation is first shown with the title `Table Documentation`. Column-level documentation is available in the `DOC` column, although it is truncated if longer than a fixed amount or if it spans more than one line. If the column-level documentation is truncated, a note is printed that will direct the user to use `-O json` to receive the full documentation. In the JSON output, table-level documentation is at `properties.comment` rather than a top-level key, and column-level documentation is at `fields[].doc`.

head: Bauplan > Looking up documentation > Embedded data documentation
text: **With the Python SDK.** When `bauplan.Client.get_table` is called, a `bauplan.schema.Table` instance is returned; the table-level documentation is accessible by the `bauplan.schema.Table.comment` property. The column-level documentation is accessible by the `bauplan.schema.TableField.doc` property, which is never truncated.

head: Bauplan > Looking up documentation > Embedded data documentation
text: **Authoring.** Documentation is only written for materialized models when running a pipeline. Table-level documentation is set from the model's function docstring if defined, or from the output schema's class docstring otherwise. Column-level documentation is set from the `doc` parameter of the `TableField` annotation. Both docstrings pass through `inspect.cleandoc`, so indentation is normalized and a whitespace-only docstring means no documentation at all.

head: Bauplan > Skills
text: Skills whose names start with `bauplan-` contain use-case-specific instructions (e.g., building pipelines, ingesting data, debugging failed runs); when a relevant skill is available, follow its guidance for that workflow.

head: Bauplan > Authentication
text: Assume Bauplan credentials are available via local CLI config, environment variables, or a profile. Do not ever prompt for API keys, nor ask the user to tell you their API key: if there are no keys set, tell the user to visit https://app.bauplanlabs.com/dashboard, get the key and do the setup following the instructions on the screen.

head: CLAUDE.md
text:
Guidance for working on **rproc** — a resource & process monitor for Linux,
built with `Slint` (software renderer). This file captures the project's
conventions so changes stay consistent and pass CI on the first try.

head: CLAUDE.md > Project shape
text: - Rust **edition 2024**, binary crate `rproc`.

head: CLAUDE.md > Project shape
text:
- GUI on `Slint`, rendered by the **software backend** (no GPU context, lowest
  resident footprint); system data via `sysinfo`, GPU via `nvml-wrapper`.

head: CLAUDE.md > Project shape
text:
- The `.slint` views live at the crate root under `ui/` and are compiled by
  `build.rs` (`slint::include_modules!()` in `main.rs` generates the Rust
  bindings). `ui/` holds `app.slint` (the `MainWindow`), one file per tab,
  plus `sidebar`, `widgets`, `structs`, `theme`.

head: CLAUDE.md > Project shape
text:
- Layout:
  - `src/main.rs` — entry point + `slint::include_modules!()`.
  - `src/app.rs` — owns the `MainWindow`, the `Sampler`, per-tab state and the
    `slint::Timer` that polls the snapshot and drives all callbacks.
  - `src/monitor/` — data collection (system, processes, services, startup,
    gpu, sampler). No UI here.
  - `src/ui/` — the **glue**: each tab maps a `Snapshot` into the Slint models
    (`performance`, `processes`, `services`, `startup`, `settings`), plus
    `icons`, `graph`, `model`, and the pure formatting/sorting/filter helpers.
    No drawing here (that's the `.slint` files).
  - `src/daemon/` — background sampling daemon (`pidfile`, `storage`).
  - `src/settings.rs`, `src/theme.rs` — config and a few `slint::Color`s.

head: CLAUDE.md > Project shape
text:
Keep the **monitor (data) / ui (glue) / .slint (render)** separation intact:
collection belongs under `src/monitor`, model-building under `src/ui`, drawing
in `ui/*.slint`. The UI is retained-mode: update Slint model properties from
the glue, don't try to "redraw". New optional or self-contained features go in
their own module with minimal hooks elsewhere.

head: CLAUDE.md > Project shape > Slint / software-renderer gotchas
text:
- The software renderer can't take a dynamic `Path.commands` string, and `for`
  is not allowed inside a `Path` — use a fixed set of child line elements
  (graphs are 60-point polylines fed exactly 60 values; see `src/ui/graph.rs`).

head: CLAUDE.md > Project shape > Slint / software-renderer gotchas
text:
- Don't replace a list's `ModelRc` every tick (it recreates delegates and drops
  in-flight clicks); reconcile a persistent `VecModel` in place via
  `ui::model::sync`.

head: CLAUDE.md > Project shape > Slint / software-renderer gotchas
text: - `Rectangle`'s `color` is reserved; name custom color props something else.

head: CLAUDE.md > Project shape > Slint / software-renderer gotchas
text:
- std-widgets follow the system light scheme — `MainWindow` forces
  `Palette.color-scheme = ColorScheme.dark` so their scrollbars/sliders match.

head: CLAUDE.md > The hygiene loop — run before every commit
text:
CI runs `fmt`, `clippy`, `test`, and `build`, all with `RUSTFLAGS="-D warnings"`.
Mirror that locally so nothing fails after push:

head: CLAUDE.md > The hygiene loop — run before every commit
text:
- **Warnings are errors.** CI sets `-D warnings`; do not merge code that warns.
  Don't blanket-`#[allow(...)]` to silence clippy — fix the cause, or add a
  narrowly scoped allow with a comment explaining why.

head: CLAUDE.md > The hygiene loop — run before every commit
text:
- **`--locked` is mandatory.** `Cargo.lock` is committed and CI builds with
  `--locked`. Never let a build silently update the lockfile; if you change
  deps, commit the updated `Cargo.lock` in the same change.

head: CLAUDE.md > The hygiene loop — run before every commit
text: - Run `cargo fmt` before committing — the `Format` job fails on any diff.

head: CLAUDE.md > Dependencies
text:
- Add deps deliberately; this is a lean monitor. Prefer the standard library
  and existing crates over pulling in new ones.

head: CLAUDE.md > Dependencies
text:
- Pin sensible versions in `Cargo.toml` and keep `default-features = false`
  with explicit feature lists where the project already does (see `slint`,
  `image`, `resvg`). `slint` is pinned to an exact version and enables only
  `backend-winit`, `renderer-software` and `software-renderer-path`; `resvg`
  drops its `text` feature (icons are shapes, and `text` would pull `fontdb` +
  system fontconfig).

head: CLAUDE.md > Dependencies
text:
- **System build deps:** Slint's winit/font stack links `fontconfig` on Linux,
  so building needs `libfontconfig1-dev` (plus `libxkbcommon-dev`, `libx11-dev`,
  `libxcb1-dev`, `libwayland-dev`). The CI/release workflows install these; keep
  them in sync if the dep set changes. No OpenGL dev package is needed (software
  renderer).

head: CLAUDE.md > Dependencies
text:
- After any dependency change: `cargo build --locked` and commit the resulting
  `Cargo.lock`.

head: CLAUDE.md > Dependencies
text:
- The release profile is tuned for a small binary (`lto = "thin"`,
  `codegen-units = 1`, `strip`, `panic = "abort"`). Don't undo these casually —
  note that `panic = "abort"` means no unwinding, so don't write code that
  relies on catching panics.

head: CLAUDE.md > Rust conventions
text:
- **Error handling:** use `anyhow::Result` with `?` for fallible paths
  (`anyhow` is the project's error crate). Add context with `.context(...)`
  rather than bare `?` when the failure site would otherwise be ambiguous.

head: CLAUDE.md > Rust conventions
text:
- **No panics on the hot path.** This is a long-running UI sampling at a fixed
  cadence — avoid `unwrap()`/`expect()` on values that depend on the live
  system (process lists, GPU handles, file reads). Reserve `expect()` for
  genuine invariants and give it a message that states the invariant.

head: CLAUDE.md > Rust conventions
text:
- **`unsafe`:** the crate uses `libc` for some syscalls. Any `unsafe` block
  must carry a `// SAFETY:` comment justifying it. Keep `unsafe` minimal and
  wrapped in a safe API.

head: CLAUDE.md > Rust conventions
text:
- **Don't block the UI thread.** Sampling that can stall (disk, NVML, process
  enumeration) runs on the sampler thread; the UI only reads the published
  `Snapshot`. Keep blocking work out of the timer tick and Slint callbacks so
  the event loop stays responsive.

head: CLAUDE.md > Rust conventions
text:
- Follow existing idioms: borrow over clone where cheap, iterators over manual
  loops, `match` over nested `if let` when it reads clearer. Match the
  surrounding code's naming and comment density.

head: CLAUDE.md > Comments & docs
text:
- **Self-explanatory code first.** Clear names and small functions beat
  comments. If a comment is needed to explain *what* code does, rename or
  refactor instead.

head: CLAUDE.md > Comments & docs
text:
- Keep comments sleek and rare. Comment only the *why* behind a non-obvious
  decision (see the `panic = "abort"` note in `Cargo.toml`) — never the *what*.
  Avoid comment blocks and section banners.

head: CLAUDE.md > Comments & docs
text:
- A short `///` on a public item is fine when the name alone isn't enough;
  don't document the obvious.

head: CLAUDE.md > Tests
CLAUDE.md > Tests
text:
- Cover pure data transforms in `monitor` (parsing, aggregation, sorting)
  especially. UI rendering is hard to unit-test — keep logic out of draw code
  so it *can* be tested from a sibling test file.

head: CLAUDE.md > Tests
text: - `cargo test --all-features --locked` must pass before pushing.

head: CLAUDE.md > Packaging & release (don't touch unless asked)
text:
- Packaging lives in `packaging/` and the `Makefile` (`make deb`, `make rpm`,
  `make flatpak`). The version is read from `Cargo.toml`.

head: CLAUDE.md > Packaging & release (don't touch unless asked)
text:
- Releases go through `make release` (interactive: bump, tag `vX.Y.Z`, push) —
  CI's release workflow then publishes artifacts. Don't hand-edit version
  numbers or tags outside that flow.

head: CLAUDE.md > Pull requests
text:
- Keep PRs focused and the diff minimal — match the prefix style of recent
  commits (`fix(ui):`, `feat(ui):`, `chore:`).

head: CLAUDE.md > Pull requests
text: - Before opening a PR, confirm the full hygiene loop above passes locally.

head: LangLib project policies
text:
LangLib is a Lean 4 library of esoteric programming language semantics, with a
human-readable front-end language (Turpentine) and verified compilers from it.

head: LangLib project policies > This file
text:
`AGENTS.md` is a symbolic link to this file, so every coding agent reads the
same policies whichever name it looks for. There is one copy: edit
`CLAUDE.md`, never replace the link with a second copy of the text. If your
tool rewrote `AGENTS.md` into a regular file, restore it with
`git checkout AGENTS.md` and put the change in `CLAUDE.md` instead.

head: LangLib project policies > This file
text:
These are the conventions. The contribution checklist, what a complete
language or compiler contribution consists of, and the rules on
computational-class claims live in `CONTRIBUTING.md`; read it before adding
a language, an example, or a compiler. Keep both files true of the
repository as you go: anything you learn that the next agent would have to
rediscover belongs in one of them, in the same commit as the change that
taught it to you.

head: LangLib project policies > Toolchain and layout
text:
* Lean toolchain is pinned in `lean-toolchain` (currently 4.33.x). Do not
  upgrade without an explicit request.

head: LangLib project policies > Toolchain and layout
text:
* Standard Lake layout with a single library, `Langlib`. Everything lives
  under the `Langlib/` folder. Test driver: `Langlib/Tests/Main.lean`, run
  with `lake test`.

head: LangLib project policies > Toolchain and layout
text:
* Each language lives in `Langlib/Languages/<Langname>/` with, at minimum:
  `Syntax.lean` (AST), `Parser.lean`, `Semantics.lean` (pure, fuel-based
  evaluator), `Main.lean` (runner executable), and a `README.md`.

head: LangLib project policies > Toolchain and layout
text:
* Shared infrastructure (byte I/O model, machine execution results, parser
  helpers, test harness) lives in `Langlib/Common/`.

head: LangLib project policies > Toolchain and layout
text:
* Documentation for each language goes to `docs/<langname>/` (lowercase),
  Lean code to `Langlib/Languages/<Langname>/` (capitalised Lean module name).
  Per-language computability accounts live in `docs/<langname>/computability.md`.
  Numbered source links must point to the exact declaration line; update
  both the path and line number when moving a definition or its proof.

head: LangLib project policies > Toolchain and layout
text:
* Example programs go to `Langlib/Examples/<Langname>/`, using the
  language's customary file extension. Language READMEs link their example
  folder and test module with relative markdown links (e.g.
  `[examples](../../Examples/Brainfuck/)` from
  `Langlib/Languages/Brainfuck/README.md`).

head: LangLib project policies > Toolchain and layout
text:
* An example that reads input or needs flags explains its own usage in a
  comment (e.g. `Usage: echo -n 34 | lake exe brainfuck ...`), where the
  language has any comment syntax at all; otherwise the usage goes in the
  language README's examples table.

head: LangLib project policies > Toolchain and layout
text:
* The front-end language is called Turpentine; it is a language like any
  other in the library, so its sources use the `.turp` extension and its
  Lean code lives under `Langlib/Languages/Turpentine/` (module
  `Langlib.Languages.Turpentine.*`, namespace `Langlib.Turpentine`, like
  every other language). Compilers to targets go in
  `Langlib/Languages/Turpentine/Compile/<Langname>.lean`, and the derived
  compilers obtained from completeness witnesses go in
  `Langlib/Languages/Turpentine/Compile/Derived.lean`.

head: LangLib project policies > Workplan and progress
text:
* The staged workplan for agents is `docs/PLAN.md`. Keep it current: when you
  finish, start, or re-scope a stage, update it in the same commit.

head: LangLib project policies > Workplan and progress
text: * Progress notes go to `docs/PROGRESS.md`, newest entry first, dated.

head: LangLib project policies > Workplan and progress
text: * The list of candidate future languages is `docs/ROADMAP.md`.

head: LangLib project policies > Semantics conventions
text:
* Reference interpreters have a **pure core**: `ByteArray` (or `List Int`)
  input, fuel parameter, explicit result type (`Langlib.Common.RunResult`,
  with `Langlib.Common.Exit`, both in `Langlib/Common/Io.lean`).
  The IO runner wraps the pure core; proofs and tests target the pure core.

head: LangLib project policies > Semantics conventions
text:
* Semantics decisions (cell width, EOF behaviour, tape bounds) must match the
  language's canonical reference implementation, and every such decision must
  be recorded in the language's doc page with a source.

head: LangLib project policies > Semantics conventions
text:
* No `sorry` on master. Proofs may be staged, but stubs must be `axiom`-free
  and clearly tracked in `docs/PLAN.md`.

head: LangLib project policies > Semantics conventions
text:
* `TuringComplete` requires both forward answer preservation and divergence
  preservation: divergent URM inputs must yield `.outOfFuel` at every finite
  target fuel, independently of decoding. Prove both fields for each runnable
  compiler; a decoded-result iff alone allows undecodable halts. The shared
  consequences and proof routes are in `docs/divergence-preservation.md`.
  Put compilers, forward proofs and language instances in
  `Langlib/Computability/<Language>/Simulation.lean`, operational divergence
  proofs in its sibling `Divergence.lean`, and assemble `<lang>Complete` in
  the public `Langlib/Computability/<Language>/Main.lean` module, which imports
  `Divergence`. Every language's computability development lives entirely in
  its own folder; negative or unfinished claims also use `Main.lean` as the
  entry point. Shared proof infrastructure lives in `Computability/Common/`.
  This order avoids a circular dependency. Shared positive-cost
  simulation lives in `Langlib/Common/Divergence.lean` (`ReachesPlus`, free
  of Mathlib); continuing URM execution lives in
  `Langlib/Computability/Common/Divergence.lean`. A zero-cost `Reaches` cycle does
  not prove divergence; self-jumps must also consume positive target fuel.

head: LangLib project policies > Documentation policy
text:
* Do not update READMEs for an in-progress language until its specification,
  parser, interpreter, runner and tests are all in place. Until then, track
  the work in its design notes, `docs/PLAN.md`, `docs/PROGRESS.md` and
  `docs/ROADMAP.md`.

head: LangLib project policies > Documentation policy
text:
* Before **every commit**, double-check all project documentation for
  consistency with the code and for link validity, including the root
  documents, `docs/`, every language README and the site documentation.
  Every local target and heading anchor must resolve. Every numbered source
  link must point to the exact referenced definition or theorem, not a nearby
  comment or field. Check both incoming and outgoing links after moves, and
  repeat the check after the last edit that changes paths or line numbers.

head: LangLib project policies > Documentation policy
text:
* Every language doc credits the original author(s), year, and the canonical
  specification or implementation. Respect copyright: summarise
  specifications in our own words, never paste licensed text or licensed
  example programs. Only implement languages that are freely implementable.

head: LangLib project policies > Documentation policy
text:
* Every spec page opens with the same preamble: a bullet list with
  **Author**, **Year**, **Canonical sources** and **In LangLib**. The last
  two are nested lists, one item per source and one item per artefact (source
  folder, runner, examples, tests, computability result, Turpentine
  backend), each artefact a relative link; a single source stays inline.
  `docs/velato/spec.md` is the model.

head: LangLib project policies > Documentation policy
text:
* Documentation should be precise and entertaining to read. These languages
  are jokes with formal content; keep both.

head: LangLib project policies > Documentation policy
text:
* Every spec page has a "Trying it" section: one command per code
  block, each preceded by a sentence saying what to expect. Never collate
  several commands into one block.

head: LangLib project policies > Documentation policy
text:
* Every spec page **ends** with an "Example programs" section: at least
  three or four complete program texts in the language, each quoted in full
  (or, where a program is too large or is an image, rendered in a stated
  transliteration) with a paragraph saying how to read it and what it does.
  Prefer programs that already live in `Langlib/Examples/<Langname>/`, and
  verify every claimed output by running it.

head: LangLib project policies > Documentation policy
text:
* Keep the command and its output in **separate** blocks, so a reader can
  copy the command without picking the output out of it. Write the command
  block with no `$` prefix, then `Output:`, then a second block with the
  output the command actually produced (verified by running it, never
  guessed). Omit the output block when the command prints nothing.

head: LangLib project policies > Documentation policy
text:
* **Graphical languages** (Piet, Brainloller: languages whose programs are
  images) additionally show every example as a rendered picture, and their
  spec page ends its "Example programs" section with a "Rendering these
  pictures" subsection giving the commands that produce them. Images live
  in `docs/<langname>/img/` and are **derived files**: never hand-edit one,
  and never check in a picture that no example produces. The single source
  of truth is `scripts/render-docs-images.sh`, which regenerates every
  image byte-for-byte; `scripts/render-docs-images.sh --check` fails if a
  committed image is stale. Add new examples to that script, and run it in
  the same commit as any change to a graphical example. Render through the
  language's own runner where it has one (`lake exe piet --svg`), so a
  picture cannot drift from what the interpreter reads.

head: LangLib project policies > Dependencies
text:
* `langlib` depends on **cslib** (pinned by revision in `lakefile.toml`),
  which brings **Mathlib**. The revision is the last one matching our
  `lean-toolchain`; bump the two together, never separately.

head: LangLib project policies > Dependencies
text:
* Keep Mathlib and cslib confined to `Langlib/Computability/` plus
  `Langlib/Common/Computability.lean`. Interpreters, parsers, runners and
  hand-written compilers under `Langlib/Languages/` must not import them,
  so they stay light and compile fast. Three places are the documented
  exceptions, all of them proof-side rather than runner-side:
  `Langlib/Languages/Turpentine/Compile/Derived.lean` and the `--tc` half
  of `Langlib/Languages/Turpentine/Main.lean`, both built out of
  completeness witnesses, and everything under
  `Langlib/Languages/Turpentine/Compile/Certified/`.

head: LangLib project policies > Dependencies
text:
* `Langlib/Languages/Turpentine/Compile/Certified/` holds the correctness proofs of
  the hand-written Turpentine backends (namespace
  `Langlib.Turpentine.Certified`, one file per target, plus `Shared.lean`
  for the Turpentine-side facts every such proof needs: the fragment
  predicates, the evaluator inversion lemmas, the `answer` epilogue and its
  decoder. A lemma that mentions no target belongs there). Those proofs sit
  next to the backends they are about rather than in
  `Langlib/Computability/`, which is reserved for the Turing-completeness
  results and their URM bridges. Nothing a runner imports may import
  `Compile/Certified/`: the executables keep compiling without Mathlib.
  Note that `Langlib.Turpentine.Certified` nests inside `Langlib.Turpentine`,
  so unqualified names resolve to the front end first — write
  `Langlib.Subleq.exec`, not `exec`, when you mean the target language's.

head: LangLib project policies > Dependencies
text:
* `Langlib/Common/Compilation.lean` — `ProgLang`, `CertifiedCompilerNoIO`,
  `CertifiedCompiler` — is deliberately free of both, and
  `Langlib/Common.lean` rolls it up while leaving
  `Langlib/Common/Computability.lean` out. State a compiler's correctness
  against those definitions; do not move them anywhere that needs Mathlib.

head: LangLib project policies > Dependencies
text:
* Compiler contracts distinguish closed computations from runtime input:
  `CertifiedCompilerNoIO spec diverges L` has no input parameter and runs targets
  on `Input.empty`; `CertifiedCompiler spec diverges targetInput L` quantifies
  over source streams under an explicit encoding. Forgetting traces does not
  close a computation: use `correct_answer` to retain input, or `toClosed`
  with proof that empty source input encodes to empty target input.

head: LangLib project policies > Dependencies
text:
* First build on a fresh machine needs Mathlib's cache
  (`lake exe cache get`).

head: LangLib project policies > Testing
text:
* Every language gets golden tests (program + input + expected output) wired
  into `lake test`.

head: LangLib project policies > Testing
text:
* Differential testing against a non-Lean reference implementation is done by
  `scripts/difftest.sh`; it must skip gracefully when the reference binary is
  not installed.

head: LangLib project policies > Testing
text:
* Compiler tests: compile Turpentine examples to each target and compare the
  target-language run against the Turpentine reference interpreter's run.

head: LangLib project policies > Testing
text:
* JavaGen reuses the FRACTRAN Minsky pass with `allowArrays := true`; the
  FRACTRAN frontend keeps its scalar-only default. Array cells have distinct
  registers, and Boolean guards must short-circuit to skip invalid indices.
  Indexed writes evaluate the RHS before the index, matching Turpentine's
  `exec`/`storeIndex` order. Generated JavaGen tables can be large: validation
  lookups are indexed, while closure rows and equal-diamond paths retain
  source order. The validator uses ordered maps so its concrete
  `decide +kernel` regressions can also reduce the lookup structures cheaply.

head: LangLib project policies > Testing
text:
* JavaGen's hand-written Turpentine backend reuses the Mathlib-free Minsky
  pass in `Compile/Fractran.lean`. The executable sweep generator lives in
  `Langlib/Languages/JavaGen/Sweep.lean`; the computability module re-exports
  it for the existing proofs. Compiled counter queries use the standalone
  `--compiled-answer` observation, not the numeric `answer`-hole certification
  script. Keep these two answer paths distinct in code and documentation.

head: LangLib project policies > Git
text:
* Commit and push regularly, at natural checkpoints (a stage, a language, a
  compiler). Master is the main branch; keep it building (`lake build` and
  `lake test` clean) at every commit.

head: AGENTS.md
text: This file provides guidance to AI coding agents (Claude Code, etc.) when working with code in this repository. CLAUDE.md is a symlink to this file.

head: AGENTS.md
text: This repository holds AGPL-3.0 licensed MATLAB tools for machine-learning Earth observation, combining neutron monitor data, MCNP transport maps, and NOAA sources into geospatial visualizations exportable to Google Maps and WebGL Earth. The main workflows are `NMDB/MAGELLAN.m`, `data/run1day.m`, and `MCNPMap/fcnMCNPmap.m`, which require MATLAB R2018a or newer plus the `functions-matlab` repository on the MATLAB path.

head: AGENTS.md > Core Principles (CRITICAL)
text: **Less is more. The simplest solution is the best solution.** The action hierarchy for every change: **Delete > Replace > Add**.

head: AGENTS.md > Core Principles (CRITICAL)
text: 1. **Solve at the owner**: Put behavior in the code path that owns or observes it. For fixes, never guard a symptom with a staleness check, initialization flag, skip-first-call branch, or `try/except` around broken logic; relocate the trigger and delete the wrong path. For features, extend the existing owner rather than creating a parallel abstraction.

head: AGENTS.md > Core Principles (CRITICAL)
text: 2. **Search and reuse first**: Search the whole repository before creating a feature, component, helper, workflow, or utility. Reuse or adapt what exists, consolidate in-scope duplication in the shared owner, and delete duplicate paths. Three similar lines beat a helper nobody else calls.

head: AGENTS.md > Core Principles (CRITICAL)
text: 3. **Delete and modify existing code before creating new code**: Bugfixes are net-negative by default unless deletion and relocation are demonstrably impossible. A new file must first prove it cannot fit cleanly in an existing owner.

head: AGENTS.md > Core Principles (CRITICAL)
text: 4. **Keep scope minimal**: Implement only the simplest complete solution. Avoid impossible-state handling, speculative flags, compatibility shims, policy scaffolding, and unrelated cleanup. Tests are out of scope by default — rely on existing coverage and focused validation; only an uncovered, high-risk regression path justifies minimal new test code.

head: AGENTS.md > Core Principles (CRITICAL)
text: 5. **Ship zero-regression, production-ready changes**: Understand what you remove instead of retaining broken code as insurance. Remove unused imports, functions, types, files, and comments; run relevant cleanup checks; and thoroughly debug and validate the changed owner. Do not break existing features or workflows unless the PR intentionally removes them with evidence.

head: AGENTS.md > Core Principles (CRITICAL)
text: **Review gate:** for every addition, the reviewer decides whether deleting or changing existing code would have fixed the problem instead — if it would, that is a blocking finding. A missing or thin PR description is never itself a finding.

head: AGENTS.md > Core Principles (CRITICAL)
text: NEVER push to `main`. NEVER force push. Always start work in a new git worktree (`git worktree add`) on a feature branch and open a PR — never edit the primary checkout directly, it may hold in-flight work.

head: AGENTS.md > PR Workflow
text: 1. Wait for the automated PR review and auto-format commit from Ultralytics Actions (`format.yml`), then pull and address every finding.

head: AGENTS.md > PR Workflow
text: 2. Review the full diff in-session against the Core Principles, performance, and the review gate above, then batch the fixes into one commit and push. After each round of bot or human commits, pull and resume the same reviewer on `<last-reviewed-sha>..HEAD` plus anything that delta could have invalidated. Repeat until the local head matches the live head.

head: AGENTS.md > PR Workflow
text: 3. Hand off or merge only on a clean final pass: one cold full-diff review returning LGTM with no findings, on a head that is still live at merge time.

head: AGENTS.md > PR Workflow
text: 4. Never fight other commits: Ultralytics Actions pushes auto-format and header commits, and multiple users may work on the same PR. `git pull --rebase` before pushing; never reset or revert commits you did not author.

head: AGENTS.md > PR Workflow
text: 5. After the PR merges, clean up: remove local worktrees and branches for it, then `git checkout main && git pull`.

head: AGENTS.md > Overview
text: Copenhagen Theme is the default Zendesk Guide (Help Center) theme. It's a Curlybars-based theme with React components for complex UI elements, built using Rollup and SCSS.

head: AGENTS.md > Common Commands
text: **Note:** Preview requires Zendesk authentication. Run `yarn zcli login` first if needed.

head: AGENTS.md > Architecture > Build System
text: - **Rollup** compiles everything - outputs `script.js`, `style.css`, and ES module bundles in `assets/`

head: AGENTS.md > Architecture > Build System
text: - **Do not edit** `script.js`, `style.css`, or files in `assets/` directly - they are generated

head: AGENTS.md > Architecture > Build System
text: - ES2015 only for `script.js` (no Babel) - avoid newer JavaScript features in `src/*.js` files

head: AGENTS.md > Architecture > Directory Structure
text: - `templates/` - Curlybars templates (`.hbs`) for Help Center pages. Curlybars is a subset of Handlebars and may not support all Handlebars features.

head: AGENTS.md > Architecture > Directory Structure
text:
- `src/` - JavaScript source
  - `src/*.js` - Legacy vanilla JS (bundled into `script.js` as IIFE)
  - `src/modules/` - React components (bundled as ES modules into `assets/`)

head: AGENTS.md > Architecture > Directory Structure
text: - `styles/` - SCSS files (compiled into `style.css`)

head: AGENTS.md > Architecture > Directory Structure
text: - `manifest.json` - Theme settings configuration

head: AGENTS.md > Architecture > React Modules
text: Located in `src/modules/`, bundled to `assets/*-bundle.js`:

head: AGENTS.md > Architecture > React Modules
text: - `new-request-form` - Ticket submission form

head: AGENTS.md > Architecture > React Modules
text: - `request-list` - User's requests page

head: AGENTS.md > Architecture > React Modules
text: - `service-catalog` - Service catalog pages

head: AGENTS.md > Architecture > React Modules
text: - `approval-requests` - Approval workflow UI

head: AGENTS.md > Architecture > React Modules
text: - `flash-notifications` - Toast notifications

head: AGENTS.md > Architecture > React Modules
text: - `shared/` - Shared utilities (Garden theme, i18n, error boundary)

head: AGENTS.md > Architecture > React Modules
text: - `ticket-fields/` - Reusable ticket field components

head: AGENTS.md > Architecture > React Modules
text: Modules are isolated - ESLint enforces that modules only import from `shared/`, `test/`, `ticket-fields/`, or `flash-notifications/`.

head: AGENTS.md > Architecture > Import Maps
text: React modules are loaded via import maps generated during build. The `document_head.hbs` template contains the import map mapping module names to asset URLs.

head: AGENTS.md > Architecture > i18n in React
AGENTS.md > Architecture > Translations: what goes where
text: - `translations.yml` (repo root) is only for strings referenced by `manifest.json` (theme settings labels/descriptions shown in the Settings panel). Don't add template or React strings here.

head: AGENTS.md > Architecture > Translations: what goes where
text: - In Curlybars templates (`templates/*.hbs`), the `{{t "key"}}` helper only resolves keys that Help Center exposes to the theme's `t` helper. A new key must be added there first; defining it in `translations.yml` or a module's `translations/` folder does not make it available to `{{t}}`.

head: AGENTS.md > Architecture > Translations: what goes where
text: - React component strings live in `src/modules/[module]/translations/` and are loaded via `react-i18next` (see README for the extraction/update workflow).

head: AGENTS.md > File Naming Conventions
text: - Folders in `src/`: kebab-case

head: AGENTS.md > File Naming Conventions
text: - TypeScript/JavaScript files in `src/`: PascalCase or camelCase

MCP revision is `2026-07-28`; `2025-11-25` is the immediately prior revision.
Treat `2026-07-28` as a released version, not an RC or draft.

head: CLAUDE.md > Project Overview
text: xpc-connect is a Node.js native addon that provides bindings for Apple's XPC (Inter-Process Communication) Services on macOS. It allows Node.js applications to communicate with macOS system services using XPC connections.

head: CLAUDE.md > Project Overview
text:
**Platform:** macOS only (specified in package.json os field)
**Node Version:** >=18.0

head: CLAUDE.md > Common Commands > Committing
text:
This project uses **commitizen** for standardized commits:
```bash
git add -A
git commit -m "your message"   # Triggers commitizen workflow
```
The commit hook will guide you through creating a conventional changelog-formatted commit. All commits must follow `cz-conventional-changelog` standards.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Layer Structure
text:
1. **JavaScript Layer** (`index.js`)
   - Thin wrapper that loads the native addon via `bindings` package
   - Extends the native XpcConnect class with EventEmitter functionality
   - Entry point for require('xpc-connect')

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Layer Structure
text:
2. **Native Addon Layer** (`src/XpcConnect.cpp`, `src/XpcConnect.h`)
   - C++ implementation using NAN (Native Abstractions for Node.js)
   - Wraps Apple's XPC C API for Node.js consumption
   - Handles async event processing via libuv

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Layer Structure
text:
3. **Build Configuration** (`binding.gyp`)
   - node-gyp configuration for compiling the native addon
   - macOS-specific compilation settings (ObjC++ support)

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > XPC Connection Lifecycle
text: The native addon manages XPC connections through a specific lifecycle:

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > XPC Connection Lifecycle
text: 1. **Initialization**: Create XpcConnect instance with service name

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > XPC Connection Lifecycle
text:
2. **Setup**: Call `setup()` once to establish connection
   - Creates dispatch queue
   - Creates XPC connection to mach service
   - Sets up event handler
   - Activates connection
   - **Can only be called once** (throws on multiple calls)

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > XPC Connection Lifecycle
text:
3. **Communication**: Use `sendMessage(obj)` to send messages
   - **Must be called after setup()** (throws if called before)

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > XPC Connection Lifecycle
text:
4. **Shutdown**: Call `shutdown()` to close connection
   - Cancels XPC connection
   - Cleanup happens asynchronously when XPC_ERROR_CONNECTION_INVALID is received

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Event Processing
text: The addon uses a queue-based async event processing model:

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Event Processing
text: - XPC events are queued on the dispatch queue thread

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Event Processing
text: - Events are transferred to a mutex-protected queue

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Event Processing
text: - `uv_async_send()` triggers processing on the Node.js event loop

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Event Processing
text: - Events are emitted as Node.js EventEmitter events ('error' or 'event')

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Memory Management
text: Important patterns in the native code:

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Memory Management
text: - Uses `this->Ref()` during setup to prevent garbage collection until connection closes

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Memory Management
text: - Uses `this->Unref()` when connection fully closes after XPC_ERROR_CONNECTION_INVALID

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Memory Management
text: - Properly retains/releases XPC objects using `xpc_retain()`/`xpc_release()`

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Memory Management
text: - Async resources are cleaned up via `AsyncCloseCallback` when connection closes

text: The addon supports bidirectional conversion between JavaScript and XPC types:

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Data Type Conversions
text: - int32/uint32 → XPC_TYPE_INT64

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Data Type Conversions
text: - string → XPC_TYPE_STRING

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Data Type Conversions
text: - Object → XPC_TYPE_DICTIONARY

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Data Type Conversions
text: - Buffer with `isUuid` property → XPC_TYPE_UUID

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Data Type Conversions
text: - XPC_TYPE_STRING → string

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Data Type Conversions
text: - XPC_TYPE_DICTIONARY → Object

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Data Type Conversions
text: - XPC_TYPE_UUID → Buffer (containing uuid_t bytes)

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Data Type Conversions
text: - `ValueToXpcObject()`, `ObjectToXpcObject()`, `ArrayToXpcObject()` (JS → XPC)

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Data Type Conversions
text: - `XpcObjectToValue()`, `XpcDictionaryToObject()`, `XpcArrayToArray()` (XPC → JS)

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture
text: svgMap is a single-class JavaScript library (`src/js/core/svg-map.js`) that renders an interactive SVG world map with per-country data visualisation.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Entry point and build
text: - **`src/js/index.js`** — re-exports the class and imports the SCSS entry point

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Entry point and build
text:
- **`rollup.config.js`** — compiles to six formats in `dist/`:
  - `index.js` (ESM), `index.cjs` (CommonJS)
  - `svg-map.umd.js` / `svg-map.umd.min.js` (UMD, global name `svgMap`)
  - `svgMap.js` / `svgMap.min.js` — legacy UMD aliases kept for backwards compatibility with pre-2.18 users
  - `svg-map.css` / `svg-map.min.css` (extracted from SCSS); legacy `svgMap.css` copies created after each build

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Core class (`src/js/core/svg-map.js`)
text: The `svgMap` class is instantiated directly by consumers (`new svgMap({ targetElementID, data, ... })`). Constructor calls `init()` which:

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Core class (`src/js/core/svg-map.js`)
text: 1. Validates `targetElementID` and `data` options

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Core class (`src/js/core/svg-map.js`)
text: 2. Builds the DOM structure: `.svgMap-wrapper` → `.svgMap-container` → `.svgMap-map-container` → `.svgMap-map-wrapper` → `<svg viewBox="0 0 2000 1001">`

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Core class (`src/js/core/svg-map.js`)
text: 3. Creates zoom controls and optional continent selector

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Core class (`src/js/core/svg-map.js`)
text: 4. Calls `createMap()` then `applyData()` — `applyData` computes per-country colors using `calculateColorRatio` and writes them as the CSS custom property `--svg-map-country-fill` on each country `<path>` element

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Core class (`src/js/core/svg-map.js`)
text: 5. The floating tooltip is appended to `<body>` and positioned with `showTooltip(e)` / `moveTooltip(e)`

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Core class (`src/js/core/svg-map.js`)
text: 6. Persistent tooltips (pinned labels on the map) are handled separately in `createPersistentTooltips()`

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Core class (`src/js/core/svg-map.js`)
text: Pan and zoom are delegated entirely to the `svg-pan-zoom` library (the only runtime dependency).

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Core class (`src/js/core/svg-map.js`)
text: Country paths are inlined inside the class as SVG `d` strings, keyed by ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 code. The `countries` property holds the name map; `emojiFlags` holds emoji representations. `EH` (Western Sahara) can be merged with `MA` (Morocco) via `options.countries.EH = false`.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Core class (`src/js/core/svg-map.js`)
text: Color interpolation (`getColor`) works by linearly blending two hex colors. `calculateColorRatio` supports `'linear'`, `'log'`, or an arbitrary `(value, min, max) => ratio` function.

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Styling (`src/scss/`)
text: - `svg-map.scss` — entry point, `@use`s `map` and `tooltip` partials

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Styling (`src/scss/`)
text: - `variables.scss` — all `!default` SCSS variables; consumers can override by importing with their own values before the library SCSS

head: CLAUDE.md > Architecture > Styling (`src/scss/`)
text: - Country fill is driven by the `--svg-map-country-fill` CSS custom property set at runtime, not by a static class

head: fireSeqSearch
text:
Local search server + browser extension that appends hits from your
Logseq/Obsidian notebook to Google search results. Architecture is **LLM-first**:
dense semantic retrieval over the user's notes plus per-page LLM-generated
summaries, with the goal of making search results explain themselves at a
glance.

head: fireSeqSearch > Surface area
text:
- `/query/:term` — semantic search, sub-second. Returns ranked `PageHit`s
  (`title`, `logseq_uri`, `score`, `chunk_id`, `top_snippet`, `summary`,
  `summary_status`).

head: fireSeqSearch > Surface area
text:
- `POST /ask` — deliberate Q&A. Body `{question, k?}`; SSE `meta` (sources +
  `confidence`) → `delta*` → `done` (`{cited, invalid, chars, answered,
  confidence}`) or `error`. Cited `[N]` markers validated against the retrieved
  set; anything invented lands in `done.invalid`.

head: fireSeqSearch > Surface area
text: - `POST /reindex` — manual rescan trigger.

head: fireSeqSearch > Surface area
text:
- `/server_info` — config + indexer/summarizer counts + crate version +
  capabilities. Addon hard-floors on `MIN_BACKEND_VERSION` and soft-gates UI
  on `capabilities`.

head: fireSeqSearch > Surface area
text:
- `POST /highlight` — dormant; kept as scaffolding for a future "explain this
  card" action.

head: fireSeqSearch > Locked decisions — don't relitigate without strong evidence > Retrieval
text:
- **Embedding:** `bge-m3` (1024-dim, multilingual, 8K context), Q4_K_M GGUF.
  Chosen to take retrieval quality off the debug list.

head: fireSeqSearch > Locked decisions — don't relitigate without strong evidence > Retrieval
text:
- **Index:** flat in-memory `Vec<(ChunkId, [f32; 1024])>`, brute-force cosine.
  No ANN, no vector DB. ~10K chunks fits under 50ms.

head: fireSeqSearch > Locked decisions — don't relitigate without strong evidence > Retrieval
text:
- **Storage:** SQLite (`notes` + `chunks`, raw f32 LE BLOBs). Storage, not a
  search index — all rows hydrate into the in-memory vec on startup.

head: fireSeqSearch > Locked decisions — don't relitigate without strong evidence > Retrieval
text: - **Change detection:** mtime as fast filter, Blake3 `content_hash` as truth.

head: fireSeqSearch > Locked decisions — don't relitigate without strong evidence > Retrieval
text:
- **Dual signal:** `note_score = max(best_chunk · query, summary · query)`.
  Pages whose *gist* matches rise even when no individual chunk does.

head: fireSeqSearch > Locked decisions — don't relitigate without strong evidence > Retrieval
text:
- **`CHUNKER_VERSION`** in `store.rs` — bump it when chunker logic changes.
  Stale chunks otherwise hash-match and skip re-embedding forever.

head: fireSeqSearch > Locked decisions — don't relitigate without strong evidence > Chunking (flavour-aware via `--notebook obsidian`)
text:
- **Logseq:** top-level bullets are the boundary unit; stub-only `-`/`*`
  lines dropped; adjacent bullets greedy-packed to `CAP_TOKENS = 600`;
  oversized units split at descendant-bullet boundaries. Strips `key:: value`,
  `#+BEGIN_QUERY ... #+END_QUERY`, SCHEDULED/DEADLINE/CLOSED continuation
  lines, and "Journal Template" parent bullets.

head: fireSeqSearch > Locked decisions — don't relitigate without strong evidence > Chunking (flavour-aware via `--notebook obsidian`)
text:
- **Obsidian:** single chunk per note when total ≤ `CAP_TOKENS` (notes are
  concept-granular; splitting them fragments retrieval). Big notes fall back
  to splitting at `#` ATX headings, then paragraph-splitting oversized
  sections. `#tag` (no space) is not a heading.

head: fireSeqSearch > Locked decisions — don't relitigate without strong evidence > Chunking (flavour-aware via `--notebook obsidian`)
text:
- **Both:** YAML frontmatter stripped, image embeds stripped (`![[…]]` +
  `![…](…)`), chunk text is `# {page_title}\n\n{body}` so the title
  participates in retrieval.

head: fireSeqSearch > Locked decisions — don't relitigate without strong evidence > Walker (flavour-aware)
text:
- **Logseq:** `pages/` + `journals/` only. `logseq/` and `assets/` skipped by
  construction.

head: fireSeqSearch > Locked decisions — don't relitigate without strong evidence > Walker (flavour-aware)
text:
- **Obsidian:** recursive walk over the vault; skips any dot-prefixed
  directory (`.obsidian/`, `.git/`, `.stversions/`, …) and `trash/`.

head: fireSeqSearch > Locked decisions — don't relitigate without strong evidence > URI generation
text: - **Logseq:** derived from page title (flat layout — basename is enough).

head: fireSeqSearch > Locked decisions — don't relitigate without strong evidence > URI generation
text:
- **Obsidian:** derived from `rel_path` (minus `.md`). The `file=` query
  param MUST carry the directory prefix as `%2F` segments — otherwise
  `obsidian://open` fails on nested notes or opens a basename collision.

head: fireSeqSearch > Locked decisions — don't relitigate without strong evidence > LLM serving
text:
- **Transport:** OpenAI-compat HTTP. Embed `/v1/embeddings`, chat
  `/v1/chat/completions`.

head: fireSeqSearch > Locked decisions — don't relitigate without strong evidence > LLM serving
text:
- **Backend:** subprocess `llama-server` by default; `--embed-endpoint` /
  `--chat-endpoint` point at a pre-running server (Ollama, remote llama) as
  a first-class alternative. `--chat <preset>` is shorthand for the common
  hosted cases — `local` (spawn), `ollama[:MODEL]`, `openai[:MODEL]` — and
  expands to the endpoint + flavour + model-name; it's mutually exclusive with
  the granular `--chat-endpoint`/`--chat-flavour` flags. Preset grammar +
  parsing live in `main.rs` (`parse_chat_preset`).

head: fireSeqSearch > Locked decisions — don't relitigate without strong evidence > LLM serving
text:
- **Embed model is zero-config:** with no `--embed-model` and no
  `--embed-endpoint`, the server auto-downloads a pinned `bge-m3` llamafile
  (URL + SHA-256 in `llm_backend/model_fetch.rs`) into
  `~/.cache/fire_seq_search` and spawns it. The `.llamafile` extension is what
  switches `process.rs` into llamafile mode (no `--model` arg). An explicit
  `--embed-model PATH` overrides; bump all three pin constants together.

head: fireSeqSearch > Locked decisions — don't relitigate without strong evidence > LLM serving
text:
- **One chat backend, shared between summarizer and `/ask`.** Deliberate —
  one process to warm, one set of args to tune. If quality demands more, the
  lever is `--chat-endpoint` pointed at a bigger server, which upgrades both
  paths at once. Don't fork the chat path.

head: fireSeqSearch > Locked decisions — don't relitigate without strong evidence > LLM serving
text:
- **Embed backend args:** `--embedding -ub 8192 -b 8192 -c 8192 -ngl 99`
  injected by default. `-ub 8192` is required — llama-server's default
  512-token ubatch rejects packed chunks with HTTP 500.

head: fireSeqSearch > Locked decisions — don't relitigate without strong evidence > LLM serving
text:
- **GPU:** Vulkan, not ROCm. gfx1102 + ROCm 6.4 on Fedora is rough; Vulkan
  works on stock Mesa 25.3+. We build llama-server in podman/Fedora 43
  (`scripts/Containerfile`, `scripts/build_llama_server.sh`).

head: fireSeqSearch > Locked decisions — don't relitigate without strong evidence > Summarization
text:
- One sentence per page, background worker, status lifecycle in
  `notes.summary_status`: `NONE → QUEUED_LOW → QUEUED_HIGH → IN_PROGRESS →
  OK | FAILED`.

head: fireSeqSearch > Locked decisions — don't relitigate without strong evidence > Summarization
text:
- **Deterministic content gate** (`is_summarizable`) — pages below
  `SUMMARIZABLE_MIN_CHARS` (16 narrative chars post-strip) skip the LLM call
  entirely. NOT a prompt instruction: models ignore those, and the rule
  must not depend on swappable chat backends.

head: fireSeqSearch > Locked decisions — don't relitigate without strong evidence > Summarization
text:
- **Junk-summary defense** (`is_junk_summary`) — `"Empty."`, `"Summary:"`,
  `"空页面"` and friends are dropped post-LLM, not embedded.

head: fireSeqSearch > Locked decisions — don't relitigate without strong evidence > Summarization
text:
- **Lazy-eval bump** — `/query` promotes pending top-10 pages to the
  high-priority queue, so what users actually search for gets summarized
  first.

head: fireSeqSearch > Locked decisions — don't relitigate without strong evidence > Summarization
text:
- Summary text + embedding written atomically; queries never see a
  half-applied state.

head: fireSeqSearch > Locked decisions — don't relitigate without strong evidence > Indexing lifecycle
text:
- Cold start is non-blocking — HTTP up immediately, indexer hydrates from
  SQLite, then `scan_once` in a background task.

head: fireSeqSearch > Locked decisions — don't relitigate without strong evidence > Indexing lifecycle
text: - Refresh: 10-min periodic + `POST /reindex`. No filesystem-watch dep.

head: fireSeqSearch > Locked decisions — don't relitigate without strong evidence > Indexing lifecycle
text:
- **Transactional**: `upsert_note` only fires after embeddings succeed for
  all of a note's chunks. Prior versions committed `content_hash` before
  chunks, leaving orphan rows whose hash-match fast-path then skipped
  re-embedding forever.

head: fireSeqSearch > Don't propose these
text:
- **ANN indexing** (HNSW, faiss). Brute-force cosine over ~10K vectors beats
  maintaining an ANN structure at this scale.

head: fireSeqSearch > Don't propose these
text: - **Vector database** (Qdrant, Chroma). SQLite + in-memory Vec is enough.

head: fireSeqSearch > Don't propose these
text:
- **Filesystem-watching** (notify, inotify). 10-min periodic + `/reindex`
  covers the use case.

head: fireSeqSearch > Don't propose these
text: - **Server-side HTML rendering** of results. The browser extension renders.

head: fireSeqSearch > Don't propose these
text:
- **BM25 hybrid / reranker.** Bringing tantivy back doubles complexity for
  unproven gain. Revisit only if `tests/eval_retrieval.py` shows dense failing
  on a class of queries.

head: fireSeqSearch > Don't propose these
text:
- **Per-chunk LLM context blurbs** (Anthropic-style contextual retrieval).
  Page summaries cover most of the same value at a fraction of indexing cost.

head: fireSeqSearch > Don't propose these
text:
- **Late chunking** (Jina). Requires per-token hidden states that
  llama-server's `/v1/embeddings` doesn't expose.

head: fireSeqSearch > Don't propose these
text: - **Forking the chat path** into separate summarizer / `/ask` models.

head: fireSeqSearch > Running
text:
- **/query smoke:** `.claude/agents/fsq-smoke.md` (Logseq, boots
  `tests/run_logseq.sh` against `~/logseq`). Obsidian is scripted:
  `bash tests/run_smoke.sh [llamacpp|ollama] [lite|full] [query]` composes a vault
  provisioner (`tests/vault_*.sh`) + a chat provisioner (`tests/chat_*.sh`, one per
  flavour) with the flavour-agnostic `tests/obsidian_smoke.sh`.
  - **lite** — committed `tests/astro-wiki-lite` fixture (2 notes). Fast and hermetic;
    asserts walker parity, URI integrity, summary health. Proves the plumbing only:
    with 2 notes there is nothing to outrank, so it says nothing about ranking.
  - **full** — the real `AstroWiki_2.0` vault (~366 notes), cloned + cached under
    `~/.cache/fire_seq_search`, pinned to the revision `tests/astro_wiki_eval.json`
    was tuned against. The **only** mode that can grade score priority and `/ask`
    answers: every gold query has a near-miss neighbour in the corpus (Compton vs.
    Inverse-Compton, Oort Cloud vs. Oort Constants). Grading runs through
    `tests/eval_retrieval.py --set`; a right-page-but-outranked result is a WARN,
    a right-page-missing result is a FAIL.
  `.claude/agents/obsidian-smoke.md` drives both and judges snippet and summary
  *quality* — the part the script can't assert.

head: AGENTS.md > Project Overview
text: ReoScript is an ECMAScript-like script language interpreter for .NET applications, allowing host applications to embed scripting and to expose .NET classes/objects/events directly to scripts. It is a tree-walking interpreter built on an ANTLR 3 grammar — there is no bytecode/JIT stage.

head: AGENTS.md > Project Overview
text: The library targets **.NET 10** and is cross-platform (no `System.Windows.Forms` dependency in the core). Build with `dotnet build`.
